title: Song Learning in Birds

abstract: We define a Gamma multi-layer perceptron (MLP) as an MLP with the usual synaptic weights replaced by gamma filters (as pro(cid:173) posed by de Vries and Principe (de Vries and Principe, 1992)) and associated gain terms throughout all layers. We derive gradient descent update equations and apply the model to the recognition of speech phonemes. We find that both the inclusion of gamma filters in all layers, and the inclusion of synaptic gains, improves the performance of the Gamma MLP. We compare the Gamma MLP with TDNN, Back-Tsoi FIR MLP, and Back-Tsoi I1R MLP architectures, and a local approximation scheme. We find that the Gamma MLP results in an substantial reduction in error rates.
originalAbstract: We define a Gamma multi-layer perceptron (MLP) as an MLP with the usual synaptic weights replaced by gamma filters (as pro(cid:173) posed by de Vries and Principe (de Vries and Principe, 1992)) and associated gain terms throughout all layers. We derive gradient descent update equations and apply the model to the recognition of speech phonemes. We find that both the inclusion of gamma filters in all layers, and the inclusion of synaptic gains, improves the performance of the Gamma MLP. We compare the Gamma MLP with TDNN, Back-Tsoi FIR MLP, and Back-Tsoi I1R MLP architectures, and a local approximation scheme. We find that the Gamma MLP results in an substantial reduction in error rates.

paragraphs: This paper modifies a multilayer perceptron so that its connections can process temporal information. The Gamma MLP replaces ordinary synaptic weights with gamma filters and associated gain terms throughout the network. A connection therefore has a filtering role as well as a gain, extending the network's treatment of signals across time.

The authors derive gradient-descent update equations for the architecture and apply it to speech-phoneme recognition. They examine two design choices: placing gamma filters in every layer and including synaptic gains. Both improve performance, showing that the placement of temporal processing and the accompanying gains each contribute to the reported results.

The Gamma MLP is compared with time-delay neural networks, Back-Tsoi FIR and IIR multilayer perceptrons, and a local approximation scheme. The authors report a substantial reduction in error rates. The contribution combines a trainable temporal architecture with evidence that distributing filters through all layers, together with gain terms, improves phoneme recognition in the comparisons presented.
summary.tldr: Replacing MLP weights with gamma filters and gains throughout the network substantially reduces speech-phoneme recognition errors.

title: The Gamma MLP for Speech Phoneme Recognition

abstract: We argue that human inductive generalization is best explained in a Bayesian framework, rather than by traditional models based on simi- larity computations. We go beyond previous work on Bayesian concept learning by introducing an unsupervised method for constructing ﬂex- ible hypothesis spaces, and we propose a version of the Bayesian Oc- cam’s razor that trades off priors and likelihoods to prevent under- or over-generalization in these ﬂexible spaces. We analyze two published data sets on inductive reasoning as well as the results of a new behavioral study that we have carried out.
originalAbstract: We argue that human inductive generalization is best explained in a Bayesian framework, rather than by traditional models based on simi- larity computations. We go beyond previous work on Bayesian concept learning by introducing an unsupervised method for constructing ﬂex- ible hypothesis spaces, and we propose a version of the Bayesian Oc- cam’s razor that trades off priors and likelihoods to prevent under- or over-generalization in these ﬂexible spaces. We analyze two published data sets on inductive reasoning as well as the results of a new behavioral study that we have carried out.

paragraphs: Inductive generalization concerns how people extend what they have observed to cases they have not seen. The authors argue that Bayesian reasoning provides a better explanation of this process than traditional accounts based on similarity calculations. Their approach treats generalization as reasoning over candidate hypotheses about what the observations imply.

The paper introduces an unsupervised method for constructing flexible hypothesis spaces. This addresses how the collection of candidate explanations can be formed, rather than simply assuming a fixed collection is already available. Flexible spaces also require a way to avoid conclusions that extend either too narrowly or too broadly beyond the evidence.

To address that issue, the authors propose a Bayesian Occam's razor that balances prior beliefs with how well hypotheses explain observations. They examine two previously published datasets on inductive reasoning and a new behavioral study. The contribution combines a way to construct candidate hypotheses with a principle for weighing them, grounding the proposed account in analyses of human generalization behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a Bayesian account of human generalization that learns flexible hypothesis spaces and balances evidence against prior beliefs.

title: Bayesian Models of Inductive Generalization

abstract: We present and empirically test a novel approach for categorizing 3-D free form ob- ject shapes represented by range data . In contrast to traditional surface-signature based systems that use alignment to match speciﬁc objects, we adapted the newly introduced symbolic-signature representation to classify deformable shapes [10]. Our approach con- structs an abstract description of shape classes using an ensemble of classiﬁers that learn object class parts and their corresponding geometrical relationships from a set of numeric and symbolic descriptors. We used our classiﬁcation engine in a series of large scale dis- crimination experiments on two well-deﬁned classes that share many common distinctive features. The experimental results suggest that our method outperforms traditional numeric signature-based methodologies. 1
originalAbstract: We present and empirically test a novel approach for categorizing 3-D free form ob- ject shapes represented by range data . In contrast to traditional surface-signature based systems that use alignment to match speciﬁc objects, we adapted the newly introduced symbolic-signature representation to classify deformable shapes [10]. Our approach con- structs an abstract description of shape classes using an ensemble of classiﬁers that learn object class parts and their corresponding geometrical relationships from a set of numeric and symbolic descriptors. We used our classiﬁcation engine in a series of large scale dis- crimination experiments on two well-deﬁned classes that share many common distinctive features. The experimental results suggest that our method outperforms traditional numeric signature-based methodologies. 1

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification of deformable, three-dimensional free-form shapes represented by range data. Its task is to recognize shape categories, even when members of a category vary in form. This differs from matching a particular object through alignment, which the abstract identifies as the focus of traditional systems using surface signatures.

The proposed method adapts a symbolic-signature representation to describe shape classes. An ensemble of classifiers learns parts associated with each class and the geometric relationships among those parts. It uses both numerical and symbolic descriptors, building an abstract class description from information about components and how they fit together.

The authors evaluate the classification system in large-scale discrimination experiments involving two well-defined classes that share many distinctive features. Their results suggest better performance than traditional numerical signature methods. This is evidence for the approach in the studied comparison, with the shared features making the distinction between the two classes especially relevant. The contribution is a class-oriented representation of deformable shape through learned parts and relationships.
summary.tldr: An ensemble learns shape parts and their geometric relationships, with experiments suggesting improved discrimination of two deformable 3-D shape classes.

title: Discriminating Deformable Shape Classes

abstract: We propose a novel method of dimensionality reduction for supervised learning. Given a regression or classiﬁcation problem in which we wish to predict a variable Y from an explanatory vector X, we treat the prob- lem of dimensionality reduction as that of ﬁnding a low-dimensional “ef- fective subspace” of X which retains the statistical relationship between X and Y . We show that this problem can be formulated in terms of conditional independence. To turn this formulation into an optimization problem, we characterize the notion of conditional independence using covariance operators on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces; this allows us to derive a contrast function for estimation of the effective subspace. Un- like many conventional methods, the proposed method requires neither assumptions on the marginal distribution of X, nor a parametric model of the conditional distribution of Y .
originalAbstract: We propose a novel method of dimensionality reduction for supervised learning. Given a regression or classiﬁcation problem in which we wish to predict a variable Y from an explanatory vector X, we treat the prob- lem of dimensionality reduction as that of ﬁnding a low-dimensional “ef- fective subspace” of X which retains the statistical relationship between X and Y . We show that this problem can be formulated in terms of conditional independence. To turn this formulation into an optimization problem, we characterize the notion of conditional independence using covariance operators on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces; this allows us to derive a contrast function for estimation of the effective subspace. Un- like many conventional methods, the proposed method requires neither assumptions on the marginal distribution of X, nor a parametric model of the conditional distribution of Y .

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reduce input dimensionality while preserving information needed to predict an output. For either regression or classification, the aim is to identify a low-dimensional effective subspace of the input vector. The defining requirement is that this reduced representation retain the statistical relationship between the inputs and the target.

The authors express that requirement using conditional independence. In plain terms, the desired representation should preserve the relevant relationship so that the discarded input information is unnecessary once the representation is known. They characterize conditional independence using covariance operators in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and turn that characterization into an optimization criterion.

This criterion supplies a method for estimating the effective subspace from the supervised learning problem. The authors emphasize that it requires neither assumptions about the marginal input distribution nor a parametric model for the output’s conditional distribution. The contribution is therefore a kernel-based formulation of supervised dimension reduction with these two distributional restrictions avoided.
summary.tldr: The method uses a kernel characterization of conditional independence to find low-dimensional inputs that preserve their relationship with the prediction target.

title: Kernel Dimensionality Reduction for Supervised Learning

abstract: We describe a novel method for real-time, simultaneous multi-view face detection and facial pose estimation. The method employs a convolutional network to map face images to points on a manifold, parametrized by pose, and non-face images to points far from that manifold. This network is trained by optimizing a loss function of three variables: image, pose, and face/non-face label. We test the resulting system, in a single configuration, on three standard data sets – one for frontal pose, one for rotated faces, and one for profiles – and find that its performance on each set is comparable to previous multi-view face detectors that can only handle one form of pose variation. We also show experimentally that the system’s accuracy on both face detection and pose estimation is improved by training for the two tasks together.
originalAbstract: We describe a novel method for real-time, simultaneous multi-view face detection and facial pose estimation. The method employs a convolutional network to map face images to points on a manifold, parametrized by pose, and non-face images to points far from that manifold. This network is trained by optimizing a loss function of three variables: image, pose, and face/non-face label. We test the resulting system, in a single configuration, on three standard data sets – one for frontal pose, one for rotated faces, and one for profiles – and find that its performance on each set is comparable to previous multi-view face detectors that can only handle one form of pose variation. We also show experimentally that the system’s accuracy on both face detection and pose estimation is improved by training for the two tasks together.

paragraphs: The paper combines face detection and facial pose estimation in a single real-time method. Rather than treating the presence of a face and its pose as unrelated predictions, it trains a convolutional network around a shared geometric representation. Face images are mapped onto a manifold organized by pose, while non-face images are mapped far away.

Training uses a loss involving the image, its pose, and its face-or-non-face label. The representation therefore has to capture variation among faces while also separating faces from other images. This design connects the two tasks directly: pose organizes the face representation, and detection distinguishes that representation from non-face content.

One system configuration is evaluated on three standard datasets covering frontal faces, rotated faces, and profiles. On each, its performance is comparable to earlier multi-view detectors restricted to one form of pose variation. Experiments also show that joint training improves accuracy on both detection and pose estimation. These findings support the benefit of sharing a representation across the two tasks in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A shared pose-organized face representation enables real-time detection and pose estimation, with joint training improving both tasks experimentally.

title: Synergistic Face Detection and Pose Estimation with Energy-Based Models

abstract: We examine the marriage of recent probabilistic generative models for social networks with classical frameworks from mathematical eco- nomics. We are particularly interested in how the statistical structure of such networks influences global economic quantities such as price vari- ation. Our findings are a mixture of formal analysis, simulation, and experiments on an international trade data set from the United Nations.
originalAbstract: We examine the marriage of recent probabilistic generative models for social networks with classical frameworks from mathematical eco- nomics. We are particularly interested in how the statistical structure of such networks influences global economic quantities such as price vari- ation. Our findings are a mixture of formal analysis, simulation, and experiments on an international trade data set from the United Nations.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the structure of a social network relates to economic outcomes across the network. Its central question concerns the influence of statistical network properties on global quantities, with variation in prices given as a particular example. This connects the organization of relationships to the behavior of an economic system as a whole.

The authors combine probabilistic generative models of social networks with established mathematical frameworks from economics. The network models describe how patterns of connections can arise, while the economic frameworks provide a way to study outcomes associated with those patterns. Bringing them together makes network structure an explicit part of the economic analysis.

The investigation draws on formal analysis, simulation, and experiments using a United Nations international trade dataset. These provide mathematical, computational, and empirical perspectives on the same broad question. The contribution described is this combined study of network structure and economic quantities; the abstract does not state a particular direction in which a network property changes price variation.
summary.tldr: The paper combines social-network models and mathematical economics to investigate how network structure influences outcomes such as price variation.

title: Economic Properties of Social Networks

abstract: Agents learning to act in a partially observable domain may need to overcome the problem of perceptual aliasing i.e., different states that appear similar but require different responses. This problem is exacer- bated when the agent's sensors are noisy, i.e., sensors may produce dif- ferent observations in the same state. We show that many well-known reinforcement learning methods designed to deal with perceptual alias- ing, such as Utile Suffix Memory, finite size history windows, eligibility traces, and memory bits, do not handle noisy sensors well. We suggest a new algorithm, Noisy Utile Suffix Memory (NUSM), based on USM, that uses a weighted classification of observed trajectories. We compare NUSM to the above methods and show it to be more robust to noise.
originalAbstract: Agents learning to act in a partially observable domain may need to overcome the problem of perceptual aliasing i.e., different states that appear similar but require different responses. This problem is exacer- bated when the agent's sensors are noisy, i.e., sensors may produce dif- ferent observations in the same state. We show that many well-known reinforcement learning methods designed to deal with perceptual alias- ing, such as Utile Suffix Memory, finite size history windows, eligibility traces, and memory bits, do not handle noisy sensors well. We suggest a new algorithm, Noisy Utile Suffix Memory (NUSM), based on USM, that uses a weighted classification of observed trajectories. We compare NUSM to the above methods and show it to be more robust to noise.

paragraphs: An agent can encounter different states that look alike but require different actions. This perceptual aliasing makes current observations insufficient for choosing a response. Sensor noise adds another difficulty: even a single underlying state can produce varying observations, making the relationship between what the agent sees and where it is harder to learn.

The paper examines reinforcement-learning methods intended to resolve ambiguity through information about the past. It reports that Utile Suffix Memory, fixed-size history windows, eligibility traces, and memory bits do not cope well with noisy sensors. This identifies noise sensitivity as a problem that persists even when the learner has mechanisms for using history.

The authors propose Noisy Utile Suffix Memory, an extension of Utile Suffix Memory based on weighted classification of observed trajectories. Its use of trajectory information addresses the combined challenge of ambiguous states and unreliable observations. Comparisons with the listed methods show greater robustness to noise, supporting the proposed modification for learning in the partially observable settings examined.
summary.tldr: Noisy Utile Suffix Memory uses weighted trajectory classification to improve noise robustness when different states produce ambiguous observations.

title: Resolving Perceptual Aliasing In The Presence Of Noisy Sensors

abstract: We present a novel spectral clustering method that enables users to incorporate prior knowledge of the size of clusters into the clustering process. The cost function, which is named size regularized cut (SRcut), is defined as the sum of the inter-cluster similarity and a regularization term measuring the relative size of two clusters. Finding a partition of the data set to minimize SRcut is proved to be NP-complete. An approximation algorithm is proposed to solve a relaxed version of the optimization problem as an eigenvalue problem. Evaluations over different data sets demonstrate that the method is not sensitive to outliers and performs better than normalized cut.
originalAbstract: We present a novel spectral clustering method that enables users to incorporate prior knowledge of the size of clusters into the clustering process. The cost function, which is named size regularized cut (SRcut), is defined as the sum of the inter-cluster similarity and a regularization term measuring the relative size of two clusters. Finding a partition of the data set to minimize SRcut is proved to be NP-complete. An approximation algorithm is proposed to solve a relaxed version of the optimization problem as an eigenvalue problem. Evaluations over different data sets demonstrate that the method is not sensitive to outliers and performs better than normalized cut.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a spectral clustering method that lets users incorporate prior knowledge about cluster sizes. Its objective, size regularized cut, combines similarity between clusters with a regularization term measuring the relative sizes of two clusters. The formulation makes size information an explicit part of deciding how to partition the data.

The authors prove that finding a partition minimizing this objective is NP-complete. They therefore propose an approximation algorithm for a relaxed version of the problem, expressed as an eigenvalue problem. This provides a computational route to using the objective while distinguishing the relaxed solution from an exact solution of the original partitioning problem.

Evaluations on different datasets show that the method is not sensitive to outliers and performs better than normalized cut in those comparisons. The contribution is a clustering criterion that combines similarity structure with size expectations, together with an approximation procedure and empirical evidence that the resulting partitions can improve on a standard spectral clustering approach.
summary.tldr: Size regularized cut incorporates cluster-size knowledge into spectral clustering and improves on normalized cut in the reported evaluations.

title: Size Regularized Cut for Data Clustering

abstract: Young children demonstrate the ability to make inferences about the preferences of other agents based on their choices. However, there exists no overarching account of what children are doing when they learn about preferences or how they use that knowledge. We use a rational model of preference learning, drawing on ideas from economics and computer science, to explain the behavior of children in several recent experiments. Specifically, we show how a simple econometric model can be extended to capture two- to four-year-oldsâ use of statistical information in inferring preferences, and their generalization of these preferences.
originalAbstract: Young children demonstrate the ability to make inferences about the preferences of other agents based on their choices. However, there exists no overarching account of what children are doing when they learn about preferences or how they use that knowledge. We use a rational model of preference learning, drawing on ideas from economics and computer science, to explain the behavior of children in several recent experiments. Specifically, we show how a simple econometric model can be extended to capture two- to four-year-oldsâ use of statistical information in inferring preferences, and their generalization of these preferences.

paragraphs: Young children can use someone’s choices to infer what that person likes. The paper asks for a unified explanation of this ability: how children learn preferences from observed decisions, and how they use those inferred preferences to anticipate other choices. Its focus is the connection between observing behavior and generalizing beyond it.

The authors build a rational model of preference learning using ideas from economics and computer science. They extend a simple econometric model to account for how children use statistical information when interpreting choices. This turns an informal description of preference understanding into a model that can be compared with behavior across several experiments.

The model captures reported patterns in two- to four-year-olds’ preference inferences and their generalization of those preferences. The contribution is an account that connects these behaviors within one framework. The stated evidence concerns explaining the experimental behavior through this model; it does not establish that children explicitly perform the model’s calculations.
summary.tldr: An extended econometric model explains how young children use observed choices to infer and generalize other people’s preferences.

title: A rational model of preference learning and choice prediction by children

abstract: Multitask learning addressed the problem of learning related tasks whose information can be shared each other. Traditional problem usually deal with homogeneous tasks such as regression, classification individually. In this paper we consider the problem learning multiple related tasks where tasks consist of both continuous and discrete outputs from a common set of input variables that lie in a high-dimensional space. All of the tasks are related in the sense that they share the same set of relevant input variables, but the amount of influence of each input on different outputs may vary. We formulate this problem as a combination of linear regression and logistic regression and model the joint sparsity as L1/Linf and L1/L2-norm of the model parameters. Among several possible applications, our approach addresses an important open problem in genetic association mapping, where we are interested in discovering genetic markers that influence multiple correlated traits jointly. In our experiments, we demonstrate our method in the scenario of association mapping, using simulated and asthma data, and show that the algorithm can effectively recover the relevant inputs with respect to all of the tasks.

paragraphs: Related prediction tasks can share useful information even when some outputs are continuous and others are discrete. This paper studies that mixed setting with a common, high-dimensional set of inputs. The tasks are assumed to depend on the same relevant input variables, although each variable may exert a different amount of influence on different outputs.

The method combines linear regression for continuous outputs with logistic regression for discrete outputs. Joint sparsity penalties encourage the models to select inputs together. The authors use L1/L-infinity and L1/L2 mixed norms to express this shared selection. This makes the identity of relevant inputs a common part of learning while allowing their effects to vary across tasks.

The motivating application is genetic association mapping, where the aim is to find genetic markers associated with multiple correlated traits. Experiments using simulated data and asthma data show that the method can effectively recover inputs relevant across the tasks. These findings support sharing feature selection between heterogeneous outputs when the common-relevance assumption is appropriate.
summary.tldr: Joint sparsity lets regression and classification tasks select shared relevant inputs while learning different effects for each output.

title: Heterogeneous multitask learning with joint sparsity constraints

abstract: We consider a class of learning problems that involve a structured sparsity-inducing norm defined as the sum of $\ell_\infty$-norms over groups of variables. Whereas a lot of effort has been put in developing fast optimization methods when the groups are disjoint or embedded in a specific hierarchical structure, we address here the case of general overlapping groups. To this end, we show that the corresponding optimization problem is related to network flow optimization. More precisely, the proximal problem associated with the norm we consider is dual to a quadratic min-cost flow problem. We propose an efficient procedure which computes its solution exactly in polynomial time. Our algorithm scales up to millions of groups and variables, and opens up a whole new range of applications for structured sparse models. We present several experiments on image and video data, demonstrating the applicability and scalability of our approach for various problems.

Whereas a lot of effort has been put in developing fast optimization methods when the groups are disjoint or embedded in a specific hierarchical structure, we address here the case of general overlapping groups. To this end, we show that the corresponding optimization problem is related to network flow optimization. More precisely, the proximal problem associated with the norm we consider is dual to a quadratic min-cost flow problem. We propose an efficient procedure which computes its solution exactly in polynomial time. Our algorithm scales up to millions of groups and variables, and opens up a whole new range of applications for structured sparse models. paragraphs: Structured sparsity encourages a learning model to select variables according to groups or relationships. This paper considers a penalty formed by summing the infinity norms of variable groups. Its focus is general overlapping groups, a setting beyond the disjoint or specially hierarchical group structures emphasized by many earlier optimization methods.

The authors show that the penalty’s proximal problem is dual to a quadratic minimum-cost flow problem. A proximal problem is an optimization step that combines a penalty with a preference for staying near a given point. The flow connection enables an efficient procedure that solves this step exactly in polynomial time, providing a computational tool for learning with the specified penalty.

The algorithm scales to millions of groups and variables. Experiments using image and video data demonstrate applicability and scalability across several problems. The significance is that general overlap becomes computationally manageable for this family of penalties, expanding the structures that sparse models can use without restricting groups to a simple hierarchy.
summary.tldr: A network-flow formulation solves a structured-sparsity proximal problem exactly in polynomial time, supporting general overlapping groups at large scale.

title: Network Flow Algorithms for Structured Sparsity

abstract: We derive an instantaneous (per-round) data-dependent regret bound for stochastic multiarmed bandits with side information (also known as contextual bandits). The scaling of our regret bound with the number of states (contexts) $N$ goes as $\sqrt{N I_{\rho_t}(S;A)}$, where $I_{\rho_t}(S;A)$ is the mutual information between states and actions (the side information) used by the algorithm at round $t$. If the algorithm uses all the side information, the regret bound scales as $\sqrt{N \ln K}$, where $K$ is the number of actions (arms). However, if the side information $I_{\rho_t}(S;A)$ is not fully used, the regret bound is significantly tighter. In the extreme case, when $I_{\rho_t}(S;A) = 0$, the dependence on the number of states reduces from linear to logarithmic. Our analysis allows to provide the algorithm large amount of side information, let the algorithm to decide which side information is relevant for the task, and penalize the algorithm only for the side information that it is using de facto. We also present an algorithm for multiarmed bandits with side information with computational complexity that is a linear in the number of actions.

The scaling of our regret bound with the number of states (contexts) $N$ goes as $\sqrt{N I_{\rho_t}(S;A)}$, where $I_{\rho_t}(S;A)$ is the mutual information between states and actions (the side information) used by the algorithm at round $t$. If the algorithm uses all the side information, the regret bound scales as $\sqrt{N \ln K}$, where $K$ is the number of actions (arms). However, if the side information $I_{\rho_t}(S;A)$ is not fully used, the regret bound is significantly tighter. In the extreme case, when $I_{\rho_t}(S;A) = 0$, the dependence on the number of states reduces from linear to logarithmic. Our analysis allows to provide the algorithm large amount of side information, let the algorithm to decide which side information is relevant for the task, and penalize the algorithm only for the side information that it is using de facto. We also present an algorithm for multiarmed bandits with side information with computational complexity that is a linear in the number of actions.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using side information while learning from uncertain outcomes. This paper derives a data-dependent regret bound for each round in the stochastic setting. Its distinguishing feature is that the bound accounts for how much context the algorithm actually uses to select actions, measured through mutual information between contexts and actions.

For N contexts, the stated scaling involves the square root of N times that mutual information. When the algorithm uses all side information, the bound scales as the square root of N log K, where K is the number of actions. If less information is used, the bound can be substantially tighter. In the zero-mutual-information case, the abstract reports only logarithmic dependence on the number of contexts.

This analysis supports providing abundant side information while charging the algorithm for the information that actually influences its choices. It therefore distinguishes information availability from information use. The paper also presents a contextual-bandit algorithm with computational complexity linear in the number of actions, pairing the theoretical analysis with an algorithmic contribution.
summary.tldr: A per-round contextual-bandit regret bound adapts to the mutual information between contexts and chosen actions, penalizing information actually used.

title: PAC-Bayesian Analysis of Contextual Bandits

abstract: For smooth and strongly convex optimization, the optimal iteration complexity of the gradient-based algorithm is $O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log 1/\epsilon)$, where $\kappa$ is the conditional number. In the case that the optimization problem is ill-conditioned, we need to evaluate a larger number of full gradients, which could be computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose to reduce the number of full gradient required by allowing the algorithm to access the stochastic gradients of the objective function. To this end, we present a novel algorithm named Epoch Mixed Gradient Descent (EMGD) that is able to utilize two kinds of gradients. A distinctive step in EMGD is the mixed gradient descent, where we use an combination of the gradient and the stochastic gradient to update the intermediate solutions. By performing a fixed number of mixed gradient descents, we are able to improve the sub-optimality of the solution by a constant factor, and thus achieve a linear convergence rate. Theoretical analysis shows that EMGD is able to find an $\epsilon$-optimal solution by computing $O(\log 1/\epsilon)$ full gradients and $O(\kappa^2\log 1/\epsilon)$ stochastic gradients.
originalAbstract: For smooth and strongly convex optimization, the optimal iteration complexity of the gradient-based algorithm is $O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log 1/\epsilon)$, where $\kappa$ is the conditional number. In the case that the optimization problem is ill-conditioned, we need to evaluate a larger number of full gradients, which could be computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose to reduce the number of full gradient required by allowing the algorithm to access the stochastic gradients of the objective function. To this end, we present a novel algorithm named Epoch Mixed Gradient Descent (EMGD) that is able to utilize two kinds of gradients. A distinctive step in EMGD is the mixed gradient descent, where we use an combination of the gradient and the stochastic gradient to update the intermediate solutions. By performing a fixed number of mixed gradient descents, we are able to improve the sub-optimality of the solution by a constant factor, and thus achieve a linear convergence rate. Theoretical analysis shows that EMGD is able to find an $\epsilon$-optimal solution by computing $O(\log 1/\epsilon)$ full gradients and $O(\kappa^2\log 1/\epsilon)$ stochastic gradients.

paragraphs: For smooth, strongly convex optimization, poor conditioning can make gradient-based optimization expensive by increasing the required number of full-gradient evaluations. This paper asks whether access to stochastic gradients can reduce that particular expense. The goal is to retain linear convergence while limiting how often the algorithm needs a full gradient.

The proposed Epoch Mixed Gradient Descent algorithm combines full and stochastic gradients in its updates. After a fixed number of mixed-gradient steps, it reduces solution suboptimality by a constant factor. Repeating those improvements produces linear convergence, meaning that successive stages shrink the remaining optimization error geometrically.

The analysis gives O(log(1/epsilon)) full-gradient evaluations and O(kappa² log(1/epsilon)) stochastic-gradient evaluations to reach epsilon accuracy, where kappa is the condition number. Thus the full-gradient count is independent of conditioning, while the stochastic-gradient count retains a quadratic dependence on it. The result identifies a specific computational tradeoff: conditioning-related work is shifted toward stochastic evaluations while expensive full-gradient access is controlled.
summary.tldr: Epoch Mixed Gradient Descent achieves linear convergence with a condition-number-independent full-gradient count by also using stochastic gradients.

title: Linear Convergence with Condition Number Independent Access of Full Gradients

abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for provably learning the structure and parameters of bipartite noisy-or Bayesian networks of binary variables where the top layer is completely hidden. Unsupervised learning of these models is a form of discrete factor analysis, enabling the discovery of hidden variables and their causal relationships with observed data. We obtain an efficient learning algorithm for a family of Bayesian networks that we call quartet-learnable, meaning that every latent variable has four children that do not have any other parents in common. We show that the existence of such a quartet allows us to uniquely identify each latent variable and to learn all parameters involving that latent variable. Underlying our algorithm are two new techniques for structure learning: a quartet test to determine whether a set of binary variables are singly coupled, and a conditional mutual information test that we use to learn parameters. We also show how to subtract already learned latent variables from the model to create new singly-coupled quartets, which substantially expands the class of structures that we can learn. Finally, we give a proof of the polynomial sample complexity of our learning algorithm, and experimentally compare it to variational EM.
originalAbstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for provably learning the structure and parameters of bipartite noisy-or Bayesian networks of binary variables where the top layer is completely hidden. Unsupervised learning of these models is a form of discrete factor analysis, enabling the discovery of hidden variables and their causal relationships with observed data. We obtain an efficient learning algorithm for a family of Bayesian networks that we call quartet-learnable, meaning that every latent variable has four children that do not have any other parents in common. We show that the existence of such a quartet allows us to uniquely identify each latent variable and to learn all parameters involving that latent variable. Underlying our algorithm are two new techniques for structure learning: a quartet test to determine whether a set of binary variables are singly coupled, and a conditional mutual information test that we use to learn parameters. We also show how to subtract already learned latent variables from the model to create new singly-coupled quartets, which substantially expands the class of structures that we can learn. Finally, we give a proof of the polynomial sample complexity of our learning algorithm, and experimentally compare it to variational EM.

paragraphs: The paper studies binary Bayesian networks with two layers, where every variable in the upper layer is hidden. Learning such noisy-or models means discovering the hidden variables, their connections to observed variables, and the associated parameters. The authors provide a polynomial-time learning algorithm with provable guarantees for a structurally defined family of these networks.

The key condition is quartet learnability: each hidden variable has four children that share no other parents. Such a quartet uniquely identifies its hidden parent and allows the parameters involving that parent to be learned. The algorithm combines a quartet test for detecting this shared-parent pattern with a conditional mutual information test for parameter estimation.

Already learned hidden variables can also be subtracted from the model, revealing new qualifying quartets and substantially enlarging the class of learnable structures. The authors prove polynomial sample complexity and compare the method experimentally with variational EM. Its guarantees depend on the stated structural conditions, making the quartet pattern central to both identifiability and efficient learning.
summary.tldr: Quartet-based tests enable provably efficient recovery of hidden variables and parameters in a structured family of noisy-or networks.

title: Discovering Hidden Variables in Noisy-Or Networks using Quartet Tests

abstract: Despite growing interest and practical use in various scientific areas, variable importances derived from tree-based ensemble methods are not well understood from a theoretical point of view. In this work we characterize the Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) variable importances as measured by an ensemble of totally randomized trees in asymptotic sample and ensemble size conditions. We derive a three-level decomposition of the information jointly provided by all input variables about the output in terms of i) the MDI importance of each input variable, ii) the degree of interaction of a given input variable with the other input variables, iii) the different interaction terms of a given degree. We then show that this MDI importance of a variable is equal to zero if and only if the variable is irrelevant and that the MDI importance of a relevant variable is invariant with respect to the removal or the addition of irrelevant variables. We illustrate these properties on a simple example and discuss how they may change in the case of non-totally randomized trees such as Random Forests and Extra-Trees.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles commonly assign importance scores to input variables, but interpreting those scores requires understanding what they measure. This paper characterizes Mean Decrease Impurity importance for ensembles of totally randomized trees under asymptotic conditions on both the number of samples and the number of trees.

The authors decompose the information that all inputs jointly provide about the output at three levels: individual variable importance, the degree of interaction with other variables, and the specific interactions within each degree. This connects a variable's overall score to the information it contributes through different combinations with other inputs.

Within the analyzed setting, a variable has zero importance exactly when it is irrelevant. A relevant variable's importance also remains unchanged when irrelevant variables are added or removed. These are precise properties of the specified randomized, asymptotic setting. The paper illustrates them with a simple example and discusses how they may change for trees that are not totally randomized, including Random Forests and Extra-Trees. That distinction is essential when applying the theoretical interpretation to practical ensemble scores.
summary.tldr: For totally randomized forests in an asymptotic setting, impurity importance decomposes predictive information and is zero exactly for irrelevant variables.

title: Understanding variable importances in forests of randomized trees

abstract: We investigate the power of voting among diverse, randomized software agents. With teams of computer Go agents in mind, we develop a novel theoretical model of two-stage noisy voting that builds on recent work in machine learning. This model allows us to reason about a collection of agents with different biases (determined by the first-stage noise models), which, furthermore, apply randomized algorithms to evaluate alternatives and produce votes (captured by the second-stage noise models). We analytically demonstrate that a uniform team, consisting of multiple instances of any single agent, must make a significant number of mistakes, whereas a diverse team converges to perfection as the number of agents grows. Our experiments, which pit teams of computer Go agents against strong agents, provide evidence for the effectiveness of voting when agents are diverse.

paragraphs: The paper asks when voting can turn a collection of randomized software agents into a stronger decision maker. Computer Go provides the motivating setting. A central distinction is between running many copies of the same agent and combining different agents whose judgments have different biases.

To study this distinction, the authors introduce a voting model with two stages of noise. The first represents differences in agents' biases, while the second represents randomness in the algorithms they use to evaluate alternatives and cast votes. Separating these sources of variation lets the analysis distinguish diversity across agent types from repeated randomized runs of one type.

Within this theoretical model, a uniform team must make a significant number of mistakes, whereas a diverse team's decisions converge to perfection as the team grows. Experiments against strong Go agents provide evidence that diverse voting teams are effective in practice. The asymptotic perfection claim belongs to the model; the experiments support the practical value of diversity without establishing that arbitrary collections of agents become flawless.
summary.tldr: A two-stage voting model and Go experiments show how diversity among randomized agents can improve collective decisions.

title: Diverse Randomized Agents Vote to Win

abstract: Despite the prevalence of collaborative filtering in recommendation systems, there has been little theoretical development on why and how well it works, especially in the ``online'' setting, where items are recommended to users over time. We address this theoretical gap by introducing a model for online recommendation systems, cast item recommendation under the model as a learning problem, and analyze the performance of a cosine-similarity collaborative filtering method. In our model, each of $n$ users either likes or dislikes each of $m$ items. We assume there to be $k$ types of users, and all the users of a given type share a common string of probabilities determining the chance of liking each item. At each time step, we recommend an item to each user, where a key distinction from related bandit literature is that once a user consumes an item (e.g., watches a movie), then that item cannot be recommended to the same user again. The goal is to maximize the number of likable items recommended to users over time. Our main result establishes that after nearly $\log(km)$ initial learning time steps, a simple collaborative filtering algorithm achieves essentially optimal performance without knowing $k$. The algorithm has an exploitation step that uses cosine similarity and two types of exploration steps, one to explore the space of items (standard in the literature) and the other to explore similarity between users (novel to this work).

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical explanation for collaborative filtering when recommendations arrive over time. Its model groups users into unknown types: users of the same type share probabilities of liking each item. Feedback is binary, and an item cannot be recommended again to a user who has already consumed it. The objective is to recommend as many likable items as possible.

The algorithm combines recommendations based on cosine similarity with two forms of exploration. One explores items to learn what users like. The other explores similarities between users, helping determine whose preferences provide useful evidence for someone else. Learning these relationships is part of the recommendation process, rather than information assumed available beforehand.

Under the proposed model, the analysis establishes essentially optimal performance after an initial learning period of nearly log(km) steps, where k counts user types and m counts items. The algorithm does not need to know k. This connects successful online recommendations to learning both item preferences and the structure shared across users.
summary.tldr: A user-type model explains how collaborative filtering can achieve essentially optimal online recommendations after a short learning period.

title: A Latent Source Model for Online Collaborative Filtering

abstract: Normalized random measures (NRMs) provide a broad class of discrete random measures that are often used as priors for Bayesian nonparametric models. Dirichlet process is a well-known example of NRMs. Most of posterior inference methods for NRM mixture models rely on MCMC methods since they are easy to implement and their convergence is well studied. However, MCMC often suffers from slow convergence when the acceptance rate is low. Tree-based inference is an alternative deterministic posterior inference method, where Bayesian hierarchical clustering (BHC) or incremental Bayesian hierarchical clustering (IBHC) have been developed for DP or NRM mixture (NRMM) models, respectively. Although IBHC is a promising method for posterior inference for NRMM models due to its efficiency and applicability to online inference, its convergence is not guaranteed since it uses heuristics that simply selects the best solution after multiple trials are made. In this paper, we present a hybrid inference algorithm for NRMM models, which combines the merits of both MCMC and IBHC. Trees built by IBHC outlinespartitions of data, which guides Metropolis-Hastings procedure to employ appropriate proposals. Inheriting the nature of MCMC, our tree-guided MCMC (tgMCMC) is guaranteed to converge, and enjoys the fast convergence thanks to the effective proposals guided by trees. Experiments on both synthetic and real world datasets demonstrate the benefit of our method.

The paper combines these approaches in tree-guided MCMC. Trees constructed by incremental Bayesian hierarchical clustering outline plausible data partitions and guide proposals within a Metropolis-Hastings procedure. The tree therefore supplies useful structure for choosing candidate moves, while the sampling procedure provides the basis for the method's convergence guarantee.

The authors state that the hybrid inherits MCMC convergence and converges quickly through effective tree-guided proposals. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate benefits of the approach. Its main significance is the division of responsibilities between the two components: hierarchical clustering guides exploration, and MCMC supplies a convergent inference mechanism, bringing together strengths that either approach alone does not provide.
summary.tldr: Tree-guided MCMC uses hierarchical clustering to propose effective moves while retaining convergence guarantees for normalized random measure mixture inference.

title: Tree-Guided MCMC Inference for Normalized Random Measure Mixture Models

abstract: Neural networks are both computationally intensive and memory intensive, making them difficult to deploy on embedded systems. Also, conventional networks fix the architecture before training starts; as a result, training cannot improve the architecture. To address these limitations, we describe a method to reduce the storage and computation required by neural networks by an order of magnitude without affecting their accuracy by learning only the important connections. Our method prunes redundant connections using a three-step method. First, we train the network to learn which connections are important. Next, we prune the unimportant connections. Finally, we retrain the network to fine tune the weights of the remaining connections. On the ImageNet dataset, our method reduced the number of parameters of AlexNet by a factor of 9×, from 61 million to 6.7 million, without incurring accuracy loss. Similar experiments with VGG-16 found that the total number of parameters can be reduced by 13×, from 138 million to 10.3 million, again with no loss of accuracy.

paragraphs: Large neural networks demand substantial memory and computation, which can make embedded deployment difficult. Conventional training adjusts weights within a fixed architecture. This paper also changes which connections remain, using training to identify a smaller network that preserves the predictive accuracy of the original in the reported experiments.

The method has three stages. First, the full network is trained so that the importance of its connections can be assessed. Next, unimportant connections are removed. Finally, the remaining weights are retrained to adapt the reduced network. This final adjustment is part of the method, so the resulting network reflects both connection selection and further weight learning.

On ImageNet, AlexNet's parameter count falls from 61 million to 6.7 million, a ninefold reduction, with no reported accuracy loss. VGG-16 falls from 138 million to 10.3 million parameters, a thirteenfold reduction, again without accuracy loss. These results demonstrate substantial redundancy in the tested networks and support learning connectivity as a way to reduce neural-network resource requirements.
summary.tldr: Training, pruning, and retraining reduce AlexNet and VGG-16 parameter counts by 9× and 13× without reported accuracy loss.

title: Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Network

abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.

Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a criterion for assessing discrimination in supervised prediction with respect to a specified sensitive attribute. The setting is a learned system that predicts a target from available features. The criterion gives the authors a defined standard against which a predictor can be evaluated and adjusted, making the intended meaning of removing discrimination explicit within their framework.

The central result is a way to optimally adjust any learned predictor so that it satisfies this standard. The result assumes access to data about the predictor, the target, and membership in the protected group. Those information requirements are part of the setting in which the adjustment is established, and the guarantee concerns discrimination according to the proposed definition.

The framework also changes who bears the cost of poor classification. The authors argue that it shifts that burden from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker. Improving predictive accuracy then becomes a way for the decision maker to respond, connecting the fairness requirement with incentives to improve the underlying classifier.
summary.tldr: The paper defines a discrimination criterion and shows how to optimally adjust learned predictors to satisfy it under stated data-access assumptions.

title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning

abstract: We investigate the statistical performance and computational efficiency of the alternating minimization procedure for nonparametric tensor learning. Tensor modeling has been widely used for capturing the higher order relations between multimodal data sources. In addition to a linear model, a nonlinear tensor model has been received much attention recently because of its high flexibility. We consider an alternating minimization procedure for a general nonlinear model where the true function consists of components in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). In this paper, we show that the alternating minimization method achieves linear convergence as an optimization algorithm and that the generalization error of the resultant estimator yields the minimax optimality. We apply our algorithm to some multitask learning problems and show that the method actually shows favorable performances.

paragraphs: Tensor models describe higher-order relationships among multiple data sources. This paper examines a nonlinear version whose true function consists of components in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. That model provides flexibility beyond a linear tensor formulation, while giving the authors a mathematical setting in which to study both computation and statistical performance.

The algorithm uses alternating minimization, optimizing different parts of the model in turn. The paper establishes linear convergence for this procedure as an optimization method. In this terminology, linear convergence describes geometric progress toward the optimization target; it does not mean that the model itself is linear or that total runtime is linear in dataset size.

The authors separately show that the resulting estimator has minimax-optimal generalization error in the considered setting. This addresses statistical accuracy as well as the speed of optimization. Applications to multitask learning also produce favorable empirical performance. Together, the results support alternating minimization for the analyzed kernel-based tensor model through complementary computational guarantees, statistical guarantees, and experiments.
summary.tldr: Alternating minimization achieves linear optimization convergence and minimax-optimal generalization for the studied nonlinear kernel tensor model.

title: Minimax Optimal Alternating Minimization for Kernel Nonparametric Tensor Learning

abstract: In many cases of network analysis, it is more attractive to study how a network varies under different conditions than an individual static network. We propose a novel graphical model, namely Latent Differential Graph Model, where the networks under two different conditions are represented by two semiparametric elliptical distributions respectively, and the variation of these two networks (i.e., differential graph) is characterized by the difference between their latent precision matrices. We propose an estimator for the differential graph based on quasi likelihood maximization with nonconvex regularization. We show that our estimator attains a faster statistical rate in parameter estimation than the state-of-the-art methods, and enjoys oracle property under mild conditions. Thorough experiments on both synthetic and real world data support our theory.

paragraphs: When a network is observed under two conditions, the scientific question may concern what changed between them. This paper makes that change the object of statistical modeling. Its Latent Differential Graph Model represents the two conditions with semiparametric elliptical distributions and describes their difference through latent precision matrices.

A precision matrix encodes a network's statistical structure in this formulation. Taking the difference between the two latent precision matrices gives the differential graph to be estimated. The proposed estimator uses quasi-likelihood maximization with nonconvex regularization, combining a criterion for fitting the model with a penalty that shapes the estimated differences.

The authors establish a faster statistical rate for parameter estimation than the state-of-the-art methods considered. They also prove an oracle property under conditions described as mild, making that guarantee conditional on the stated theoretical setting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the analysis. The contribution is a framework for estimating network variation directly, together with theoretical and empirical evidence about the accuracy of those estimates.
summary.tldr: A latent differential graph estimator models network changes and achieves improved estimation rates with a conditional oracle guarantee.

title: Semiparametric Differential Graph Models

abstract: We consider the problem of learning an unknown Markov Decision Process (MDP) that is weakly communicating in the infinite horizon setting. We propose a Thompson Sampling-based reinforcement learning algorithm with dynamic episodes (TSDE). At the beginning of each episode, the algorithm generates a sample from the posterior distribution over the unknown model parameters. It then follows the optimal stationary policy for the sampled model for the rest of the episode. The duration of each episode is dynamically determined by two stopping criteria. The first stopping criterion controls the growth rate of episode length. The second stopping criterion happens when the number of visits to any state-action pair is doubled. We establish $\tilde O(HS\sqrt{AT})$ bounds on expected regret under a Bayesian setting, where $S$ and $A$ are the sizes of the state and action spaces, $T$ is time, and $H$ is the bound of the span. This regret bound matches the best available bound for weakly communicating MDPs. Numerical results show it to perform better than existing algorithms for infinite horizon MDPs.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in an unknown, weakly communicating Markov decision process over an unlimited time horizon. The learner must choose actions while learning the environment's dynamics. The proposed algorithm, Thompson Sampling with Dynamic Episodes, uses uncertainty over model parameters to select a policy for each episode.

At the start of an episode, the algorithm samples a model from its posterior distribution and follows that model's optimal stationary policy. Episode duration is controlled by two stopping criteria. One limits how quickly episode lengths grow; the other ends an episode when the visit count for any state–action pair doubles. These rules determine when the learner resamples its model.

The authors establish a Bayesian expected-regret bound of order HS√(AT), up to logarithmic factors, where S and A count states and actions, T is elapsed time, and H bounds the span. This matches the best available bound reported for weakly communicating MDPs. Numerical results also show better performance than existing infinite-horizon algorithms in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Thompson sampling with dynamically ended episodes achieves a matching Bayesian regret bound for weakly communicating infinite-horizon MDPs.

title: Learning Unknown Markov Decision Processes: A Thompson Sampling Approach

abstract: From only positive (P) and unlabeled (U) data, a binary classifier could be trained with PU learning, in which the state of the art is unbiased PU learning. However, if its model is very flexible, empirical risks on training data will go negative, and we will suffer from serious overfitting. In this paper, we propose a non-negative risk estimator for PU learning: when getting minimized, it is more robust against overfitting, and thus we are able to use very flexible models (such as deep neural networks) given limited P data. Moreover, we analyze the bias, consistency, and mean-squared-error reduction of the proposed risk estimator, and bound the estimation error of the resulting empirical risk minimizer. Experiments demonstrate that our risk estimator fixes the overfitting problem of its unbiased counterparts.

In this paper, we propose a non-negative risk estimator for PU learning: when getting minimized, it is more robust against overfitting, and thus we are able to use very flexible models (such as deep neural networks) given limited P data. Moreover, we analyze the bias, consistency, and mean-squared-error reduction of the proposed risk estimator, and bound the estimation error of the resulting empirical risk minimizer. Experiments demonstrate that our risk estimator fixes the overfitting problem of its unbiased counterparts.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier using positive examples and examples without labels. The paper identifies a failure of the existing unbiased risk estimator when paired with very flexible models: its estimated training risk can become negative, and minimizing that estimate can lead to severe overfitting rather than better prediction.

The proposed estimator enforces non-negativity of the risk estimate. The authors report that minimizing it is more robust to overfitting, making it possible to use flexible models such as deep neural networks even when labeled positive examples are limited. The change targets the training objective itself, addressing how the learner evaluates candidate classifiers from positive and unlabeled data.

The paper studies the estimator’s bias, consistency, and reduction in mean squared error, and bounds the estimation error of the resulting empirical risk minimizer. These analyses examine the statistical consequences of modifying the unbiased estimator. Experiments show that the proposed approach resolves the overfitting observed with its unbiased counterparts, supporting non-negativity as a useful constraint in the tested PU-learning settings.
summary.tldr: A non-negative risk estimator reduces overfitting in positive-unlabeled learning and supports flexible models with limited positive data.

title: Positive-Unlabeled Learning with Non-Negative Risk Estimator

abstract: Non-discrimination is a recognized objective in algorithmic decision making. In this paper, we introduce a novel probabilistic formulation of data pre-processing for reducing discrimination. We propose a convex optimization for learning a data transformation with three goals: controlling discrimination, limiting distortion in individual data samples, and preserving utility. We characterize the impact of limited sample size in accomplishing this objective. Two instances of the proposed optimization are applied to datasets, including one on real-world criminal recidivism. Results show that discrimination can be greatly reduced at a small cost in classification accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper approaches discrimination reduction through data preprocessing. It introduces a probabilistic formulation for learning a transformation of the data before those data are used in decision making. The transformation is designed around three simultaneous goals: controlling discrimination, restricting changes to individual samples, and retaining useful information for the prediction task.

The authors express this balance as a convex optimization problem. Including sample-level distortion alongside discrimination and utility makes the treatment of individual records part of the formulation. The paper also characterizes how limited sample size affects the objective, recognizing that the transformation must be learned from the available data rather than from complete knowledge of the population.

Two instances of the optimization are evaluated on datasets, including a real-world criminal recidivism dataset. The results show that discrimination can be substantially reduced with only a small loss in classification accuracy. These findings demonstrate an empirical tradeoff achieved by the proposed preprocessing framework, while the optimization formulation makes the competing goals explicit rather than leaving data changes unconstrained.
summary.tldr: A convex preprocessing framework reduces discrimination while controlling individual data distortion and preserving predictive utility.

title: Optimized Pre-Processing for Discrimination Prevention

abstract: Recently, continuous cache models were proposed as extensions to recurrent neural network language models, to adapt their predictions to local changes in the data distribution. These models only capture the local context, of up to a few thousands tokens. In this paper, we propose an extension of continuous cache models, which can scale to larger contexts. In particular, we use a large scale non-parametric memory component that stores all the hidden activations seen in the past. We leverage recent advances in approximate nearest neighbor search and quantization algorithms to store millions of representations while searching them efficiently. We conduct extensive experiments showing that our approach significantly improves the perplexity of pre-trained language models on new distributions, and can scale efficiently to much larger contexts than previously proposed local cache models.

We conduct extensive experiments showing that our approach significantly improves the perplexity of pre-trained language models on new distributions, and can scale efficiently to much larger contexts than previously proposed local cache models.

paragraphs: A language model may encounter text whose distribution differs from what it previously learned. Continuous cache models help adapt predictions using recent context, but earlier versions cover only a limited history. This paper extends that approach so adaptation can draw on a much larger collection of past representations.

The proposed memory component stores all hidden activations observed in the past. Approximate nearest neighbor search makes it possible to search this large collection efficiently, while quantization supports storage of millions of representations. Together, these techniques make a substantially longer history usable within the cache mechanism.

Experiments show significant improvements in the perplexity of pretrained language models on new distributions, indicating better predictive fit in those evaluations. The approach also scales efficiently to contexts much larger than those supported by earlier local caches. The contribution is a practical expansion of the memory available for adaptation: previously computed activations remain accessible beyond a short local window, with search and storage methods supporting the larger scale.
summary.tldr: A large searchable cache of past hidden activations improves language-model adaptation and scales to much longer contexts.

title: Unbounded cache model for online language modeling with open vocabulary

abstract: One of the popular approaches for low-rank tensor completion is to use the latent trace norm regularization. However, most existing works in this direction learn a sparse combination of tensors. In this work, we fill this gap by proposing a variant of the latent trace norm that helps in learning a non-sparse combination of tensors. We develop a dual framework for solving the low-rank tensor completion problem. We first show a novel characterization of the dual solution space with an interesting factorization of the optimal solution. Overall, the optimal solution is shown to lie on a Cartesian product of Riemannian manifolds. Furthermore, we exploit the versatile Riemannian optimization framework for proposing computationally efficient trust region algorithm. The experiments illustrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm on several real-world datasets across applications.

paragraphs: Tensor completion concerns filling in missing entries of a multidimensional array using low-rank structure. The paper examines an approach based on latent trace norm regularization. Existing methods of this kind often favor a sparse combination of component tensors, meaning that relatively few components contribute to the recovered result.

The authors introduce a variant of that regularizer designed to support a non-sparse combination. They then develop a dual formulation of the completion problem and characterize its solution space. Their analysis reveals a factorization of the optimal solution, placing it on a Cartesian product of Riemannian manifolds: a collection of spaces with structured geometry.

That geometric characterization supplies a route to computation. The authors use Riemannian optimization to construct a computationally efficient trust region algorithm suited to the solution space. Experiments on real-world datasets across several applications illustrate its effectiveness. The contribution therefore connects a different preference about how tensor components combine with a mathematical formulation and an algorithm for finding the resulting completion.
summary.tldr: A modified tensor regularizer and geometric dual formulation enable efficient completion using non-sparse combinations of component tensors.

title: A Dual Framework for Low-rank Tensor Completion

abstract: We consider adaptive control of the Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR), where an unknown linear system is controlled subject to quadratic costs. Leveraging recent developments in the estimation of linear systems and in robust controller synthesis, we present the first provably polynomial time algorithm that achieves sub-linear regret on this problem. We further study the interplay between regret minimization and parameter estimation by proving a lower bound on the expected regret in terms of the exploration schedule used by any algorithm. Finally, we conduct a numerical study comparing our robust adaptive algorithm to other methods from the adaptive LQR literature, and demonstrate the flexibility of our proposed method by extending it to a demand forecasting problem subject to state constraints.

paragraphs: An adaptive linear quadratic regulator must control an unknown linear system while incurring quadratic costs. Learning the system and controlling it are intertwined: actions affect immediate costs and the information available for future decisions. This paper combines advances in linear-system estimation with robust controller synthesis to address that joint problem.

The authors present what they identify as the first provably polynomial-time algorithm achieving sublinear regret for this problem. Sublinear regret means that accumulated excess cost grows more slowly than the time horizon. They also prove a lower bound on expected regret in terms of an algorithm's exploration schedule, making the connection between information gathering and control performance explicit.

A numerical study compares the robust adaptive method with other approaches from the adaptive LQR literature. The authors additionally extend it to a demand-forecasting problem with state constraints, demonstrating flexibility beyond the initial formulation. The main contribution is the combination of computational efficiency and a regret guarantee, accompanied by an analysis of the cost of exploration.
summary.tldr: A robust adaptive LQR algorithm achieves sublinear regret in polynomial time and exposes how exploration affects achievable regret.

title: Regret Bounds for Robust Adaptive Control of the Linear Quadratic Regulator

abstract: This paper presents KeypointNet, an end-to-end geometric reasoning framework to learn an optimal set of category-specific keypoints, along with their detectors to predict 3D keypoints in a single 2D input image. We demonstrate this framework on 3D pose estimation task by proposing a differentiable pose objective that seeks the optimal set of keypoints for recovering the relative pose between two views of an object. Our network automatically discovers a consistent set of keypoints across viewpoints of a single object as well as across all object instances of a given object class. Importantly, we find that our end-to-end approach using no ground-truth keypoint annotations outperforms a fully supervised baseline using the same neural network architecture for the pose estimation task. The discovered 3D keypoints across the car, chair, and plane categories of ShapeNet are visualized at https://keypoints.github.io/
