paragraphs: Keypoints provide a compact way to describe an object's geometry, but choosing which points to detect can itself be a learning problem. KeypointNet learns both a category-specific set of points and detectors that predict their three-dimensional positions from one two-dimensional image. The aim is to discover points useful for geometric reasoning.

The framework is trained through a differentiable pose objective that evaluates how well the keypoints recover the relative pose between two views of an object. This connects the choice of points directly to the task they should support. The network discovers consistent points across different views of one object and across different instances within an object category.

The authors report that this end-to-end approach, without ground-truth keypoint annotations, outperforms a fully supervised baseline using the same network architecture on pose estimation. This comparison suggests that points selected through the geometric task can be more useful than the annotated points used by that baseline. The paper presents discovered keypoints for cars, chairs, and planes from ShapeNet.
summary.tldr: KeypointNet discovers consistent 3D keypoints through a pose objective and outperforms a supervised pose-estimation baseline without keypoint annotations.

title: Discovery of Latent 3D Keypoints via End-to-end Geometric Reasoning

abstract: We develop deep Poisson-gamma dynamical systems (DPGDS) to model sequentially observed multivariate count data, improving previously proposed models by not only mining deep hierarchical latent structure from the data, but also capturing both first-order and long-range temporal dependencies. Using sophisticated but simple-to-implement data augmentation techniques, we derived closed-form Gibbs sampling update equations by first backward and upward propagating auxiliary latent counts, and then forward and downward sampling latent variables. Moreover, we develop stochastic gradient MCMC inference that is scalable to very long multivariate count time series. Experiments on both synthetic and a variety of real-world data demonstrate that the proposed model not only has excellent predictive performance, but also provides highly interpretable multilayer latent structure to represent hierarchical and temporal information propagation.

paragraphs: This paper models sequences in which several count-valued quantities are observed over time. Its deep Poisson-gamma dynamical system learns multiple layers of hidden structure while capturing both immediate temporal dependencies and relationships extending further into the past. The aim is to represent hierarchical organization and temporal behavior together within a single probabilistic model.

The authors derive closed-form Gibbs sampling updates using data augmentation. Auxiliary hidden counts first propagate backward through time and upward through the hierarchy; latent variables are then sampled forward and downward. This arrangement supplies an inference procedure for the interacting layers and time steps. A stochastic gradient MCMC method further makes inference scalable to very long multivariate count sequences.

Experiments on synthetic and varied real-world data report excellent predictive performance. The learned layers also provide interpretable representations of how hierarchical and temporal information propagates. The findings therefore concern both prediction and understanding: the model produces useful forecasts while exposing structured hidden factors that organize the observed count data.
summary.tldr: Deep Poisson-gamma dynamical systems combine hierarchical structure and temporal dependencies to predict and interpret multivariate count sequences.

title: Deep Poisson gamma dynamical systems

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have recently achieved great success in single-image super-resolution (SISR). However, these methods tend to produce over-smoothed outputs and miss some textural details. To solve these problems, we propose the Super-Resolution CliqueNet (SRCliqueNet) to reconstruct the high resolution (HR) image with better textural details in the wavelet domain. The proposed SRCliqueNet firstly extracts a set of feature maps from the low resolution (LR) image by the clique blocks group. Then we send the set of feature maps to the clique up-sampling module to reconstruct the HR image. The clique up-sampling module consists of four sub-nets which predict the high resolution wavelet coefficients of four sub-bands. Since we consider the edge feature properties of four sub-bands, the four sub-nets are connected to the others so that they can learn the coefficients of four sub-bands jointly. Finally we apply inverse discrete wavelet transform (IDWT) to the output of four sub-nets at the end of the clique up-sampling module to increase the resolution and reconstruct the HR image. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments on benchmark datasets show that our method achieves superior performance over the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution aims to reconstruct a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution input. The paper addresses a common problem in convolutional approaches: outputs can look overly smooth and lose texture. Its proposed SRCliqueNet reconstructs the image through wavelet coefficients, using relationships among different sub-bands to improve detail.

A group of clique blocks first extracts feature maps from the input image. A subsequent upsampling module contains four subnetworks, each predicting the high-resolution coefficients of one wavelet sub-band. These subnetworks are connected so that their predictions can be learned jointly, taking account of the edge-related properties of the four sub-bands.

An inverse discrete wavelet transform combines the predicted coefficients to produce the higher-resolution image. This design makes coordination among sub-bands part of reconstruction, connecting feature extraction to a structured representation of image detail. Quantitative and qualitative benchmark experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support jointly predicting related wavelet components as an effective way to address texture loss in the super-resolution settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: SRCliqueNet jointly predicts four wavelet sub-bands to reconstruct higher-resolution images with improved texture detail.

title: Joint Sub-bands Learning with Clique Structures for Wavelet Domain Super-Resolution

abstract: Learning how to act when there are many available actions in each state is a challenging task for Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents, especially when many of the actions are redundant or irrelevant. In such cases, it is easier to learn which actions not to take. In this work, we propose the Action-Elimination Deep Q-Network (AE-DQN) architecture that combines a Deep RL algorithm with an Action Elimination Network (AEN) that eliminates sub-optimal actions. The AEN is trained to predict invalid actions, supervised by an external elimination signal provided by the environment. Simulations demonstrate a considerable speedup and added robustness over vanilla DQN in text-based games with over a thousand discrete actions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when each state offers many possible actions, especially when a large fraction are irrelevant or redundant. This paper explores the idea that identifying actions to avoid can be easier than learning the best action directly. It uses that information to assist a deep reinforcement learning agent.

The proposed Action-Elimination Deep Q-Network, or AE-DQN, combines a deep reinforcement learning algorithm with an Action Elimination Network. This additional network predicts invalid actions and eliminates suboptimal choices. Its supervision comes from an external elimination signal supplied by the environment, making that signal an explicit part of the proposed learning setup.

Simulations evaluate the architecture in text-based games containing more than a thousand discrete actions. The authors report considerable speed gains and greater robustness compared with vanilla DQN. These results suggest that a dedicated action-elimination component can help learning in large action spaces when suitable environmental feedback is available. The method's practical idea is to use learned exclusion information to reduce the burden placed on the action-learning process.
summary.tldr: AE-DQN uses an environment-supervised action-elimination network to accelerate and stabilize learning in text games with large action spaces.

title: Learn What Not to Learn: Action Elimination with Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Graph embedding methods represent nodes in a continuous vector space, preserving different types of relational information from the graph. There are many hyper-parameters to these methods (e.g. the length of a random walk) which have to be manually tuned for every graph. In this paper, we replace previously fixed hyper-parameters with trainable ones that we automatically learn via backpropagation. In particular, we propose a novel attention model on the power series of the transition matrix, which guides the random walk to optimize an upstream objective. Unlike previous approaches to attention models, the method that we propose utilizes attention parameters exclusively on the data itself (e.g. on the random walk), and are not used by the model for inference. We experiment on link prediction tasks, as we aim to produce embeddings that best-preserve the graph structure, generalizing to unseen information. We improve state-of-the-art results on a comprehensive suite of real-world graph datasets including social, collaboration, and biological networks, where we observe that our graph attention model can reduce the error by up to 20\%-40\%. We show that our automatically-learned attention parameters can vary significantly per graph, and correspond to the optimal choice of hyper-parameter if we manually tune existing methods.

Their quality often depends on manually chosen settings, such as random-walk length, that need adjustment for each graph. This paper replaces previously fixed choices with parameters learned through backpropagation, allowing the graph representation’s construction to adapt to the task.

The method places attention over the power series of the graph’s transition matrix, guiding the random walk toward the training objective. Its attention parameters act on the data-generation process used to learn embeddings and are not needed during inference. This makes attention a way to learn which graph relationships training should emphasize.

On link-prediction tasks across social, collaboration, and biological networks, the method improves on state-of-the-art results, with reported error reductions reaching 20–40%. Learned attention differs substantially between graphs and corresponds to optimal hyperparameter choices found by manual tuning of existing methods. The findings support adapting the walk-based training information to each graph instead of expecting one fixed configuration to preserve all graph structures equally well.
summary.tldr: Learning attention over random-walk structure improves node embeddings while removing some manual graph-specific tuning.

title: Watch Your Step: Learning Node Embeddings via Graph Attention

abstract: We address the problem of finding reliable dense correspondences between a pair of images. This is a challenging task due to strong appearance differences between the corresponding scene elements and ambiguities generated by repetitive patterns. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, inspired by the classic idea of disambiguating feature matches using semi-local constraints, we develop an end-to-end trainable convolutional neural network architecture that identifies sets of spatially consistent matches by analyzing neighbourhood consensus patterns in the 4D space of all possible correspondences between a pair of images without the need for a global geometric model. Second, we demonstrate that the model can be trained effectively from weak supervision in the form of matching and non-matching image pairs without the need for costly manual annotation of point to point correspondences. Third, we show the proposed neighbourhood consensus network can be applied to a range of matching tasks including both category- and instance-level matching, obtaining the state-of-the-art results on the PF Pascal dataset and the InLoc indoor visual localization benchmark.

paragraphs: Finding dense correspondences means identifying which locations in two images depict matching content. Appearance changes and repeated patterns make individual matches ambiguous. The paper uses agreement among nearby candidate matches to identify spatially consistent sets, building on the idea that neighboring correspondences can help resolve uncertainty.

Its trainable convolutional architecture analyzes neighborhood-consensus patterns in the four-dimensional space of all possible correspondences between two images. This space records a location in each image for every candidate match. The method searches for local patterns of agreement without requiring a global geometric model to describe the relationship between the images.

The authors show that the network can learn effectively from image pairs labeled as matching or nonmatching. This avoids requiring manual annotations of individual point correspondences. They apply the approach to both category-level and instance-level matching, reporting state-of-the-art results on PF Pascal and the InLoc indoor localization benchmark. Together, the findings support learning spatial consistency from relatively weak supervision and using it across multiple image-matching tasks.
summary.tldr: Neighbourhood consensus networks learn spatially consistent image matches from image-pair supervision without requiring a global geometric model.

title: Neighbourhood Consensus Networks

abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have enabled prosthetic device control by decoding motor movements from neural activities. Neural signals recorded from cortex exhibit nonstationary property due to abrupt noises and neuroplastic changes in brain activities during motor control. Current state-of-the-art neural signal decoders such as Kalman filter assume fixed relationship between neural activities and motor movements, thus will fail if this assumption is not satisfied. We propose a dynamic ensemble modeling (DyEnsemble) approach that is capable of adapting to changes in neural signals by employing a proper combination of decoding functions. The DyEnsemble method firstly learns a set of diverse candidate models. Then, it dynamically selects and combines these models online according to Bayesian updating mechanism. Our method can mitigate the effect of noises and cope with different task behaviors by automatic model switching, thus gives more accurate predictions. Experiments with neural data demonstrate that the DyEnsemble method outperforms Kalman filters remarkably, and its advantage is more obvious with noisy signals.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces infer intended movements from neural activity, but the relationship between those signals and movement can change. Abrupt noise and changes in brain activity during motor control make the signals nonstationary. The paper addresses the resulting difficulty for decoders, such as the Kalman filters described in the abstract, that assume a fixed relationship.

The proposed DyEnsemble method first learns a diverse collection of candidate decoding models. During operation, it uses Bayesian updating to select and combine those models dynamically. This gives the decoder a way to change which functions it relies on as incoming neural evidence changes, rather than depending on a single fixed decoding relationship.

Automatic model switching is intended to reduce the effects of noise and accommodate different task behaviors. Experiments with neural data show substantially better predictions than Kalman filters, with a more pronounced advantage when signals are noisy. These findings support adapting the combination of decoders online as a practical response to changing neural signals in the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: DyEnsemble adapts neural movement decoding through Bayesian selection and combination of candidate models, improving predictions especially with noisy signals.

title: Dynamic Ensemble Modeling Approach to Nonstationary Neural Decoding in Brain-Computer Interfaces

abstract: Learning representations with diversified information remains as an open problem. Towards learning diversified representations, a new approach, termed Information Competing Process (ICP), is proposed in this paper. Aiming to enrich the information carried by feature representations, ICP separates a representation into two parts with different mutual information constraints. The separated parts are forced to accomplish the downstream task independently in a competitive environment which prevents the two parts from learning what each other learned for the downstream task. Such competing parts are then combined synergistically to complete the task. By fusing representation parts learned competitively under different conditions, ICP facilitates obtaining diversified representations which contain rich information. Experiments on image classification and image reconstruction tasks demonstrate the great potential of ICP to learn discriminative and disentangled representations in both supervised and self-supervised learning settings.

paragraphs: A learned representation can devote multiple parts to overlapping information, leaving other useful information underrepresented. This paper proposes Information Competing Process, or ICP, to encourage richer representations. Its central idea is to make separate parts develop useful information under different constraints before combining them for the final task.

ICP divides a representation into two parts and applies different mutual information constraints to them. Each part must independently accomplish the downstream task in a competitive setting designed to prevent it from learning the same task information as the other. The parts are then brought together so their different contributions can support the task jointly.

The authors evaluate this approach on image classification and image reconstruction in supervised and self-supervised settings. The experiments demonstrate potential for learning representations that both distinguish relevant categories and separate underlying information. The findings support competition followed by combination as a useful strategy for representation diversity, rather than establishing a universal guarantee that the learned parts will be fully disentangled.
summary.tldr: ICP trains competing parts of a representation under different information constraints, then combines them to capture more diverse task-relevant information.

title: Information Competing Process for Learning Diversified Representations

abstract: Estimating graphical model structure from high-dimensional and undersampled data is a fundamental problem in many scientific fields. Existing approaches, such as GLASSO, latent variable GLASSO, and latent tree models, suffer from high computational complexity and may impose unrealistic sparsity priors in some cases. We introduce a novel method that leverages a newly discovered connection between information-theoretic measures and structured latent factor models to derive an optimization objective which encourages modular structures where each observed variable has a single latent parent. The proposed method has linear stepwise computational complexity w.r.t. the number of observed variables. Our experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that our approach is the only method that recovers modular structure better as the dimensionality increases. We also use our approach for estimating covariance structure for a number of real-world datasets and show that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art estimators at a fraction of the computational cost. Finally, we apply the proposed method to high-resolution fMRI data (with more than 10^5 voxels) and show that it is capable of extracting meaningful patterns.

paragraphs: Recovering relationships among many variables is difficult when observations are scarce. The paper targets graphical structure learning in this setting, where existing methods can be computationally expensive and may impose unsuitable sparsity assumptions. It proposes a different structural preference: modules in which each observed variable has a single latent parent.

The method derives its optimization objective from a connection between information-theoretic measures and structured latent factor models. The objective encourages this modular organization, and each optimization step has computational cost linear in the number of observed variables. This makes the proposed approach relevant to settings where the number of variables itself is a major computational obstacle.

In synthetic experiments, the method is the only evaluated approach whose modular structure recovery improves as dimensionality increases. On real-world covariance estimation datasets, it consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art estimators at substantially lower computational cost. An application to high-resolution fMRI data with more than 100,000 voxels also extracts meaningful patterns, demonstrating the method's use at a large observational scale.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic objective encourages modular latent structure, enabling linear-cost optimization steps and strong empirical covariance estimation performance.

title: Fast structure learning with modular regularization

abstract: This paper presents a new mechanism for producing sanitized statistical summaries that achieve {\it differential privacy}, called the {\it K-Norm Gradient} Mechanism, or KNG. This new approach maintains the strong flexibility of the exponential mechanism, while achieving the powerful utility performance of objective perturbation. KNG starts with an inherent objective function (often an empirical risk), and promotes summaries that are close to minimizing the objective by weighting according to how far the gradient of the objective function is from zero. Working with the gradient instead of the original objective function allows for additional flexibility as one can penalize using different norms. We show that, unlike the exponential mechanism, the noise added by KNG is asymptotically negligible compared to the statistical error for many problems. In addition to theoretical guarantees on privacy and utility, we confirm the utility of KNG empirically in the settings of linear and quantile regression through simulations.

In addition to theoretical guarantees on privacy and utility, we confirm the utility of KNG empirically in the settings of linear and quantile regression through simulations.

paragraphs: Producing a differentially private statistical summary requires balancing protection of individual data with the usefulness of the result. This paper introduces the K-Norm Gradient mechanism, or KNG, for doing so through an objective function such as empirical risk. It seeks the flexibility of the exponential mechanism together with the utility performance associated with objective perturbation.

KNG weights candidate summaries according to how close the objective's gradient is to zero. This promotes summaries near an objective minimum through gradient information rather than through the objective value itself. Working with gradients also allows different norms to express the penalty, providing flexibility in how candidate summaries are assessed.

The authors prove privacy and utility guarantees and show that, for many problems, KNG's added noise becomes asymptotically negligible relative to statistical error. This compares the privacy contribution to the error already present in estimation as the sample grows. It is a qualified result for many problems, not a claim of zero privacy cost at finite sample sizes. Simulations in linear and quantile regression provide empirical support for the mechanism's utility.
summary.tldr: KNG uses gradient-based weighting to produce private statistical summaries whose privacy noise is asymptotically negligible relative to statistical error for many problems.

title: KNG: The K-Norm Gradient Mechanism

abstract: Explanations of time series models are useful for high stakes applications like healthcare but have received little attention in machine learning literature. We propose FIT, a framework that evaluates the importance of observations for a multivariate time-series black-box model by quantifying the shift in the predictive distribution over time. FIT defines the importance of an observation based on its contribution to the distributional shift under a KL-divergence that contrasts the predictive distribution against a counterfactual where the rest of the features are unobserved. We also demonstrate the need to control for time-dependent distribution shifts. We compare with state-of-the-art baselines on simulated and real-world clinical data and demonstrate that our approach is superior in identifying important time points and observations throughout the time series.

paragraphs: A time-series explanation needs to identify both which observations matter and when they matter. This paper introduces FIT, a framework for explaining individual predictions from black-box models of multivariate time series. It focuses on how observations contribute to changes in the model's predictive distribution as the sequence unfolds.

FIT measures an observation's importance through its contribution to a distributional shift. Its definition uses KL-divergence to compare the predictive distribution with a counterfactual in which the remaining features are unobserved. This ties importance to a specific contrast about the information available to the model, giving the explanation a way to distinguish contributions from different observations over time.

The authors also demonstrate the need to control for distribution shifts that depend on time, which matters when interpreting changes in predictions across a sequence. Comparisons on simulated data and real clinical data show that FIT identifies important observations and time points better than the tested state-of-the-art baselines. The reported findings support an explanation framework that treats temporal change as an essential part of feature importance.
summary.tldr: FIT explains time-series predictions by measuring how individual observations contribute to changes in predictive distributions over time.

title: What went wrong and when? Instance-wise feature importance for time-series black-box models

abstract: We study the problem of switching-constrained online convex optimization (OCO), where the player has a limited number of opportunities to change her action. While the discrete analog of this online learning task has been studied extensively, previous work in the continuous setting has neither established the minimax rate nor algorithmically achieved it. In this paper, we show that $ T $-round switching-constrained OCO with fewer than $ K $ switches has a minimax regret of $ \Theta(\frac{T}{\sqrt{K}}) $. In particular, it is at least $ \frac{T}{\sqrt{2K}} $ for one dimension and at least $ \frac{T}{\sqrt{K}} $ for higher dimensions. The lower bound in higher dimensions is attained by an orthogonal subspace argument. In one dimension, a novel adversarial strategy yields the lower bound of $O(\frac{T}{\sqrt{K}})$, but a precise minimax analysis including constants is more involved. To establish the tighter one-dimensional result, we introduce the \emph{fugal game} relaxation, whose minimax regret lower bounds that of switching-constrained OCO. We show that the minimax regret of the fugal game is at least $ \frac{T}{\sqrt{2K}} $ and thereby establish the optimal minimax lower bound in one dimension. To establish the dimension-independent upper bound, we next show that a mini-batching algorithm provides an $ O(\frac{T}{\sqrt{K}}) $ upper bound, and therefore conclude that the minimax regret of switching-constrained OCO is $ \Theta(\frac{T}{\sqrt{K}}) $ for any $K$. This is in sharp contrast to its discrete counterpart, the switching-constrained prediction-from-experts problem, which exhibits a phase transition in minimax regret between the low-switching and high-switching regimes.

The distinction shows that the continuous action setting has a different switching-performance relationship.
summary.tldr: Switching-constrained online convex optimization has minimax regret Θ(T/√K), with a matching mini-batching algorithm and no discrete-style phase transition.

title: Minimax Regret of Switching-Constrained Online Convex Optimization: No Phase Transition

abstract: Making an adaptive prediction based on input is an important ability for general artificial intelligence. In this work, we step forward in this direction and propose a semi-parametric method, Meta-Neighborhoods, where predictions are made adaptively to the neighborhood of the input. We show that Meta-Neighborhoods is a generalization of k-nearest-neighbors. Due to the simpler manifold structure around a local neighborhood, Meta-Neighborhoods represent the predictive distribution p(y | x) more accurately. To reduce memory and computation overheads, we propose induced neighborhoods that summarize the training data into a much smaller dictionary. A meta-learning based training mechanism is then exploited to jointly learn the induced neighborhoods and the model. Extensive studies demonstrate the superiority of our method.

paragraphs: A prediction can depend on the local context surrounding an input, rather than applying the same predictive behavior everywhere. Meta-Neighborhoods develops this idea through a semi-parametric method that adapts predictions to an input's neighborhood. The authors show that the method generalizes k-nearest-neighbors, connecting a familiar local prediction approach to a learned adaptive model.

The motivation is that the structure of the data manifold is simpler within a local neighborhood. Working with this simpler local structure lets the method represent the conditional predictive distribution more accurately. The neighborhood therefore contributes to how a prediction is formed, making local information part of the model's adaptation to each input.

To reduce the memory and computation associated with retaining neighborhood data, the authors introduce induced neighborhoods summarized in a much smaller dictionary. A meta-learning procedure trains this dictionary and the predictive model jointly. The reported studies support the method's superiority, linking adaptive local prediction with a compact learned representation of the training data.
summary.tldr: Meta-Neighborhoods generalizes nearest-neighbor prediction with jointly learned local adaptation and a compact dictionary of induced neighborhoods.

title: Meta-Neighborhoods

abstract: To improve the sample efficiency of policy-gradient based reinforcement learning algorithms, we propose implicit distributional actor-critic (IDAC) that consists of a distributional critic, built on two deep generator networks (DGNs), and a semi-implicit actor (SIA), powered by a flexible policy distribution. We adopt a distributional perspective on the discounted cumulative return and model it with a state-action-dependent implicit distribution, which is approximated by the DGNs that take state-action pairs and random noises as their input. Moreover, we use the SIA to provide a semi-implicit policy distribution, which mixes the policy parameters with a reparameterizable distribution that is not constrained by an analytic density function. In this way, the policy's marginal distribution is implicit, providing the potential to model complex properties such as covariance structure and skewness, but its parameter and entropy can still be estimated. We incorporate these features with an off-policy algorithm framework to solve problems with continuous action space and compare IDAC with state-of-the-art algorithms on representative OpenAI Gym environments. We observe that IDAC outperforms these baselines in most tasks. Python code is provided.

paragraphs: Implicit distributional actor-critic, or IDAC, aims to improve the sample efficiency of policy-gradient reinforcement learning. It combines a critic that models a distribution of discounted returns with an actor that uses a flexible policy distribution. The resulting method operates within an off-policy framework for continuous-action problems.

The critic uses two deep generator networks that receive a state-action pair and random noise. Their outputs approximate a return distribution conditioned on that pair, allowing the critic to represent more than an expected return. The actor mixes policy parameters using a reparameterizable distribution that does not require an analytic density function.

This construction makes the actor's marginal policy implicit while still allowing its parameters and entropy to be estimated. It potentially captures complex covariance and skewness in the policy distribution. On representative OpenAI Gym environments, the authors report that IDAC outperforms leading comparison algorithms on most tasks. The findings support combining flexible return and policy distributions, while the reported advantage remains an empirical result across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: IDAC combines an implicit return-distribution critic with a flexible semi-implicit actor and outperforms comparison methods on most evaluated continuous-control tasks.

title: Implicit Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep learning methods for graphs achieve remarkable performance on many tasks. However, despite the proliferation of such methods and their success, recent findings indicate that small, unnoticeable perturbations of graph structure can catastrophically reduce performance of even the strongest and most popular Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Here, we develop GNNGuard, a general defense approach against a variety of training-time attacks that perturb the discrete graph structure. GNNGuard can be straightforwardly incorporated into any GNN. Its core principle is to detect and quantify the relationship between the graph structure and node features, if one exists, and then exploit that relationship to mitigate the negative effects of the attack. GNNGuard learns how to best assign higher weights to edges connecting similar nodes while pruning edges between unrelated nodes. The revised edges then allow the underlying GNN to robustly propagate neural messages in the graph. GNNGuard introduces two novel components, the neighbor importance estimation, and the layer-wise graph memory, and we show empirically that both components are necessary for a successful defense. Across five GNNs, three defense methods, and four datasets, including a challenging human disease graph, experiments show that GNNGuard outperforms existing defense approaches by 15.3% on average. Remarkably, GNNGuard can effectively restore state-of-the-art performance of GNNs in the face of various adversarial attacks, including targeted and non-targeted attacks, and can defend against attacks on heterophily graphs.

paragraphs: Small changes to graph connections can severely damage a graph neural network's performance. GNNGuard addresses attacks that alter graph structure during training. It is designed as a general defense that can be incorporated into a GNN, modifying how information travels along edges when the graph may have been manipulated.

The defense looks for a relationship between node features and graph structure, when such a relationship exists. It learns to give greater weight to edges between similar nodes and prune connections between unrelated nodes. Neighbor importance estimation and memory across layers support these adjustments. The authors find empirically that both components are needed for successful defense in their evaluation.

Across five GNNs, three defense methods, and four datasets, GNNGuard outperforms existing defenses by 15.3% on average. The results include targeted and non-targeted attacks, a human disease graph, and graphs with heterophily. The experiments show that the approach can restore strong GNN performance under attacks by revising the connections used for message propagation.
summary.tldr: GNNGuard reweights and prunes graph edges to defend graph neural networks against training-time structural attacks.

title: GNNGuard: Defending Graph Neural Networks against Adversarial Attacks

abstract: It is a popular belief that model-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) is more sample efficient than model-free RL, but in practice, it is not always true due to overweighed model errors. In complex and noisy settings, model-based RL tends to have trouble using the model if it does not know when to trust the model. In this work, we find that better model usage can make a huge difference. We show theoretically that if the use of model-generated data is restricted to state-action pairs where the model error is small, the performance gap between model and real rollouts can be reduced. It motivates us to use model rollouts only when the model is confident about its predictions. We propose Masked Model-based Actor-Critic (M2AC), a novel policy optimization algorithm that maximizes a model-based lower-bound of the true value function. M2AC implements a masking mechanism based on the model's uncertainty estimation to decide whether the model should be used or not. Consequently, the new algorithm tends to give robust policy improvements. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that M2AC has strong performance even when using long model rollouts in very noisy environments, and significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can supply simulated experience for reinforcement learning, but inaccurate predictions can undermine the benefit. This paper focuses on deciding when model-generated data should be trusted. Its theoretical analysis shows that restricting model use to state-action pairs with small model error can reduce the performance gap between simulated and real rollouts.

Masked Model-based Actor-Critic, or M2AC, turns that motivation into a policy optimization algorithm. It optimizes a model-based lower bound on the true value function and uses estimated model uncertainty to decide where the model should contribute. The masking mechanism is intended to keep learning from relying too heavily on predictions in places where the model lacks confidence.

Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks show strong performance even with long model rollouts in very noisy environments, and substantial improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support selective model use as an important ingredient in robust policy improvement. The theoretical condition concerns small actual model error, while the practical algorithm uses uncertainty estimates to guide its selection.
summary.tldr: M2AC uses uncertainty-based masking to select model-generated experience, improving policy learning in the tested noisy continuous-control environments.

title: Trust the Model When It Is Confident: Masked Model-based Actor-Critic

abstract: Potential-based reward shaping provides an approach for designing good reward functions, with the purpose of speeding up learning. However, automatically finding potential functions for complex environments is a difficult problem (in fact, of the same difficulty as learning a value function from scratch). We propose a new framework for learning potential functions by leveraging ideas from graph representation learning. Our approach relies on Graph Convolutional Networks which we use as a key ingredient in combination with the probabilistic inference view of reinforcement learning. More precisely, we leverage Graph Convolutional Networks to perform message passing from rewarding states. The propagated messages can then be used as potential functions for reward shaping to accelerate learning. We verify empirically that our approach can achieve considerable improvements in both small and high-dimensional control problems.

paragraphs: Reward shaping modifies the learning signal to help a reinforcement-learning agent learn faster. In potential-based shaping, a potential function supplies the information used to construct that signal. Automatically finding a useful potential is difficult: the abstract describes the problem as being as hard as learning a value function from scratch.

This paper proposes learning potentials through graph representation learning. Graph convolutional networks pass messages from rewarding states, combining this propagation process with a probabilistic-inference view of reinforcement learning. The propagated information is then used as a potential function for reward shaping.

The approach connects the availability of reward at particular states with a mechanism for spreading useful information through a graph. Experiments show that it can produce considerable learning improvements in both small and high-dimensional control problems. These results support graph-based propagation as a practical way to construct shaping potentials in the evaluated environments, addressing a component that would otherwise be difficult to design automatically.
summary.tldr: Graph convolutional networks propagate information from rewarding states to learn potential functions that can accelerate reinforcement learning.

title: Reward Propagation Using Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Quantization is an effective method for reducing memory footprint and inference time of Neural Networks. However, ultra low precision quantization could lead to significant degradation in model accuracy. A promising method to address this is to perform mixed-precision quantization, where more sensitive layers are kept at higher precision. However, the search space for a mixed-precision quantization is exponential in the number of layers. Recent work has proposed a novel Hessian based framework, with the aim of reducing this exponential search space by using second-order information. While promising, this prior work has three major limitations: (i) they only use a heuristic metric based on top Hessian eigenvalue as a measure of sensitivity and do not consider the rest of the Hessian spectrum; (ii) their approach only provides relative sensitivity of different layers and therefore requires a manual selection of the mixed-precision setting; and (iii) they do not consider mixed-precision activation quantization. Here, we present HAWQ-V2 which addresses these shortcomings. For (i), we theoretically prove that the right sensitivity metric is the average Hessian trace, instead of just top Hessian eigenvalue. For (ii), we develop a Pareto frontier based method for automatic bit precision selection of different layers without any manual intervention. For (iii), we develop the first Hessian based analysis for mixed-precision activation quantization, which is very beneficial for object detection. We show that HAWQ-V2 achieves new state-of-the-art results for a wide range of tasks. In particular, we present quantization results for InceptionV3, ResNet50, and SqueezeNext, all without any manual bit selection. Furthermore, we present results for object detection on Microsoft COCO, where we achieve 2.6 higher mAP than direct uniform quantization and 1.6 higher mAP than the recently proposed method of FQN, with a smaller model size of 17.9MB.

title: HAWQ-V2: Hessian Aware trace-Weighted Quantization of Neural Networks

abstract: When machine learning systems meet real world applications, accuracy is only one of several requirements. In this paper, we assay a complementary perspective originating from the increasing availability of pre-trained and regularly improving state-of-the-art models. While new improved models develop at a fast pace, downstream tasks vary more slowly or stay constant. Assume that we have a large unlabelled data set for which we want to maintain accurate predictions. Whenever a new and presumably better ML models becomes available, we encounter two problems: (i) given a limited budget, which data points should be re-evaluated using the new model?; and (ii) if the new predictions differ from the current ones, should we update? Problem (i) is about compute cost, which matters for very large data sets and models. Problem (ii) is about maintaining consistency of the predictions, which can be highly relevant for downstream applications; our demand is to avoid negative flips, i.e., changing correct to incorrect predictions. In this paper, we formalize the Prediction Update Problem and present an efficient probabilistic approach as answer to the above questions. In extensive experiments on standard classification benchmark data sets, we show that our method outperforms alternative strategies along key metrics for backward-compatible prediction updates.

paragraphs: A newer model can be more accurate overall while still making mistakes on examples that an older model handled correctly. This paper studies how to maintain predictions for a large unlabeled dataset as improved models become available. Its setting includes a limited computation budget and downstream applications that benefit from consistent predictions.

The authors formalize two linked decisions. First, which examples should be evaluated again using the new model? Second, when the new prediction disagrees with the stored prediction, should it replace it? The first decision allocates computation; the second addresses backward compatibility, especially the desire to avoid negative flips from correct predictions to incorrect ones.

The paper proposes an efficient probabilistic approach to both decisions. Experiments on standard classification benchmarks show better performance than alternative strategies on key measures of backward-compatible updates. The contribution treats updating a prediction collection as its own decision problem: adopting a newer model involves choosing where to spend computation and when its changed answers warrant replacing existing ones.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic update strategy decides which examples to reevaluate and when to replace predictions, balancing computation with the goal of avoiding harmful changes.

title: Backward-Compatible Prediction Updates: A Probabilistic Approach

abstract: Private data analysis suffers a costly curse of dimensionality. However, the data often has an underlying low-dimensional structure. For example, when optimizing via gradient descent, the gradients often lie in or near a low-dimensional subspace. If that low-dimensional structure can be identified, then we can avoid paying (in terms of privacy or accuracy) for the high ambient dimension. We present differentially private algorithms that take input data sampled from a low-dimensional linear subspace (possibly with a small amount of error) and output that subspace (or an approximation to it). These algorithms can serve as a pre-processing step for other procedures.

paragraphs: Private data analysis can become costly when data have many coordinates, even when their underlying variation occupies far fewer dimensions. This paper studies how to identify that smaller linear space while preserving differential privacy. The motivating distinction is between the dimension of the surrounding representation and the dimension of the structure actually present in the data.

The authors present algorithms for data sampled from a low-dimensional linear subspace, allowing a small amount of error in the input. The algorithms return the subspace itself or an approximation. Their task is therefore to recover useful geometric structure privately, including the case where observations lie only approximately within that structure.

The abstract highlights gradients in optimization as one setting where such low-dimensional structure can arise. Identifying it can avoid privacy or accuracy costs tied to the full ambient dimension. The proposed algorithms can serve as preprocessing for other procedures, making private structural recovery a preliminary step toward analysis that takes advantage of the data's lower-dimensional organization.
summary.tldr: Differentially private algorithms recover exact or approximate low-dimensional subspaces to help subsequent analysis avoid costs tied to ambient dimension.

title: Privately Learning Subspaces

abstract: With the explosive growth of information technology, multi-view graph data have become increasingly prevalent and valuable. Most existing multi-view clustering techniques either focus on the scenario of multiple graphs or multi-view attributes. In this paper, we propose a generic framework to cluster multi-view attributed graph data. Specifically, inspired by the success of contrastive learning, we propose multi-view contrastive graph clustering (MCGC) method to learn a consensus graph since the original graph could be noisy or incomplete and is not directly applicable. Our method composes of two key steps: we first filter out the undesirable high-frequency noise while preserving the graph geometric features via graph filtering and obtain a smooth representation of nodes; we then learn a consensus graph regularized by graph contrastive loss. Results on several benchmark datasets show the superiority of our method with respect to state-of-the-art approaches. In particular, our simple approach outperforms existing deep learning-based methods.

This paper proposes a general framework for multi-view attributed graphs, with particular attention to the fact that an original graph may be noisy or incomplete.

The method, MCGC, first filters the graph information to suppress unwanted high-frequency noise while preserving geometric features. This produces smoother node representations. It then learns a consensus graph using a graph-contrastive loss as a regularizer. The learned graph brings the views together and supplies structure for clustering when the original graph is not directly suitable.

Results on several benchmark datasets show improvements over compared state-of-the-art approaches, including existing deep-learning methods. These findings support the combination of graph filtering and contrastive consensus learning in the evaluated tasks. The paper’s contribution is a relatively simple two-step route from imperfect, multi-view input to a graph representation that better supports clustering.
summary.tldr: MCGC combines graph filtering with contrastive consensus-graph learning to improve clustering of multi-view attributed graphs.

title: Multi-view Contrastive Graph Clustering

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely applied to various fields for learning over graph-structured data. They have shown significant improvements over traditional heuristic methods in various tasks such as node classification and graph classification. However, since GNNs heavily rely on smoothed node features rather than graph structure, they often show poor performance than simple heuristic methods in link prediction where the structural information, e.g., overlapped neighborhoods, degrees, and shortest paths, is crucial. To address this limitation, we propose Neighborhood Overlap-aware Graph Neural Networks (Neo-GNNs) that learn useful structural features from an adjacency matrix and estimate overlapped neighborhoods for link prediction. Our Neo-GNNs generalize neighborhood overlap-based heuristic methods and handle overlapped multi-hop neighborhoods. Our extensive experiments on Open Graph Benchmark datasets (OGB) demonstrate that Neo-GNNs consistently achieve state-of-the-art performance in link prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting whether two graph nodes should be connected often depends on graph structure, such as shared neighbors, node degrees, and distances. The paper observes that graph neural networks can underperform simple structural heuristics on this task because they rely heavily on smoothed node features. Success on node or graph classification does not automatically resolve that mismatch.

Neo-GNNs address it by learning structural features directly from the adjacency matrix, which records the graph's connections. They estimate overlap between neighborhoods and extend the idea to neighborhoods spanning multiple hops. The architecture also generalizes heuristic methods based on neighborhood overlap, incorporating that useful structural principle into a learned model.

Across the evaluated Open Graph Benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently state-of-the-art link prediction performance. These findings support explicitly representing structural relationships between candidate endpoints. The contribution is particularly relevant to link prediction, where whether two neighborhoods overlap can provide information that feature smoothing alone does not adequately capture.
summary.tldr: Neo-GNNs learn neighborhood-overlap structure for link prediction and achieve consistently state-of-the-art results on the evaluated OGB datasets.

title: Neo-GNNs: Neighborhood Overlap-aware Graph Neural Networks for Link Prediction

abstract: We present a novel generative modeling method called diffusion normalizing flow based on stochastic differential equations (SDEs). The algorithm consists of two neural SDEs: a forward SDE that gradually adds noise to the data to transform the data into Gaussian random noise, and a backward SDE that gradually removes the noise to sample from the data distribution. By jointly training the two neural SDEs to minimize a common cost function that quantifies the difference between the two, the backward SDE converges to a diffusion process the starts with a Gaussian distribution and ends with the desired data distribution. Our method is closely related to normalizing flow and diffusion probabilistic models, and can be viewed as a combination of the two. Compared with normalizing flow, diffusion normalizing flow is able to learn distributions with sharp boundaries. Compared with diffusion probabilistic models, diffusion normalizing flow requires fewer discretization steps and thus has better sampling efficiency. Our algorithm demonstrates competitive performance in both high-dimension data density estimation and image generation tasks.

paragraphs: Diffusion normalizing flow generates data by learning a relationship between the data distribution and Gaussian noise. It uses two neural stochastic differential equations, which describe transformations that include randomness. One gradually adds noise to data; the other gradually removes noise to produce samples.

The two directions are trained jointly using a shared cost that measures their difference. Through this training, the backward process converges to a diffusion that begins with a Gaussian distribution and ends with the desired data distribution. The forward transformation and the generative transformation are therefore learned together as parts of one objective.

The approach combines ideas from normalizing flows and diffusion probabilistic models. The authors report that it can learn distributions with sharp boundaries, an advantage over normalizing flow, and requires fewer discretization steps than diffusion probabilistic models, improving sampling efficiency. It also achieves competitive results in high-dimensional density estimation and image generation. These findings connect the method's distribution-modeling capabilities with the computational work needed to draw samples.
summary.tldr: Diffusion normalizing flow jointly learns noise-adding and noise-removing stochastic processes to combine flexible density modeling with more efficient sampling.

title: Diffusion Normalizing Flow

abstract: Methods for Visual Question Anwering (VQA) are notorious for leveraging dataset biases rather than performing reasoning, hindering generalization. It has been recently shown that better reasoning patterns emerge in attention layers of a state-of-the-art VQA model when they are trained on perfect (oracle) visual inputs. This provides evidence that deep neural networks can learn to reason when training conditions are favorable enough. However, transferring this learned knowledge to deployable models is a challenge, as much of it is lost during the transfer.We propose a method for knowledge transfer based on a regularization term in our loss function, supervising the sequence of required reasoning operations.We provide a theoretical analysis based on PAC-learning, showing that such program prediction can lead to decreased sample complexity under mild hypotheses. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach experimentally on the GQA dataset and show its complementarity to BERT-like self-supervised pre-training.

paragraphs: Visual question answering models can exploit dataset biases instead of learning the reasoning needed to answer questions about images. Prior observations described in the paper show that better reasoning patterns emerge when a strong model receives perfect visual inputs. The challenge is preserving that learned reasoning when transferring it to a deployable model.

The authors propose a transfer method that adds a regularization term to the training loss. This term supervises the sequence of reasoning operations required for the task, giving the receiving model guidance about the reasoning process. The approach targets the loss of useful reasoning knowledge that can occur during transfer from favorable training conditions.

A theoretical analysis using PAC-learning shows that predicting these reasoning programs can reduce sample complexity under mild hypotheses. The claim is conditional: the analysis identifies a potential data-efficiency benefit under its assumptions. Experiments on GQA demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and show that it complements BERT-like self-supervised pre-training. Together, these findings support explicit reasoning supervision as an additional source of useful learning signal during knowledge transfer.
summary.tldr: Supervising reasoning-operation sequences improves knowledge transfer in visual question answering and can reduce sample complexity under the paper’s hypotheses.

title: Supervising the Transfer of Reasoning Patterns in VQA

abstract: Multilingual Spoken Words Corpus is a large and growing audio dataset of spoken words in 50 languages collectively spoken by over 5 billion people, for academic research and commercial applications in keyword spotting and spoken term search, licensed under CC-BY 4.0. The dataset contains more than 340,000 keywords, totaling 23.4 million 1-second spoken examples (over 6,000 hours). The dataset has many use cases, ranging from voice-enabled consumer devices to call center automation. We generate this dataset by applying forced alignment on crowd-sourced sentence-level audio to produce per-word timing estimates for extraction. All alignments are included in the dataset. We provide a detailed analysis of the contents of the data and contribute methods for detecting potential outliers. We report baseline accuracy metrics on keyword spotting models trained from our dataset compared to models trained on a manually-recorded keyword dataset. We conclude with our plans for dataset maintenance, updates, and open-sourced code.

It contains over 340,000 keywords and 23.4 million one-second examples, totaling more than 6,000 hours. The resource supports both academic research and commercial applications under a CC-BY 4.0 license.

The authors build the collection from crowdsourced recordings of complete sentences. They apply forced alignment to estimate where individual words occur, then extract word-level audio using those timing estimates. Including all alignments makes the timing information part of the released dataset, alongside the extracted examples.

The paper analyzes the collection and introduces methods for identifying potential outliers. It also reports keyword-spotting baseline accuracies and compares models trained on this corpus with models trained on manually recorded keywords. These comparisons help assess the resulting training resource. The contribution combines multilingual scale with a documented construction process and plans for maintenance, updates, and open-source code.
summary.tldr: This corpus extracts 23.4 million spoken-word examples in 50 languages from crowdsourced sentence recordings for keyword and speech-search research.

title: Multilingual Spoken Words Corpus

abstract: Much recent work has been devoted to the problem of ensuring that a neural network's confidence scores match the true probability of being correct, i.e. the calibration problem. Of note, it was found that training with focal loss leads to better calibration than cross-entropy while achieving similar level of accuracy \cite{mukhoti2020}. This success stems from focal loss regularizing the entropy of the model's prediction (controlled by the parameter $\gamma$), thereby reining in the model's overconfidence. Further improvement is expected if $\gamma$ is selected independently for each training sample (Sample-Dependent Focal Loss (FLSD-53) \cite{mukhoti2020}). However, FLSD-53 is based on heuristics and does not generalize well. In this paper, we propose a calibration-aware adaptive focal loss called AdaFocal that utilizes the calibration properties of focal (and inverse-focal) loss and adaptively modifies $\gamma_t$ for different groups of samples based on $\gamma_{t-1}$ from the previous step and the knowledge of model's under/over-confidence on the validation set. We evaluate AdaFocal on various image recognition and one NLP task, covering a wide variety of network architectures, to confirm the improvement in calibration while achieving similar levels of accuracy. Additionally, we show that models trained with AdaFocal achieve a significant boost in out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict the right label while giving misleading confidence scores. Calibration asks whether those scores reflect how often predictions are correct. This paper develops AdaFocal, a training loss that adjusts its behavior using evidence about whether the model is too confident or insufficiently confident.

The approach builds on focal loss, whose parameter gamma controls an effect that can reduce overconfidence. Earlier sample-dependent choices relied on heuristics. AdaFocal instead updates gamma for different groups of samples using both its previous value and calibration information from a validation set. It draws on the calibration behavior of focal and inverse-focal losses, allowing the adjustment to respond to the direction of the confidence error.

Across image recognition tasks and one language task, covering multiple network architectures, the authors report improved calibration with similar accuracy. They also report substantially better detection of inputs from outside the training distribution. These findings suggest that adapting the loss to observed confidence errors can improve the usefulness of uncertainty estimates alongside ordinary classification performance.
summary.tldr: AdaFocal adjusts focal-loss parameters using validation-set confidence errors, improving calibration and out-of-distribution detection in the reported experiments.

title: AdaFocal: Calibration-aware Adaptive Focal Loss

abstract: Having similar behavior at training time and test time—what we call a “What You See Is What You Get” (WYSIWYG) property—is desirable in machine learning. Models trained with standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD), however, do not necessarily have this property, as their complex behaviors such as robustness or subgroup performance can differ drastically between training and test time. In contrast, we show that Differentially-Private (DP) training provably ensures the high-level WYSIWYG property, which we quantify using a notion of distributional generalization. Applying this connection, we introduce new conceptual tools for designing deep-learning methods by reducing generalization concerns to optimization ones: to mitigate unwanted behavior at test time, it is provably sufficient to mitigate this behavior on the training data. By applying this novel design principle, which bypasses “pathologies” of SGD, we construct simple algorithms that are competitive with SOTA in several distributional-robustness applications, significantly improve the privacy vs. disparate impact trade-off of DP-SGD, and mitigate robust overfitting in adversarial training. Finally, we also improve on theoretical bounds relating DP, stability, and distributional generalization.

paragraphs: A model's behavior on training data may differ sharply from its behavior on unseen data, including in robustness and subgroup performance. This paper formalizes the desirable correspondence between those behaviors through distributional generalization. The authors call it a What You See Is What You Get property and show that differentially private training provably provides it.

The connection gives a design principle: within the established framework, mitigating unwanted behavior on training data is sufficient to mitigate it at test time. This turns a generalization concern into an optimization problem. The principle is a sufficiency result tied to the paper's differential-privacy connection, rather than a claim that arbitrary training procedures transfer every observed behavior.

Using this principle, the authors construct simple methods competitive with leading approaches in several distributional-robustness applications. They also improve the privacy-versus-disparate-impact trade-off of DP-SGD and reduce robust overfitting in adversarial training. Additional theoretical results tighten relationships among differential privacy, stability, and distributional generalization, supporting both the conceptual framework and its applications.
summary.tldr: Differentially private training provides a distributional-generalization principle for translating improvements in training behavior into improvements at test time.

title: What You See is What You Get: Principled Deep Learning via Distributional Generalization

abstract: Estimation and inference on causal parameters is typically reduced to a generalized method of moments problem, which involves auxiliary functions that correspond to solutions to a regression or classification problem. Recent line of work on debiased machine learning shows how one can use generic machine learning estimators for these auxiliary problems, while maintaining asymptotic normality and root-$n$ consistency of the target parameter of interest, while only requiring mean-squared-error guarantees from the auxiliary estimation algorithms. The literature typically requires that these auxiliary problems are fitted on a separate sample or in a cross-fitting manner. We show that when these auxiliary estimation algorithms satisfy natural leave-one-out stability properties, then sample splitting is not required. This allows for sample re-use, which can be beneficial in moderately sized sample regimes. For instance, we show that the stability properties that we propose are satisfied for ensemble bagged estimators, built via sub-sampling without replacement, a popular technique in machine learning practice.

paragraphs: Estimating causal parameters often requires first learning auxiliary regression or classification functions. Debiased machine learning makes it possible to use flexible estimators for those functions while retaining useful large-sample guarantees for the target parameter. Standard approaches typically fit the auxiliary functions on separate observations or use cross-fitting to separate the roles of the data.

This paper establishes a condition under which that separation is unnecessary. If the auxiliary learning algorithms satisfy suitable leave-one-out stability properties, the observations can be reused. The stability requirement concerns how the fitted procedure behaves when an individual observation is left out; it supplies the control needed to retain the inference guarantees.

The result preserves asymptotic normality and root-n consistency under the paper's conditions while allowing sample reuse, which can benefit moderately sized datasets. The authors also show that their proposed stability properties hold for bagged ensembles constructed by subsampling without replacement. This gives a concrete family of learning procedures to which the argument applies, rather than removing sample splitting for arbitrary auxiliary estimators.
summary.tldr: Suitable leave-one-out stability allows debiased machine learning to reuse samples while retaining asymptotic inference guarantees.

title: Debiased Machine Learning without Sample-Splitting for Stable Estimators

abstract: Lifelong learners must recognize concept vocabularies that evolve over time. A common yet underexplored scenario is learning with class labels that continually refine/expand old classes. For example, humans learn to recognize ${\tt dog}$ before dog breeds. In practical settings, dataset ${\it versioning}$ often introduces refinement to ontologies, such as autonomous vehicle benchmarks that refine a previous ${\tt vehicle}$ class into ${\tt school-bus}$ as autonomous operations expand to new cities. This paper formalizes a protocol for studying the problem of ${\it Learning with Evolving Class Ontology}$ (LECO). LECO requires learning classifiers in distinct time periods (TPs); each TP introduces a new ontology of "fine" labels that refines old ontologies of "coarse" labels (e.g., dog breeds that refine the previous ${\tt dog}$). LECO explores such questions as whether to annotate new data or relabel the old, how to exploit coarse labels, and whether to finetune the previous TP's model or train from scratch. To answer these questions, we leverage insights from related problems such as class-incremental learning. We validate them under the LECO protocol through the lens of image classification (on CIFAR and iNaturalist) and semantic segmentation (on Mapillary). Extensive experiments lead to some surprising conclusions; while the current status quo in the field is to relabel existing datasets with new class ontologies (such as COCO-to-LVIS or Mapillary1.2-to-2.0), LECO demonstrates that a far better strategy is to annotate ${\it new}$ data with the new ontology. However, this produces an aggregate dataset with inconsistent old-vs-new labels, complicating learning. To address this challenge, we adopt methods from semi-supervised and partial-label learning. We demonstrate that such strategies can surprisingly be made near-optimal, in the sense of approaching an "oracle" that learns on the aggregate dataset exhaustively labeled with the newest ontology.

paragraphs: A classifier's vocabulary can become more detailed over time: an earlier label such as dog may later be divided into individual breeds. This paper formalizes that situation through Learning with Evolving Class Ontology, or LECO. Each time period introduces finer labels that refine the categories available in previous periods.

The protocol examines practical choices about handling these changes. Should developers relabel existing examples or annotate new ones? How should older coarse labels be used? Should the previous model be fine-tuned or replaced by one trained from scratch? The authors investigate these questions through image classification on CIFAR and iNaturalist and semantic segmentation on Mapillary.

Their experiments find that labeling new data with the updated vocabulary is substantially better than relabeling the existing dataset. This leaves a mixture of old coarse labels and new fine labels. Methods adapted from semi-supervised and partial-label learning handle that inconsistency effectively, approaching an oracle trained on the combined data fully relabeled with the newest vocabulary. The result supports expanding annotated data while retaining useful information from older labels.
summary.tldr: When categories become finer, LECO experiments favor labeling new data and learning jointly from old coarse and new fine labels.

title: Continual Learning with Evolving Class Ontologies

abstract: Random reshuffling, which randomly permutes the dataset each epoch, is widely adopted in model training because it yields faster convergence than with-replacement sampling. Recent studies indicate greedily chosen data orderings can further speed up convergence empirically, at the cost of using more computation and memory. However, greedy ordering lacks theoretical justification and has limited utility due to its non-trivial memory and computation overhead. In this paper, we first formulate an example-ordering framework named \emph{herding} and answer affirmatively that SGD with herding converges at the rate $O(T^{-2/3})$ on smooth, non-convex objectives, faster than the $O(n^{1/3}T^{-2/3})$ obtained by random reshuffling, where $n$ denotes the number of data points and $T$ denotes the total number of iterations. To reduce the memory overhead, we leverage discrepancy minimization theory to propose an online Gradient Balancing algorithm (GraB) that enjoys the same rate as herding, while reducing the memory usage from $O(nd)$ to just $O(d)$ and computation from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$, where $d$ denotes the model dimension. We show empirically on applications including MNIST, CIFAR10, WikiText and GLUE that GraB can outperform random reshuffling in terms of both training and validation performance, and even outperform state-of-the-art greedy ordering while reducing memory usage over $100\times$.

paragraphs: The order in which training examples are processed can affect optimization. Random reshuffling selects a new permutation each epoch, while greedy ordering methods can improve convergence empirically but require substantial resources. This paper develops a theoretically justified ordering framework called herding and then makes its benefits more practical through Gradient Balancing, or GraB.

For smooth, non-convex objectives, the authors establish a convergence rate of O(T^(-2/3)) for SGD with herding, compared with O(n^(1/3)T^(-2/3)) for random reshuffling. Here n counts examples and T counts iterations. The improvement removes the displayed dependence on dataset size while retaining the same iteration exponent.

GraB uses discrepancy minimization to achieve the same rate with an online procedure. It reduces memory from O(nd) to O(d), where d is model dimension, and computation from O(n²) to O(n). Experiments across image and language tasks show that GraB can improve training and validation performance over random reshuffling and outperform greedy ordering while using over 100 times less memory.
summary.tldr: GraB balances gradients to choose data orders with a stronger convergence rate than random reshuffling and much lower overhead than greedy ordering.

title: GraB: Finding Provably Better Data Permutations than Random Reshuffling

abstract: Most popular dimension reduction (DR) methods like t-SNE and UMAP are based on minimizing a cost between input and latent pairwise similarities. Though widely used, these approaches lack clear probabilistic foundations to enable a full understanding of their properties and limitations. To that extent, we introduce a unifying statistical framework based on the coupling of hidden graphs using cross entropy. These graphs induce a Markov random field dependency structure among the observations in both input and latent spaces. We show that existing pairwise similarity DR methods can be retrieved from our framework with particular choices of priors for the graphs. Moreover this reveals that these methods relying on shift-invariant kernels suffer from a statistical degeneracy that explains poor performances in conserving coarse-grain dependencies. originalAbstract: Most popular dimension reduction (DR) methods like t-SNE and UMAP are based on minimizing a cost between input and latent pairwise similarities. Though widely used, these approaches lack clear probabilistic foundations to enable a full understanding of their properties and limitations. To that extent, we introduce a unifying statistical framework based on the coupling of hidden graphs using cross entropy. These graphs induce a Markov random field dependency structure among the observations in both input and latent spaces. We show that existing pairwise similarity DR methods can be retrieved from our framework with particular choices of priors for the graphs. Moreover this reveals that these methods relying on shift-invariant kernels suffer from a statistical degeneracy that explains poor performances in conserving coarse-grain dependencies. New links are drawn with PCA which appears as a non-degenerate graph coupling model.

paragraphs: Dimension reduction methods turn complex data into a smaller representation by trying to preserve relationships between observations. Popular methods such as t-SNE and UMAP compare pairwise similarities in the original and reduced spaces. This paper asks what statistical model could explain those objectives and help clarify which relationships they preserve poorly.

The authors introduce a framework built around hidden graphs in both spaces. These graphs describe dependencies among observations through a Markov random field, and cross entropy connects the two graph models. Particular choices of graph priors recover existing methods based on pairwise similarities. This gives several familiar algorithms a common probabilistic interpretation rather than treating their objectives as unrelated constructions.

The framework also exposes a statistical degeneracy in the methods that use shift-invariant kernels. The authors connect this degeneracy to poor preservation of coarse relationships across the data. They additionally show that PCA fits into the framework as a graph coupling model without this degeneracy. The contribution is therefore both a unification of methods and an explanation of a specific weakness in part of that family.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic framework unifies similarity-based dimension reduction and reveals a statistical degeneracy linked to poor preservation of coarse relationships.

title: A Probabilistic Graph Coupling View of Dimension Reduction

abstract: Predictor screening rules, which discard predictors before fitting a model, have had considerable impact on the speed with which sparse regression problems, such as the lasso, can be solved. In this paper we present a new screening rule for solving the lasso path: the Hessian Screening Rule. The rule uses second-order information from the model to provide both effective screening, particularly in the case of high correlation, as well as accurate warm starts. The proposed rule outperforms all alternatives we study on simulated data sets with both low and high correlation for \(\ell_1\)-regularized least-squares (the lasso) and logistic regression. It also performs best in general on the real data sets that we examine.
