This paper introduces the Hessian Screening Rule for computing the lasso path, the sequence of solutions obtained as the strength of regularization changes.

The rule uses second-order information from the model, which describes curvature rather than only the direction of local change. That information supports both effective predictor screening and accurate warm starts for subsequent optimization problems. The authors emphasize screening effectiveness when predictors are highly correlated, a setting where relationships among predictors are particularly relevant to deciding what to retain.

In simulations with both low and high correlation, the proposed rule outperforms every alternative studied for l1-regularized least-squares and logistic regression. It also generally performs best on the real datasets examined. The findings support curvature information as a practical way to accelerate sparse-model fitting across a regularization path, with empirical advantages in both correlated and less-correlated settings.
summary.tldr: The Hessian Screening Rule uses model curvature to discard predictors and improve warm starts when fitting sparse regression paths.

title: The Hessian Screening Rule

abstract: We consider the combinatorial bandits problem with semi-bandit feedback under finite sampling budget constraints, in which the learner can carry out its action only for a limited number of times specified by an overall budget. The action is to choose a set of arms, whereupon feedback for each arm in the chosen set is received. Unlike existing works, we study this problem in a non-stochastic setting with subset-dependent feedback, i.e., the semi-bandit feedback received could be generated by an oblivious adversary and also might depend on the chosen set of arms. In addition, we consider a general feedback scenario covering both the numerical-based as well as preference-based case and introduce a sound theoretical framework for this setting guaranteeing sensible notions of optimal arms, which a learner seeks to find. We suggest a generic algorithm suitable to cover the full spectrum of conceivable arm elimination strategies from aggressive to conservative. Theoretical questions about the sufficient and necessary budget of the algorithm to find the best arm are answered and complemented by deriving lower bounds for any learning algorithm for this problem scenario.

The aim is to identify optimal arms before the budget runs out. Unlike simpler formulations, an arm's feedback may depend on which other arms were selected alongside it.

The setting is also non-stochastic: feedback may be generated by an oblivious adversary rather than by a fixed random reward distribution. The authors build a theoretical framework covering both numerical feedback and preference-based feedback, while ensuring that meaningful notions of optimal arms can still be defined under these broader conditions.

They propose a generic algorithm encompassing elimination strategies ranging from aggressive removal of candidates to more conservative decisions. The analysis establishes sufficient and necessary sampling budgets for the algorithm to find the best arm and derives lower bounds applying to any learning algorithm in this setting. These results clarify how the available budget constrains identification when feedback depends on the selected group.
summary.tldr: The paper develops an arm-elimination framework and budget guarantees for non-stochastic combinatorial bandits with subset-dependent feedback.

title: Finding Optimal Arms in Non-stochastic Combinatorial Bandits with Semi-bandit Feedback and Finite Budget

abstract: We introduce the first direct policy search algorithm which provably converges to the globally optimal dynamic filter for the classical problem of predicting the outputs of a linear dynamical system, given noisy, partial observations. Despite the ubiquity of partial observability in practice, theoretical guarantees for direct policy search algorithms, one of the backbones of modern reinforcement learning, have proven difficult to achieve. This is primarily due to the degeneracies which arise when optimizing over filters that maintain an internal state. In this paper, we provide a new perspective on this challenging problem based on the notion of informativity, which intuitively requires that all components of a filter’s internal state are representative of the true state of the underlying dynamical system. We show that informativity overcomes the aforementioned degeneracy. Specifically, we propose a regularizer which explicitly enforces informativity, and establish that gradient descent on this regularized objective - combined with a “reconditioning step” – converges to the globally optimal cost at a $O(1/T)$ rate.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict the outputs of a linear dynamical system when observations are noisy and incomplete. A dynamic filter maintains an internal state to make those predictions. Directly optimizing such a filter is difficult because its internal-state representation can introduce degeneracies that obstruct convergence guarantees.

The authors address this issue through informativity. Intuitively, every component of the filter's internal state should represent something about the true state of the underlying system. They show that this property overcomes the degeneracy and introduce a regularizer that explicitly enforces it. The regularizer changes the optimization problem so that useful internal representations are maintained.

The proposed algorithm combines gradient descent on the regularized objective with a reconditioning step. For this output-estimation problem, the authors prove convergence to the globally optimal cost at a rate proportional to one over the number of iterations. The result supplies a global guarantee for direct policy search in this partially observed linear setting and identifies internal-state informativity as the mechanism that makes the guarantee possible.
summary.tldr: An informativity regularizer and reconditioning step give direct policy search a global convergence guarantee for filtering partially observed linear systems.

title: Globally Convergent Policy Search for Output Estimation

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) provides a promising direction to exploit massive amount of offline data for complex decision-making tasks. Due to the distribution shift issue, current offline RL algorithms are generally designed to be conservative in value estimation and action selection. However, such conservatism can impair the robustness of learned policies when encountering observation deviation under realistic conditions, such as sensor errors and adversarial attacks. To trade off robustness and conservatism, we propose Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning (RORL) with a novel conservative smoothing technique. In RORL, we explicitly introduce regularization on the policy and the value function for states near the dataset, as well as additional conservative value estimation on these states. Theoretically, we show RORL enjoys a tighter suboptimality bound than recent theoretical results in linear MDPs. We demonstrate that RORL can achieve state-of-the-art performance on the general offline RL benchmark and is considerably robust to adversarial observation perturbations.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns decision policies from an existing dataset. Because deployment can differ from the recorded data, many methods use conservative value estimates and action choices. This paper highlights a tension: that conservatism can impair robustness when observations deviate because of sensor errors or adversarial perturbations.

Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning, or RORL, introduces conservative smoothing to address this tradeoff. It regularizes both the policy and the value function at states near the dataset, while also applying additional conservative value estimation to those states. The design therefore explicitly considers nearby observations when shaping decisions and estimates, rather than focusing only on the recorded states.

For linear Markov decision processes, the authors prove a tighter suboptimality bound than recent theoretical results. Empirically, they report state-of-the-art performance on a general offline reinforcement-learning benchmark and substantial robustness to adversarial observation perturbations. The theoretical result is tied to the linear setting, while the experiments support the practical value of combining local smoothing with conservatism in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: RORL combines conservative value estimation with smoothing around dataset states to improve offline policy performance and robustness.

title: RORL: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning via Conservative Smoothing

abstract: As shown by recent studies, machine intelligence-enabled systems are vulnerable to test cases resulting from either adversarial manipulation or natural distribution shifts. This has raised great concerns about deploying machine learning algorithms for real-world applications, especially in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving (AD). On the other hand, traditional AD testing on naturalistic scenarios requires hundreds of millions of driving miles due to the high dimensionality and rareness of the safety-critical scenarios in the real world. As a result, several approaches for autonomous driving evaluation have been explored, which are usually, however, based on different simulation platforms, types of safety-critical scenarios, scenario generation algorithms, and driving route variations. Thus, despite a large amount of effort in autonomous driving testing, it is still challenging to compare and understand the effectiveness and efficiency of different testing scenario generation algorithms and testing mechanisms under similar conditions. In this paper, we aim to provide the first unified platform SafeBench to integrate different types of safety-critical testing scenarios, scenario generation algorithms, and other variations such as driving routes and environments. In particular, we consider 8 safety-critical testing scenarios following National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and develop 4 scenario generation algorithms considering 10 variations for each scenario. Meanwhile, we implement 4 deep reinforcement learning-based AD algorithms with 4 types of input (e.g., bird’s-eye view, camera) to perform fair comparisons on SafeBench. We find our generated testing scenarios are indeed more challenging and observe the trade-off between the performance of AD agents under benign and safety-critical testing scenarios. We believe our unified platform SafeBench for large-scale and effective autonomous driving testing will motivate the development of new testing scenario generation and safe AD algorithms. SafeBench is available at https://safebench.github.io.

Existing evaluation approaches also differ in simulators, routes, scenarios, and generation methods, complicating comparisons. SafeBench brings these elements into a unified platform so autonomous-driving systems and testing methods can be compared under more consistent conditions.

summary.tldr: SafeBench unifies autonomous-driving safety evaluation and reveals trade-offs between performance in benign and safety-critical scenarios.

title: SafeBench: A Benchmarking Platform for Safety Evaluation of Autonomous Vehicles

abstract: Vision transformers have demonstrated remarkable performance on a variety of computer vision tasks. In this paper, we illustrate the effectiveness of the deformable vision transformer for single-stage pedestrian detection and propose a spatial and multi-scale feature enhancement module, which aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and accuracy. Performance improvement with the use of vision transformers on various commonly used single-stage structures is demonstrated. The design of the proposed architecture is investigated in depth. Comprehensive comparisons with state-of-the-art single- and two-stage detectors on various pedestrian datasets are performed. The proposed detector achieves leading performance on Caltech and Citypersons datasets among single- and two-stage methods using fewer parameters than the baseline. The log-average miss rates for Reasonable and Heavy are decreased to 2.6% and 28.0% on the Caltech test set, and 10.9% and 38.6% on the Citypersons validation set respectively. The proposed method outperforms SOTA two-stage detectors in the Heavy subset on the Citypersons validation set with considerably faster inference speed.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a deformable vision transformer can improve single-stage pedestrian detection while retaining fast inference. Its focus is the balance between detection accuracy and computational cost. The authors study transformer use across several common single-stage detector structures, rather than presenting performance improvements for only one architectural arrangement.

The proposed detector includes a module that enhances spatial features and features at multiple scales. The authors examine the architecture's design in depth and compare it with both single-stage and two-stage detectors. They report leading performance on Caltech and Citypersons while using fewer parameters than their baseline, connecting the accuracy improvements to a relatively compact model.

Reported log-average miss rates are 2.6% and 28.0% for the Reasonable and Heavy subsets of the Caltech test set, and 10.9% and 38.6% on the corresponding Citypersons validation subsets. On the Citypersons Heavy subset, the method also outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage detectors with considerably faster inference. These are results on the specified evaluations, supporting the proposed architecture's speed–accuracy balance.
summary.tldr: A deformable vision transformer with spatial and multi-scale feature enhancement delivers strong pedestrian detection results with fast inference.

title: Effectiveness of Vision Transformer for Fast and Accurate Single-Stage Pedestrian Detection

abstract: Does prompting a large language model (LLM) like GPT-3 with explanations improve in-context learning? We study this question on two NLP tasks that involve reasoning over text, namely question answering and natural language inference. We test the performance of four LLMs on three textual reasoning datasets using prompts that include explanations in multiple different styles. For these tasks, we find that including explanations in the prompts for OPT, GPT-3 (davinci), and InstructGPT (text-davinci-001) only yields small to moderate accuracy improvements over standard few-show learning. However, text-davinci-002 is able to benefit more substantially.We further show that explanations generated by the LLMs may not entail the models’ predictions nor be factually grounded in the input, even on simple tasks with extractive explanations. However, these flawed explanations can still be useful as a way to verify LLMs’ predictions post-hoc. Through analysis in our three settings, we show that explanations judged by humans to be good—logically consistent with the input and the prediction—more likely cooccur with accurate predictions. Following these observations, we train calibrators using automatically extracted scores that assess the reliability of explanations, allowing us to improve performance post-hoc across all of our datasets.

paragraphs: This paper tests whether adding explanations to example prompts improves language models' reasoning over text. The study covers question answering and natural language inference, using four models, three datasets, and several explanation styles. For OPT, GPT-3 davinci, and text-davinci-001, the gains are small to moderate; text-davinci-002 benefits more substantially.

The authors also examine whether generated explanations actually support the associated answers. They find that explanations can fail to entail the prediction or remain grounded in the input, even when explanations simply extract text. An explanation accompanying an answer therefore cannot automatically be treated as reliable evidence that the answer follows from the supplied information.

Nevertheless, explanation quality carries useful information. Across the three settings, explanations that people judge logically consistent with the input and prediction more often accompany correct answers. The authors train calibrators using automatically extracted explanation-reliability scores and improve performance after prediction across all evaluated datasets. Thus, explanations show value as signals for checking predictions even when their generation is itself unreliable.
summary.tldr: Explanations offer model-dependent prompting gains and can be unreliable, yet their assessed quality helps improve prediction calibration.

title: The Unreliability of Explanations in Few-shot Prompting for Textual Reasoning

abstract: Understanding genetic variation, e.g., through mutations, in organisms is crucial to unravel their effects on the environment and human health. A fundamental characterization can be obtained by solving the haplotype assembly problem, which yields the variation across multiple copies of chromosomes. Variations among fast evolving viruses that lead to different strains (called quasispecies) are also deciphered with similar approaches. In both these cases, high-throughput sequencing technologies that provide oversampled mixtures of large noisy fragments (reads) of genomes, are used to infer constituent components (haplotypes or quasispecies). The problem is harder for polyploid species where there are more than two copies of chromosomes. State-of-the-art neural approaches to solve this NP-hard problem do not adequately model relations among the reads that are important for deconvolving the input signal. We address this problem by developing a new method, called NeurHap, that combines graph representation learning with combinatorial optimization. Our experiments demonstrate the substantially better performance of NeurHap in real and synthetic datasets compared to competing approaches.

paragraphs: Sequencing produces mixtures of noisy genome fragments, and reconstructing their constituent sequences requires disentangling which fragments belong together. The paper's graph-coloring approach brings a discrete organization problem together with learned representations of read relationships.

The contribution is therefore a combination of relational modeling and structured optimization for an NP-hard reconstruction problem. Its stated results support treating interactions among reads as a central part of recovering genetic components from noisy sequencing mixtures.
summary.tldr: NeurHap combines graph learning and combinatorial optimization to improve reconstruction of chromosome copies and viral strains from noisy reads.

title: Graph Coloring via Neural Networks for Haplotype Assembly and Viral Quasispecies Reconstruction

abstract: We consider a structured multi-label prediction problem where the labels are organized under implication and mutual exclusion constraints. A major concern is to produce predictions that are logically consistent with these constraints. To do so, we formulate this problem as an embedding inference problem where the constraints are imposed onto the embeddings of labels by geometric construction. Particularly, we consider a hyperbolic Poincaré ball model in which we encode labels as Poincaré hyperplanes that work as linear decision boundaries. The hyperplanes are interpreted as convex regions such that the logical relationships (implication and exclusion) are geometrically encoded using the insideness and disjointedness of these regions, respectively. We show theoretical groundings of the method for preserving logical relationships in the embedding space. Extensive experiments on 12 datasets show 1) significant improvements in mean average precision; 2) lower number of constraint violations; 3) an order of magnitude fewer dimensions than baselines.

The hyperplanes are interpreted as convex regions such that the logical relationships (implication and exclusion) are geometrically encoded using the insideness and disjointedness of these regions, respectively. paragraphs: In structured multi-label prediction, labels can have logical relationships: one may imply another, while two others may exclude each other. Predicting labels separately can conflict with those relationships. This paper incorporates the constraints into a geometric representation of labels so that logical structure directly shapes the prediction problem.

The method uses the hyperbolic Poincaré ball and represents labels with hyperplanes that serve as decision boundaries. Interpreting them through convex regions makes the logic geometric. A region contained inside another expresses implication, while disjoint regions express mutual exclusion. The authors provide theoretical grounding for preserving these relationships in the embedding space.

Across 12 datasets, the experiments report significant improvements in mean average precision, fewer constraint violations, and an order of magnitude fewer dimensions than the baselines. These findings connect predictive performance, logical consistency, and representation size. The reported reduction in violations is an empirical improvement, while the geometric construction supplies the structural mechanism intended to keep related label decisions consistent.
summary.tldr: Hyperbolic label regions encode implication and exclusion, improving prediction quality and reducing logical violations in experiments.

title: Hyperbolic Embedding Inference for Structured Multi-Label Prediction

abstract: We aim to understand grokking, a phenomenon where models generalize long after overfitting their training set. We present both a microscopic analysis anchored by an effective theory and a macroscopic analysis of phase diagrams describing learning performance across hyperparameters. We find that generalization originates from structured representations, whose training dynamics and dependence on training set size can be predicted by our effective theory (in a toy setting). We observe empirically the presence of four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion. We find representation learning to occur only in a "Goldilocks zone" (including comprehension and grokking) between memorization and confusion. Compared to the comprehension phase, the grokking phase stays closer to the memorization phase, leading to delayed generalization. The Goldilocks phase is reminiscent of "intelligence from starvation" in Darwinian evolution, where resource limitations drive discovery of more efficient solutions. This study not only provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking, but also highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, e.g., effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a surprising training pattern: a model first overfits its training examples and only much later begins to generalize. This paper investigates that delay by connecting the formation of internal representations with broader patterns of learning behavior. It combines an effective theory of representation dynamics with phase diagrams showing outcomes across hyperparameter choices.

In a toy setting, the theory predicts how structured representations develop and how their dynamics depend on training-set size. The authors connect those representations to generalization. Their empirical analysis identifies four phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion. Representation learning appears only in an intermediate region containing comprehension and grokking, between the other two phases.

Within this picture, grokking lies closer to memorization than comprehension does, helping explain its delayed transition to generalization. The authors compare the intermediate region to situations where resource limitations encourage more efficient solutions. The study offers a mechanistic interpretation within its analyzed setting and demonstrates how physics-inspired theories and phase diagrams can organize otherwise puzzling learning behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper explains grokking through delayed structured-representation learning in a region between memorization and confusion.

title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning

abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), it is easier to solve a task if given a good representation. While deep RL should automatically acquire such good representations, prior work often finds that learning representations in an end-to-end fashion is unstable and instead equip RL algorithms with additional representation learning parts (e.g., auxiliary losses, data augmentation). How can we design RL algorithms that directly acquire good representations? In this paper, instead of adding representation learning parts to an existing RL algorithm, we show (contrastive) representation learning methods are already RL algorithms in their own right. To do this, we build upon prior work and apply contrastive representation learning to action-labeled trajectories, in such a way that the (inner product of) learned representations exactly corresponds to a goal-conditioned value function. We use this idea to reinterpret a prior RL method as performing contrastive learning, and then use the idea to propose a much simpler method that achieves similar performance. Across a range of goal-conditioned RL tasks, we demonstrate that contrastive RL methods achieve higher success rates than prior non-contrastive methods. We also show that contrastive RL outperforms prior methods on image-based tasks, without using data augmentation or auxiliary objectives

With their construction, the inner product between learned representations corresponds exactly to a goal-conditioned value function. abstract: Recent advancements in vision backbones have significantly improved their performance by simultaneously modeling images’ local and global contexts. However, the bidirectional interaction between these two contexts has not been well explored and exploited, which is important in the human visual system. This paper proposes a **F**ully **A**daptive **S**elf-**A**ttention (FASA) mechanism for vision transformer to model the local and global information as well as the bidirectional interaction between them in context-aware ways. Specifically, FASA employs self-modulated convolutions to adaptively extract local representation while utilizing self-attention in down-sampled space to extract global representation. Subsequently, it conducts a bidirectional adaptation process between local and global representation to model their interaction. In addition, we introduce a fine-grained downsampling strategy to enhance the down-sampled self-attention mechanism for finer-grained global perception capability. Based on FASA, we develop a family of lightweight vision backbones, **F**ully **A**daptive **T**ransformer (FAT) family. Extensive experiments on multiple vision tasks demonstrate that FAT achieves impressive performance. Notably, FAT accomplishes a **77.6%** accuracy on ImageNet-1K using only **4.5M** parameters and **0.7G** FLOPs, which surpasses the most advanced ConvNets and Transformers with similar model size and computational costs. Moreover, our model exhibits faster speed on modern GPU compared to other models.

title: Lightweight Vision Transformer with Bidirectional Interaction

abstract: Multi-agent systems are characterized by environmental uncertainty, varying policies of agents, and partial observability, which result in significant risks. In the context of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), learning coordinated and decentralized policies that are sensitive to risk is challenging. To formulate the coordination requirements in risk-sensitive MARL, we introduce the Risk-sensitive Individual-Global-Max (RIGM) principle as a generalization of the Individual-Global-Max (IGM) and Distributional IGM (DIGM) principles. This principle requires that the collection of risk-sensitive action selections of each agent should be equivalent to the risk-sensitive action selection of the central policy. Current MARL value factorization methods do not satisfy the RIGM principle for common risk metrics such as the Value at Risk (VaR) metric or distorted risk measurements. Therefore, we propose RiskQ to address this limitation, which models the joint return distribution by modeling quantiles of it as weighted quantile mixtures of per-agent return distribution utilities. RiskQ satisfies the RIGM principle for the VaR and distorted risk metrics. We show that RiskQ can obtain promising performance through extensive experiments. The source code of RiskQ is available in https://github.com/xmu-rl-3dv/RiskQ.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents must make decisions under environmental uncertainty, changing behavior from other agents, and incomplete observations. When decisions also account for risk, coordinating independently acting agents becomes harder. This paper asks how each agent's risk-sensitive choices can agree with the risk-sensitive choice of a centralized policy.

The authors formalize that requirement through the Risk-sensitive Individual-Global-Max principle, or RIGM. It extends earlier coordination principles by requiring agreement under risk-sensitive action selection. Existing value-factorization methods do not satisfy this requirement for common measures such as Value at Risk and distorted risk measures. RiskQ addresses the mismatch by representing joint-return quantiles as weighted mixtures of quantiles from individual agents' return utilities.

The paper shows that RiskQ satisfies RIGM for Value at Risk and distorted risk metrics. This supplies a formal connection between decentralized choices and the central risk objective. Extensive experiments also show promising performance. The contribution combines a precise coordination criterion with a distributional representation designed to meet it, making risk sensitivity part of how cooperative value estimates are assembled.
summary.tldr: RiskQ factorizes return distributions so decentralized risk-sensitive choices agree with a centralized policy for specified risk metrics.

title: RiskQ: Risk-sensitive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Value Factorization

abstract: In the field of behavior-related brain computation, it is necessary to align raw neural signals against the drastic domain shift among them. A foundational framework within neuroscience research posits that trial-based neural population activities rely on low-dimensional latent dynamics, thus focusing on the latter greatly facilitates the alignment procedure. Despite this field's progress, existing methods ignore the intrinsic spatio-temporal structure during the alignment phase. Hence, their solutions usually lead to poor quality in latent dynamics structures and overall performance. To tackle this problem, we propose an alignment method ERDiff, which leverages the expressivity of the diffusion model to preserve the spatio-temporal structure of latent dynamics. Specifically, the latent dynamics structures of the source domain are first extracted by a diffusion model. Then, under the guidance of this diffusion model, such structures are well-recovered through a maximum likelihood alignment procedure in the target domain. We first demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method on a synthetic dataset. Then, when applied to neural recordings from the non-human primate motor cortex, under both cross-day and inter-subject settings, our method consistently manifests its capability of preserving the spatio-temporal structure of latent dynamics and outperforms existing approaches in alignment goodness-of-fit and neural decoding performance.

paragraphs: Neural recordings can differ substantially across recording days or subjects, making it difficult to align signals for studying behavior. The paper adopts a neuroscience framework in which population activity depends on lower-dimensional latent dynamics. Aligning these dynamics simplifies the problem, but the authors argue that existing methods neglect their internal spatial and temporal structure.

ERDiff uses a diffusion model to capture that structure before aligning a new domain. First, the model learns the organization of latent dynamics in the source domain. The approach makes preservation of how latent activity is organized across space and time central to alignment.

In both cross-day and inter-subject experiments, ERDiff preserves latent structure and improves alignment goodness-of-fit and neural decoding relative to existing approaches. These findings connect better structural preservation with better performance on the evaluated neural analysis tasks.
summary.tldr: ERDiff uses diffusion-learned latent structure to improve neural-recording alignment and decoding across days and subjects.

title: Extraction and Recovery of Spatio-Temporal Structure in Latent Dynamics Alignment with Diffusion Models

abstract: We propose A-Crab (Actor-Critic Regularized by Average Bellman error), a new practical algorithm for offline reinforcement learning (RL) in complex environments with insufficient data coverage. Our algorithm combines the marginalized importance sampling framework with the actor-critic paradigm, where the critic returns evaluations of the actor (policy) that are pessimistic relative to the offline data and have a small average (importance-weighted) Bellman error. Compared to existing methods, our algorithm simultaneously offers a number of advantages:(1) It achieves the optimal statistical rate of $1/\sqrt{N}$---where $N$ is the size of offline dataset---in converging to the best policy covered in the offline dataset, even when combined with general function approximators.(2) It relies on a weaker \textit{average} notion of policy coverage (compared to the $\ell_\infty$ single-policy concentrability) that exploits the structure of policy visitations.(3) It outperforms the data-collection behavior policy over a wide range of specific hyperparameters. We provide both theoretical analysis and experimental results to validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm. The code is available at https://github.com/zhuhl98/ACrab.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from an existing dataset, which may provide insufficient coverage of the environment. A-Crab addresses this setting by making policy evaluation conservative relative to the available data. Its target is the best policy covered by that dataset.

The algorithm combines marginalized importance sampling with an actor–critic structure. The actor supplies a policy, while the critic evaluates it pessimistically and keeps its average importance-weighted Bellman error small. This error measures consistency in the critic’s value estimates, with importance weighting incorporated into the average. The method uses an average notion of policy coverage that exploits visitation structure and is weaker than the worst-case coverage condition discussed in the paper.

The analysis establishes the optimal statistical rate of 1/√N for convergence to the best covered policy, including with general function approximators. The authors also report improvement over the data-collection policy across a wide range of particular hyperparameters. Theory and experiments together support this combination of conservative evaluation, importance weighting, and actor–critic learning.
summary.tldr: A-Crab combines conservative actor–critic evaluation with importance weighting to learn the best dataset-covered policy at an optimal statistical rate.

title: Importance Weighted Actor-Critic for Optimal Conservative Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reward-free data is abundant and contains rich prior knowledge of human behaviors, but it is not well exploited by offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. In this paper, we propose UBER, an unsupervised approach to extract useful behaviors from offline reward-free datasets via diversified rewards. UBER assigns different pseudo-rewards sampled from a given prior distribution to different agents to extract a diverse set of behaviors, and reuse them as candidate policies to facilitate the learning of new tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that rewards generated from random neural networks are sufficient to extract diverse and useful behaviors, some even close to expert ones. We provide both empirical and theoretical evidences to justify the use of random priors for the reward function. Experiments on multiple benchmarks showcase UBER's ability to learn effective and diverse behavior sets that enhance sample efficiency for online RL, outperforming existing baselines. By reducing reliance on human supervision, UBER broadens the applicability of RL to real-world scenarios with abundant reward-free data.

paragraphs: Recorded behavior often comes without rewards specifying which actions are desirable. Such data still contains useful knowledge, but offline reinforcement learning does not fully exploit it. UBER proposes extracting a collection of behaviors from reward-free datasets before using those behaviors to help learn new tasks.

The approach assigns different agents different artificial rewards sampled from a prior distribution. Each reward encourages the extraction of a different behavior from the same offline data, producing candidate policies for later reuse. The authors show that rewards generated by random neural networks are sufficient to recover diverse, useful behaviors, including some close to expert behavior.

The paper provides both theoretical and empirical evidence for using these random reward priors. Across multiple benchmarks, the resulting behavior collections improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning and outperform existing baselines. The significance is that useful behavioral starting points can be obtained without manually specifying rewards for the original dataset. This reduces reliance on human supervision while allowing later task learning to benefit from previously recorded behavior.
summary.tldr: UBER uses random artificial rewards to extract diverse policies from reward-free data and improve subsequent reinforcement learning.

title: Unsupervised Behavior Extraction via Random Intent Priors

abstract: A room’s acoustic properties are a product of the room’s geometry, the objects within the room, and their specific positions. A room’s acoustic properties can be characterized by its impulse response (RIR) between a source and listener location, or roughly inferred from recordings of natural signals present in the room. Variations in the positions of objects in a room can effect measurable changes in the room’s acoustic properties, as characterized by the RIR. Existing datasets of RIRs either do not systematically vary positions of objects in an environment, or they consist of only simulated RIRs. We present SoundCam, the largest dataset of unique RIRs from in-the-wild rooms publicly released to date. It includes 5,000 10-channel real-world measurements of room impulse responses and 2,000 10-channel recordings of music in three different rooms, including a controlled acoustic lab, an in-the-wild living room, and a conference room, with different humans in positions throughout each room. We show that these measurements can be used for interesting tasks, such as detecting and identifying humans, and tracking their positions.

paragraphs: A room’s sound depends on its shape, its contents, and where those contents are positioned. Moving a person can therefore change how sound travels through the room. SoundCam provides measurements for studying whether those changes reveal human presence, identity, and position, using room acoustics as a source of information.

The dataset contains 5,000 ten-channel room impulse-response measurements and 2,000 ten-channel music recordings. Collection covers an acoustic laboratory, a living room, and a conference room, with different people positioned throughout each space. Impulse responses characterize the acoustic path between a source and listener, while music recordings offer another way to observe the room’s acoustic properties.

Earlier datasets either lacked systematic object-position variation or relied entirely on simulation. SoundCam addresses that gap with real measurements and varied human locations. The authors describe it as the largest publicly released collection of unique impulse responses from in-the-wild rooms at the time, and demonstrate uses including human detection, identification, and position tracking.
summary.tldr: SoundCam records how people change room acoustics and demonstrates that these measurements can support detection, identification, and tracking.

title: SoundCam: A Dataset for Finding Humans Using Room Acoustics

abstract: Synthesizing images with user-specified subjects has received growing attention due to its practical applications. Despite the recent success in single subject customization, existing algorithms suffer from high training cost and low success rate along with increased number of subjects. Towards controllable image synthesis with multiple subjects as the constraints, this work studies how to efficiently represent a particular subject as well as how to appropriately compose different subjects. We find that the text embedding regarding the subject token already serves as a simple yet effective representation that supports arbitrary combinations without any model tuning. Through learning a residual on top of the base embedding, we manage to robustly shift the raw subject to the customized subject given various text conditions. We then propose to employ layout, a very abstract and easy-to-obtain prior, as the spatial guidance for subject arrangement. By rectifying the activations in the cross-attention map, the layout appoints and separates the location of different subjects in the image, significantly alleviating the interference across them. Using cross-attention map as the intermediary, we could strengthen the signal of target subjects and weaken the signal of irrelevant subjects within a certain region, significantly alleviating the interference across subjects. Both qualitative and quantitative experimental results demonstrate our superiority over state-of-the-art alternatives under a variety of settings for multi-subject customization.

paragraphs: Generating an image containing several user-specified subjects raises two linked problems: representing each subject efficiently and preventing subjects from interfering with one another. The paper addresses both, motivated by existing customization methods whose training costs rise and success rates fall as more subjects are included in a requested image.

For representation, the authors find that a subject token's text embedding can support arbitrary combinations without tuning the image model. They learn a residual added to a base embedding, shifting the generic subject representation toward the customized subject under different text conditions. This concentrates customization in the representation used to describe the subject.

For composition, the method uses a layout to specify where subjects should appear. It adjusts cross-attention maps to strengthen a target subject's signal within its region and suppress irrelevant subject signals there. This spatial separation reduces interference between subjects. Qualitative and quantitative experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art alternatives across several multi-subject customization settings, supporting the combination of compact subject representations and explicit spatial guidance.
summary.tldr: Learned subject embeddings and layout-guided cross-attention improve the composition of multiple customized subjects in generated images.

title: Customizable Image Synthesis with Multiple Subjects

abstract: Spatio-temporal predictive learning is a learning paradigm that enables models to learn spatial and temporal patterns by predicting future frames from given past frames in an unsupervised manner. Despite remarkable progress in recent years, a lack of systematic understanding persists due to the diverse settings, complex implementation, and difficult reproducibility. Without standardization, comparisons can be unfair and insights inconclusive. To address this dilemma, we propose OpenSTL, a comprehensive benchmark for spatio-temporal predictive learning that categorizes prevalent approaches into recurrent-based and recurrent-free models. OpenSTL provides a modular and extensible framework implementing various state-of-the-art methods. We conduct standard evaluations on datasets across various domains, including synthetic moving object trajectory, human motion, driving scenes, traffic flow, and weather forecasting. Based on our observations, we provide a detailed analysis of how model architecture and dataset properties affect spatio-temporal predictive learning performance. Surprisingly, we find that recurrent-free models achieve a good balance between efficiency and performance than recurrent models. Thus, we further extend the common MetaFormers to boost recurrent-free spatial-temporal predictive learning. We open-source the code and models at https://github.com/chengtan9907/OpenSTL.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal predictive learning trains models to predict future frames from past ones, learning spatial and temporal patterns without separate labels. Comparing approaches is difficult when experimental settings and implementations differ. OpenSTL provides a standardized benchmark and software framework to make those comparisons more systematic and reproducible.

The framework groups approaches into recurrent and recurrent-free models and implements multiple leading methods in a modular, extensible form. Evaluations span synthetic moving objects, human motion, driving scenes, traffic flow, and weather forecasting. This range supports analysis of how both architecture and dataset properties affect performance, rather than treating one setting as representative of the entire field.

The authors find that recurrent-free models offer a favorable balance of efficiency and performance compared with recurrent models in their evaluations. Motivated by this observation, they extend common MetaFormer architectures for recurrent-free prediction. OpenSTL therefore contributes both shared evaluation infrastructure and an architectural direction supported by the benchmark findings. The released code and models make these comparisons and extensions available for further research.
summary.tldr: OpenSTL standardizes spatio-temporal prediction evaluation and finds a favorable efficiency–performance balance for recurrent-free models across its benchmarks.

title: OpenSTL: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Spatio-Temporal Predictive Learning

abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular approach for enhancing the performance of "student" models, with lower representational capacity, by taking advantage of more powerful "teacher" models. Despite its apparent simplicity, the underlying mechanics behind knowledge distillation (KD) are not yet fully understood. In this work, we shed new light on the inner workings of this method, by examining it from an optimization perspective. Specifically, we show that, in the context of linear and deep linear models, KD can be interpreted as a novel type of stochastic variance reduction mechanism. We provide a detailed convergence analysis of the resulting dynamics, which hold under standard assumptions for both strongly-convex and non-convex losses, showing that KD acts as a form of \emph{partial variance reduction}, which can reduce the stochastic gradient noise, but may not eliminate it completely, depending on the properties of the ``teacher'' model. Our analysis puts further emphasis on the need for careful parametrization of KD, in particular w.r.t. the weighting of the distillation loss, and is validated empirically on both linear models and deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student using guidance from a more powerful teacher. This paper investigates why that guidance can help by examining the optimization process. For linear and deep linear models, the authors interpret distillation as a form of stochastic variance reduction: it can reduce noise in the gradient updates used during training.

The reduction is partial. Depending on the teacher's properties, distillation may leave some stochastic gradient noise rather than remove it entirely. The authors analyze convergence under standard assumptions for strongly convex and non-convex losses. This gives a mathematical account of the training dynamics while keeping the theoretical interpretation tied to the model classes studied.

The analysis also highlights the importance of how strongly the distillation loss is weighted. Teacher guidance is not simply a benefit whose effect is independent of its parametrization; its contribution to optimization depends on the chosen weighting. Experiments on linear models and deep neural networks support the analysis. The result adds an optimization-based explanation for distillation alongside its familiar role in transferring information from teacher to student.
summary.tldr: For linear and deep linear models, knowledge distillation can partially reduce gradient noise, with benefits depending on the teacher and loss weighting.

title: Knowledge Distillation Performs Partial Variance Reduction

abstract: Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) have instigated a groundbreaking shift in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations across a wide range of fields, such as physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Incorporating higher order many-body interactions can enhance the expressiveness and accuracy of models. Recent models have achieved this by explicitly including up to four-body interactions. However, five-body interactions, which have relevance in various fields, are still challenging to incorporate efficiently into MLFFs. In this work, we propose the quintuple network (QuinNet), an end-to-end graph neural network that efficiently expresses many-body interactions up to five-body interactions with \emph{ab initio} accuracy. By analyzing the topology of diverse many-body interactions, we design the model architecture to efficiently and explicitly represent these interactions. We evaluate QuinNet on public datasets of small molecules, such as MD17 and its revised version, and show that it is compatible with other state-of-the-art models on these benchmarks. Moreover, QuinNet surpasses many leading models on larger and more complex molecular systems, such as MD22 and Chignolin, without increasing the computational complexity. We also use QuinNet as a force field for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to demonstrate its accuracy and stability, and conduct an ablation study to elucidate the significance of five-body interactions. We open source our implementation at https://github.com/Zun-Wang/QuinNet.

paragraphs: Machine learning force fields support molecular dynamics simulations by modeling molecular interactions. Including interactions among larger groups of atoms can improve expressiveness and accuracy, but doing so efficiently becomes difficult. This paper introduces QuinNet, a graph neural network that explicitly represents interactions involving up to five bodies and is described as achieving ab initio accuracy.

The architecture is based on analyzing the topology of different many-body interactions. This gives the model a structured way to represent five-body effects rather than stopping at the four-body interactions explicitly included in recent models. The central design goal is to capture this richer interaction structure without increasing computational complexity.

On small-molecule datasets, including MD17 and its revised version, QuinNet performs comparably to other state-of-the-art models. On larger, more complex systems, including MD22 and Chignolin, it surpasses many leading models without increased computational complexity. Molecular dynamics simulations further demonstrate accuracy and stability, while an ablation study examines the significance of five-body interactions. Together, these evaluations support the usefulness of representing higher-order molecular structure efficiently.
summary.tldr: QuinNet efficiently models up to five-body molecular interactions and shows particular benefits on larger, more complex molecular systems.

title: Efficiently incorporating quintuple interactions into geometric deep learning force fields

abstract: Expert-designed close-ended benchmarks are indispensable in assessing the knowledge capacity of large language models (LLMs). Despite their widespread use, concerns have mounted regarding their reliability due to limited test scenarios and an unavoidable risk of data contamination. To rectify this, we present PertEval, a toolkit devised for in-depth probing of LLMs' knowledge capacity through **knowledge-invariant perturbations**. These perturbations employ human-like restatement techniques to generate on-the-fly test samples from static benchmarks, meticulously retaining knowledge-critical content while altering irrelevant details. Our toolkit further includes a suite of **response consistency analyses** that compare performance on raw vs. perturbed test sets to precisely assess LLMs' genuine knowledge capacity. Six representative LLMs are re-evaluated using PertEval. Results reveal significantly inflated performance of the LLMs on raw benchmarks, including an absolute 25.8% overestimation for GPT-4. Additionally, through a nuanced response pattern analysis, we discover that PertEval retains LLMs' uncertainty to specious knowledge, and reveals their potential rote memorization to correct options which leads to overestimated performance. We also find that the detailed response consistency analyses by PertEval could illuminate various weaknesses in existing LLMs' knowledge mastery and guide the development of refinement. Our findings provide insights for advancing more robust and genuinely knowledgeable LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/aigc-apps/PertEval.

paragraphs: A model's score on a fixed knowledge benchmark may reflect more than mastery of the underlying subject. Limited test scenarios and possible data contamination complicate interpretation. PertEval probes this issue by generating altered versions of benchmark questions that preserve knowledge-critical content while changing details irrelevant to the knowledge being tested.

The toolkit uses human-like restatements to produce new test samples on demand. It then compares responses on original and perturbed versions through consistency analyses. The aim is to examine whether apparent knowledge survives changes in presentation, and to use patterns across paired responses to identify weaknesses that an aggregate score can hide.

Reevaluation of six representative language models finds inflated performance on the original benchmarks, including a reported absolute overestimation of 25.8% for GPT-4. Response patterns also reveal potential rote memorization of correct options while retaining models' uncertainty about specious knowledge. These findings support using perturbations and consistency together to scrutinize benchmark performance, with memorization presented as a potential explanation rather than a universal diagnosis.
summary.tldr: PertEval changes knowledge-irrelevant question details and analyzes response consistency, revealing inflated original-benchmark performance in six tested language models.

title: PertEval: Unveiling Real Knowledge Capacity of LLMs with Knowledge-Invariant Perturbations

abstract: Models are expected to engage in invariance learning, which involves distinguishing the core relations that remain consistent across varying environments to ensure the predictions are safe, robust and fair. While existing works consider specific algorithms to realize invariance learning, we show that model has the potential to learn invariance through standard training procedures. In other words, this paper studies the implicit bias of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) over heterogeneous data and shows that the implicit bias drives the model learning towards an invariant solution. We call the phenomenon the implicit invariance learning. Specifically, we theoretically investigate the multi-environment low-rank matrix sensing problem where in each environment, the signal comprises (i) a lower-rank invariant part shared across all environments; and (ii) a significantly varying environment-dependent spurious component. The key insight is, through simply employing the large step size large-batch SGD sequentially in each environment without any explicit regularization, the oscillation caused by heterogeneity can provably prevent model learning spurious signals. The model reaches the invariant solution after certain iterations. In contrast, model learned using pooled SGD over all data would simultaneously learn both the invariant and spurious signals. Overall, we unveil another implicit bias that is a result of the symbiosis between the heterogeneity of data and modern algorithms, which is, to the best of our knowledge, first in the literature.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether ordinary training can favor relationships that remain stable across environments without explicit invariance regularization. It studies a low-rank matrix-sensing problem in which every environment contains a shared, lower-rank signal plus a spurious component that varies substantially between environments. That structure is central to the theoretical result.

The proposed training setup applies large-batch stochastic gradient descent with a large step size sequentially within each environment. Differences between environments create oscillations that can provably prevent the model from learning their spurious signals. After a certain number of iterations, the model reaches the invariant solution in the analyzed setting.

By contrast, pooling all the data for SGD leads the model to learn both invariant and spurious components. The comparison shows that heterogeneity can help or fail to help depending on how training encounters it. The authors call the beneficial behavior implicit invariance learning: the interaction of the data structure and optimization procedure favors the shared signal without adding an explicit penalty for environment-specific information.
summary.tldr: In a structured matrix-sensing setting, sequential large-step SGD can use environmental variation to avoid spurious signals and recover an invariant solution.

title: The Implicit Bias of Heterogeneity towards Invariance: A Study of Multi-Environment Matrix Sensing

abstract: Gaze following and social gaze prediction are fundamental tasks providing insights into human communication behaviors, intent, and social interactions. Most previous approaches addressed these tasks separately, either by designing highly specialized social gaze models that do not generalize to other social gaze tasks or by considering social gaze inference as an ad-hoc post-processing of the gaze following task. Furthermore, the vast majority of gaze following approaches have proposed models that can handle only one person at a time and are static, therefore failing to take advantage of social interactions and temporal dynamics. In this paper, we address these limitations and introduce a novel framework to jointly predict the gaze target and social gaze label for all people in the scene. It comprises (i) a temporal, transformer-based architecture that, in addition to frame tokens, handles person-specific tokens capturing the gaze information related to each individual; (ii) a new dataset, VSGaze, built from multiple gaze following and social gaze datasets by extending and validating head detections and tracks, and unifying annotation types. We demonstrate that our model can address and benefit from training on all tasks jointly, achieving state-of-the-art results for multi-person gaze following and social gaze prediction. Our annotations and code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Understanding gaze involves predicting where people look and identifying the social meaning of their gaze. Earlier approaches often separate these tasks or process one person in a static image at a time. MTGS brings them together, predicting gaze targets and social gaze labels for everyone in a scene while accounting for changes over time.

Its temporal transformer processes both frame-level tokens and person-specific tokens carrying each individual's gaze information. The authors also create VSGaze by combining existing gaze-following and social-gaze datasets. They extend and validate head detections and tracks and unify annotation types so that the combined data can support the joint framework.

The reported experiments show that the model can train on all the tasks together and benefit from doing so. It achieves state-of-the-art results for multi-person gaze following and social gaze prediction. The architecture and dataset work together to make interactions and temporal information usable within one model, addressing the fragmentation of tasks, people, and time in prior approaches.
summary.tldr: MTGS jointly predicts gaze targets and social gaze for multiple people over time, supported by the unified VSGaze dataset.

title: MTGS: A Novel Framework for Multi-Person Temporal Gaze Following and Social Gaze Prediction

abstract: The human brain exhibits a strong ability to spontaneously associate different visual attributes of the same or similar visual scene, such as associating sketches and graffiti with real-world visual objects, usually without supervising information. In contrast, in the field of artificial intelligence, controllable generation methods like ControlNet heavily rely on annotated training datasets such as depth maps, semantic segmentation maps, and poses, which limits the method’s scalability. Inspired by the neural mechanisms that may contribute to the brain’s associative power, specifically the cortical modularization and hippocampal pattern completion, here we propose a self-supervised controllable generation (SCG) framework. Firstly, we introduce an equivariance constraint to promote inter-module independence and intra-module correlation in a modular autoencoder network, thereby achieving functional specialization. Subsequently, based on these specialized modules, we employ a self-supervised pattern completion approach for controllable generation training. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed modular autoencoder effectively achieves functional specialization, including the modular processing of color, brightness, and edge detection, and exhibits brain-like features including orientation selectivity, color antagonism, and center-surround receptive fields. Through self-supervised training, associative generation capabilities spontaneously emerge in SCG, demonstrating excellent zero-shot generalization ability to various tasks such as superresolution, dehaze and associative or conditional generation on painting, sketches, and ancient graffiti. Compared to the previous representative method ControlNet, our proposed approach not only demonstrates superior robustness in more challenging high-noise scenarios but also possesses more promising scalability potential due to its self-supervised manner. Codes are released on Github and Gitee.

paragraphs: Controllable image generation often depends on annotated conditions such as depth, segmentation, or pose. This paper develops a self-supervised alternative inspired by how visual attributes can become associated without explicit supervision. Its framework, SCG, combines specialized processing modules with a pattern-completion training procedure.

First, a modular autoencoder is trained with an equivariance constraint that encourages independence between modules and correlation within each module. Experiments show specialization for properties including color, brightness, and edges, alongside reported brain-like response features. The specialized modules then provide the basis for learning controllable generation through self-supervised pattern completion.

The authors report that associative generation emerges through this training and generalizes without task-specific training to superresolution, dehazing, and generation conditioned on paintings, sketches, or ancient graffiti. They also find greater robustness than ControlNet in challenging high-noise settings. These results support learning useful visual associations without the same dependence on annotated control datasets, while the self-supervised design offers potential for greater scalability.
summary.tldr: SCG learns specialized visual modules and pattern completion to enable self-supervised controllable generation with reported zero-shot generalization.

title: Learning from Pattern Completion: Self-supervised Controllable Generation

abstract: Severe data imbalance naturally exists among web-scale vision-language datasets. Despite this, we find CLIP pre-trained thereupon exhibits notable robustness to the data imbalance compared to supervised learning, and demonstrates significant effectiveness in learning generalizable representations. With an aim to investigate the reasons behind this finding, we conduct controlled experiments to study various underlying factors, and reveal that CLIP's pretext task forms a dynamic classification problem wherein only a subset of classes is present in training. This isolates the bias from dominant classes and implicitly balances the learning signal. Furthermore, the robustness and discriminability of CLIP improve with more descriptive language supervision, larger data scale, and broader open-world concepts, which are inaccessible to supervised learning. Our study not only uncovers the mechanisms behind CLIP's generalizability beyond data imbalance but also provides transferable insights for the research community. The findings are validated in both supervised and self-supervised learning, enabling models trained on imbalanced data to achieve CLIP-level performance on diverse recognition tasks. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/clip-beyond-tail.

paragraphs: Web-scale image-and-language datasets contain large imbalances: some concepts appear much more frequently than others. The authors find that CLIP handles this imbalance better than supervised learning while learning generalizable representations. They use controlled experiments to investigate which aspects of its training explain that robustness.

The study identifies CLIP's training task as a changing classification problem in which only a subset of classes is present at a time. This isolates bias from dominant classes and implicitly balances the learning signal. The experiments also show improved robustness and discrimination with more descriptive language supervision, larger datasets, and broader open-world concepts.

The authors then test whether these insights transfer to supervised and self-supervised learning. Their results show that models trained on imbalanced data can reach CLIP-level performance across diverse recognition tasks using the resulting insights. The contribution connects an observed advantage to specific training mechanisms, making it useful beyond understanding CLIP alone. The claimed transfer is supported by the evaluated tasks rather than establishing that all imbalanced learning problems can attain the same performance.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments connect CLIP's imbalance robustness to dynamic classification and language supervision, with insights that transfer to other learning methods.

title: What Makes CLIP More Robust to Long-Tailed Pre-Training Data? A Controlled Study for Transferable Insights

abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have demonstrated success in a variety of applications, including inverse problems and neural rendering. An INR is typically trained to capture one signal of interest, resulting in learned neural features that are highly attuned to that signal. Assumed to be less generalizable, we explore the aspect of transferability of such learned neural features for fitting similar signals. We introduce a new INR training framework, STRAINER that learns transferable features for fitting INRs to new signals from a given distribution, faster and with better reconstruction quality. Owing to the sequential layer-wise affine operations in an INR, we propose to learn transferable representations by sharing initial encoder layers across multiple INRs with independent decoder layers. At test time, the learned encoder representations are transferred as initialization for an otherwise randomly initialized INR. We find STRAINER to yield extremely powerful initialization for fitting images from the same domain and allow for a ≈ +10dB gain in signal quality early on compared to an untrained INR itself. STRAINER also provides a simple way to encode data-driven priors in INRs. We evaluate STRAINER on multiple in-domain and out-of-domain signal fitting tasks and inverse problems and further provide detailed analysis and discussion on the transferability of STRAINER’s features.

paragraphs: An implicit neural representation is usually trained to capture one particular signal, making its learned features closely tied to that signal. This paper asks whether those features can nevertheless help fit other, similar signals. Its STRAINER framework learns an initialization intended to make fitting a new representation faster and improve reconstruction quality.

During training, multiple representations share their early encoder layers but have separate decoder layers. This arrangement learns common features while allowing each representation to fit its own signal. At test time, the learned encoder supplies the initialization for a new representation whose remaining components start randomly initialized. The shared features therefore act as a learned prior for subsequent fitting.

For images from the same domain, the authors report an early signal-quality gain of approximately 10 decibels compared with an untrained representation. They also evaluate fitting and inverse problems involving both in-domain and out-of-domain signals. The work shows that signal-specific representation training can produce reusable features, with particularly strong reported benefits during early fitting within the training domain.
summary.tldr: STRAINER learns shared encoder features that initialize new implicit neural representations for faster fitting and better reconstruction.

title: Learning Transferable Features for Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: We introduce Equivariant Neural Diffusion (END), a novel diffusion model for molecule generation in 3D that is equivariant to Euclidean transformations. Compared to current state-of-the-art equivariant diffusion models, the key innovation in END lies in its learnable forward process for enhanced generative modelling. Rather than pre-specified, the forward process is parameterized through a time- and data-dependent transformation that is equivariant to rigid transformations. Through a series of experiments on standard molecule generation benchmarks, we demonstrate the competitive performance of END compared to several strong baselines for both unconditional and conditional generation.

paragraphs: Equivariant Neural Diffusion, or END, generates molecules in three-dimensional space using a diffusion model. Its design respects Euclidean transformations, so the model’s behavior remains consistent with changes in a molecule’s spatial placement and orientation. This geometric property is built into the generative framework rather than treated as an incidental feature of training data.

The paper’s main change concerns the forward process of diffusion. Existing equivariant approaches use a prespecified process, while END makes that process learnable. It parameterizes the transformation so that it depends on both time and data, while preserving equivariance to rigid transformations. This introduces flexibility into how the forward process handles molecular examples without abandoning the geometric structure the model is designed to respect.

Experiments on standard molecule-generation benchmarks show competitive performance against several strong baselines. The evaluations include both unconditional generation and generation with conditioning information. The stated finding supports learnable forward processes as a viable direction for equivariant molecular diffusion, with competitive results across both tested generation settings.
summary.tldr: END makes the forward diffusion process learnable while preserving geometric equivariance, achieving competitive conditional and unconditional molecule generation.

title: Equivariant Neural Diffusion for Molecule Generation

abstract: Recent DETR-based methods have advanced the development of Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) through transformers' efficiency and capability in modeling spatial and temporal information. Despite harvesting remarkable progress, existing works follow asynchronous designs, which model video sequences via either video-level queries only or adopting query-sensitive cascade structures, resulting in difficulties when handling complex and challenging video scenarios. In this work, we analyze the cause of this phenomenon and the limitations of the current solutions, and propose to conduct synchronized modeling via a new framework named SyncVIS. Specifically, SyncVIS explicitly introduces video-level query embeddings and designs two key modules to synchronize video-level query with frame-level query embeddings: a synchronized video-frame modeling paradigm and a synchronized embedding optimization strategy. The former attempts to promote the mutual learning of frame- and video-level embeddings with each other and the latter divides large video sequences into small clips for easier optimization. Extensive experimental evaluations are conducted on the challenging YouTube-VIS 2019 & 2021 & 2022, and OVIS benchmarks, and SyncVIS achieves state-of-the-art results, which demonstrates the effectiveness and generality of the proposed approach. The code is available at https://github.com/rkzheng99/SyncVIS.

paragraphs: Video instance segmentation requires identifying individual objects across a sequence while delineating them in each frame. Transformer-based methods can model spatial and temporal information, but the paper identifies problems in asynchronous designs using only video-level queries or query-sensitive cascades. These arrangements can struggle with complex video scenarios.

SyncVIS introduces explicit video-level query embeddings and synchronizes them with frame-level embeddings. One module encourages the two representation levels to learn from each other, linking information about individual frames with information about the wider sequence. A second module divides long sequences into shorter clips to make optimization easier.

The authors evaluate the framework on YouTube-VIS 2019, 2021, and 2022, as well as OVIS, and report state-of-the-art results. Performance across these benchmarks supports the effectiveness and generality claimed for the approach. The contribution centers on coordinating representations at two temporal scales and structuring optimization around manageable clips, making frame-specific and sequence-level information work together within the same segmentation framework.
summary.tldr: SyncVIS synchronizes frame-level and video-level representations and optimizes shorter clips, achieving reported state-of-the-art video instance segmentation results.

title: SyncVIS: Synchronized Video Instance Segmentation

abstract: The trade-off between cost and performance has been a longstanding and critical issue for deep neural networks. One key factor affecting the computational cost is the width of each layer. However, in practice, the width of layers in a neural network is mostly empirically determined. In this paper, we show that a pattern regarding the variance of weight norm corresponding to different channels can indicate whether the layer is sufficiently wide and may help us better allocate computational resources across the layers.Starting from a simple intuition that channels with larger weights would have larger gradients and the difference in weight norm enlarges between channels with similar weight, we empirically validate that wide and narrow layers show two different patterns with experiments across different data modalities and network architectures. Based on the two different patterns, we identify three stages during training and explain each stage with corresponding evidence. We further propose to adjust the width based on the identified pattern and show that conventional layer width settings for CNNs could be adjusted to reduce the number of parameters while boosting the performance.
