paragraphs: Layer width strongly affects a neural network's computational cost, yet it is often chosen empirically. This paper investigates whether training behavior can indicate when a layer is sufficiently wide. Its proposed signal is the variance of weight norms across channels: how unevenly the magnitudes of different channels' weights are distributed.

The starting intuition is that channels with larger weights receive larger gradients, allowing initially similar channels to become increasingly unequal. Experiments across different data modalities and architectures reveal distinct patterns for wide and narrow layers. The authors use those patterns to identify three stages of training and provide evidence explaining the behavior in each stage.

They then propose adjusting layer widths according to the observed pattern. In their CNN experiments, this allows conventional width choices to be revised in ways that reduce parameter counts while improving performance. The findings suggest that variation in channel weight magnitudes can provide useful feedback for allocating capacity across layers. The claim is an empirically supported indicator and adjustment strategy, rather than a universal prescription for every network.
summary.tldr: Patterns in channel weight-norm variance indicate layer-width sufficiency and guide CNN width changes that reduce parameters while improving reported performance.

title: Unveiling The Matthew Effect Across Channels: Assessing Layer Width Sufficiency via Weight Norm Variance

abstract: Graph representation learning (GRL) is critical for extracting insights from complex network structures, but it also raises security concerns due to potential privacy vulnerabilities in these representations. This paper investigates the structural vulnerabilities in graph neural models where sensitive topological information can be inferred through edge reconstruction attacks. Our research primarily addresses the theoretical underpinnings of similarity-based edge reconstruction attacks (SERA), furnishing a non-asymptotic analysis of their reconstruction capacities. Moreover, we present empirical corroboration indicating that such attacks can perfectly reconstruct sparse graphs as graph size increases. Conversely, we establish that sparsity is a critical factor for SERA's effectiveness, as demonstrated through analysis and experiments on (dense) stochastic block models. Finally, we explore the resilience of private graph representations produced via noisy aggregation (NAG) mechanism against SERA. Through theoretical analysis and empirical assessments, we affirm the mitigation of SERA using NAG . In parallel, we also empirically delineate instances wherein SERA demonstrates both efficacy and deficiency in its capacity to function as an instrument for elucidating the trade-off between privacy and utility.

paragraphs: Graph representations can reveal sensitive network structure even when the original edges are not directly exposed. This paper studies similarity-based edge reconstruction attacks, or SERA, which infer connections from learned representations. Its main focus is a non-asymptotic theoretical analysis of how much graph structure these attacks can recover.

Empirical results indicate that such attacks can perfectly reconstruct sparse graphs as graph size increases. The authors also examine dense stochastic block models and show, through theory and experiments, that sparsity is a critical factor in attack effectiveness. The findings therefore connect reconstruction vulnerability to properties of the underlying graph, rather than treating attack success as uniform across graph structures.

The paper further studies representations produced with noisy aggregation, a privacy mechanism called NAG. Theory and experiments support its ability to mitigate SERA. Additional empirical analysis identifies cases where SERA is useful, and cases where it is deficient, as a tool for examining privacy–utility trade-offs. This qualifies what reconstruction attacks can reveal about representation privacy.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes graph reconstruction attacks, identifies sparsity as crucial to their effectiveness, and shows mitigation through noisy aggregation.

title: On provable privacy vulnerabilities of graph representations

abstract: We propose Any2graph, a generic framework for end-to-end Supervised Graph Prediction (SGP) i.e. a deep learning model that predicts an entire graph for any kind of input. The framework is built on a novel Optimal Transport loss, the Partially-Masked Fused Gromov-Wasserstein, that exhibits all necessary properties (permutation invariance, differentiability and scalability) and is designed to handle any-sized graphs. Numerical experiments showcase the versatility of the approach that outperform existing competitors on a novel challenging synthetic dataset and a variety of real-world tasks such as map construction from satellite image (Sat2Graph) or molecule prediction from fingerprint (Fingerprint2Graph).

paragraphs: Supervised graph prediction requires producing an entire graph from an input, including structure whose node ordering should not matter. Any2Graph proposes a generic end-to-end framework intended to work across different input types rather than relying on a separate formulation for each application.

Its central component is a Partially-Masked Fused Gromov–Wasserstein loss. The loss is designed to be permutation invariant, differentiable, and scalable while handling graphs of different sizes, allowing graph predictions to be trained through a common matching objective.

Experiments outperform existing competitors on a challenging synthetic dataset and real tasks including map construction from satellite images and molecule prediction from fingerprints. The abstract does not supply numerical results or graph-size limits. The contribution is a reusable graph-output learning framework with evidence across these tasks, not proof of equally strong performance for every possible input-to-graph mapping.
summary.tldr: Any2Graph predicts variable-sized graphs with a differentiable, permutation-invariant optimal-transport loss.

title: Any2Graph: Deep End-To-End Supervised Graph Prediction With An Optimal Transport Loss

abstract: Collecting large quantities of high-quality data can be prohibitively expensive or impractical, and a bottleneck in machine learning. One may instead augment a small set of $n$ data points from the target distribution with data from more accessible sources, e.g. data collected under different circumstances or synthesized by generative models. We refer to such data as `surrogate data'. We study a weighted empirical risk minimization (ERM) approach for integrating surrogate data into training. We analyze mathematically this method under several classical statistical models, and validate our findings empirically on datasets from different domains. Our main findings are: $(i)$ Integrating surrogate data can significantly reduce the test error on the original distribution. Surprisingly, this can happen even when the surrogate data is unrelated to the original ones. We trace back this behavior to the classical Stein's paradox. $(ii)$ In order to reap the benefit of surrogate data, it is crucial to use optimally weighted ERM. $(iii)$ The test error of models trained on mixtures of real and surrogate data is approximately described by a scaling law. This scaling law can be used to predict the optimal weighting scheme, and to choose the amount of surrogate data to add.

paragraphs: When high-quality target data are expensive, additional training examples may come from different conditions or generative models. This paper calls those examples surrogate data and studies how to combine them with a smaller target dataset. The central method is weighted empirical risk minimization, which controls how much each data source influences training.

The authors analyze this method under several classical statistical models and test their findings on datasets from different domains. They find that surrogate data can substantially lower test error on the target distribution. Surprisingly, improvement can occur even with unrelated surrogate data, a phenomenon they connect to Stein's paradox. This is a possible benefit, not a claim that arbitrary added data always help.

Obtaining the benefit depends crucially on choosing optimal weights. The paper also finds that an approximate scaling law describes test error for models trained on mixtures of target and surrogate data. That relationship can guide both the weighting scheme and the amount of surrogate data to add, linking data acquisition decisions to expected predictive performance.
summary.tldr: An approximate scaling law helps choose how much surrogate data to add and how strongly to weight it for improved target-distribution predictions.

title: Scaling laws for learning with real and surrogate data

abstract: Despite advancements in Neural Implicit models for 3D surface reconstruction, handling dynamic environments with interactions between arbitrary rigid, non-rigid, or deformable entities remains challenging. The generic reconstruction methods adaptable to such dynamic scenes often require additional inputs like depth or optical flow or rely on pre-trained image features for reasonable outcomes. These methods typically use latent codes to capture frame-by-frame deformations. Another set of dynamic scene reconstruction methods, are entity-specific, mostly focusing on humans, and relies on template models. In contrast, some template-free methods bypass these requirements and adopt traditional LBS (Linear Blend Skinning) weights for a detailed representation of deformable object motions,although they involve complex optimizations leading to lengthy training times. To this end, as a remedy, this paper introduces TFS-NeRF, a template-free 3D semantic NeRF for dynamic scenes captured from sparse or single-view RGB videos, featuring interactions among two entities and more time-efficient than other LBS-based approaches. Our framework uses an Invertible Neural Network (INN) for LBS prediction, simplifying the training process. By disentangling the motions of interacting entities and optimizing per-entity skinning weights, our method efficiently generates accurate, semantically separable geometries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach produces high-quality reconstructions of both deformable and non-deformable objects in complex interactions, with improvedtraining efficiency compared to existing methods. The code and models will be available on our github page.

Its main architectural choice is an invertible neural network for predicting the skinning representation, which simplifies training. By separating the motions of interacting entities and optimizing skinning weights for each one, the framework can model their geometry and motion distinctly.

Experiments report high-quality reconstruction of both deformable and non-deformable objects during complex interactions, together with improved training efficiency over existing methods. The stated two-entity setting is important to the scope of the result. Within that setting, the contribution combines efficient motion estimation with semantically separable reconstruction, addressing both the cost of training and the difficulty of keeping interacting entities distinguishable in 3D.
summary.tldr: TFS-NeRF reconstructs two interacting entities from sparse or single-view RGB video using template-free motion modeling with improved training efficiency.

title: TFS-NeRF: Template-Free NeRF for Semantic 3D Reconstruction of Dynamic Scene

abstract: Certified adversarial robustness of large-scale deep networks has progressed substantially after the introduction of randomized smoothing. Deep net classifiers are now provably robust in their predictions against a large class of threat models, including $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_\infty$ norm-bounded attacks. Certified robustness analysis by randomized smoothing has not been performed for deep regression networks where the output variable is continuous and unbounded. In this paper, we extend the existing results for randomized smoothing into regression models using powerful tools from robust statistics, in particular, $\alpha$-trimming filter as the smoothing function. Adjusting the hyperparameter $\alpha$ achieves a smooth trade-off between desired certified robustness and utility. For the first time, we propose a benchmark for certified robust regression in visual positioning systems using the Cambridge Landmarks dataset where robustness analysis is essential for autonomous navigation of AI agents and self-driving cars. Code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/arekavandi/Certified_adv_RRegression/}.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing has enabled mathematical robustness guarantees for deep classifiers, but regression presents a different output problem. Its predictions are continuous and can be unbounded, rather than belonging to a fixed set of classes. This paper extends smoothing-based robustness analysis to deep regression networks, bringing certification into a setting not covered by the classification results discussed in the abstract.

The method uses robust statistics, specifically an alpha-trimming filter, as its smoothing function. Alpha acts as an adjustable control over the balance between certified robustness and predictive utility. This makes the robustness objective tunable: the framework explicitly accommodates different desired balances rather than presenting robustness and utility as independent outcomes.

The authors also propose a benchmark for certified regression in visual positioning, using the Cambridge Landmarks dataset. Position estimation connects the method to autonomous navigation, where continuous outputs matter directly. Together, the certification approach and benchmark provide a way to study how a regression model’s robustness changes with its smoothing configuration and how that protection relates to useful predictions.
summary.tldr: Alpha-trimmed randomized smoothing extends robustness certification to regression with a tunable robustness–utility trade-off.

title: Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized $\alpha$-Smoothing for Regression Models

abstract: Matching objectives underpin the success of modern generative models and rely on constructing conditional paths that transform a source distribution into a target distribution. Despite being a fundamental building block, conditional paths have been designed principally under the assumption of $\textit{Euclidean geometry}$, resulting in straight interpolations. However, this can be particularly restrictive for tasks such as trajectory inference, where straight paths might lie outside the data manifold, thus failing to capture the underlying dynamics giving rise to the observed marginals. In this paper, we propose Metric Flow Matching (MFM), a novel simulation-free framework for conditional flow matching where interpolants are approximate geodesics learned by minimizing the kinetic energy of a data-induced Riemannian metric. This way, the generative model matches vector fields on the data manifold, which corresponds to lower uncertainty and more meaningful interpolations. We prescribe general metrics to instantiate MFM, independent of the task, and test it on a suite of challenging problems including LiDAR navigation, unpaired image translation, and modeling cellular dynamics. We observe that MFM outperforms the Euclidean baselines, particularly achieving SOTA on single-cell trajectory prediction.

paragraphs: Flow-matching generative models rely on paths that connect source and target distributions. Straight paths are natural under Euclidean geometry, but they can pass outside the data manifold. For trajectory inference, that can produce interpolations that fail to reflect the dynamics responsible for the observed starting and ending distributions.

Metric Flow Matching changes the geometry used to construct these paths. It learns approximate geodesics by minimizing kinetic energy under a Riemannian metric induced by the data. The resulting simulation-free framework trains the generative model to match vector fields on the data manifold, which the authors associate with lower uncertainty and more meaningful interpolations.

The paper provides general, task-independent metrics and evaluates the framework on LiDAR navigation, unpaired image translation, and cellular dynamics. It reports improvements over Euclidean baselines and state-of-the-art results for single-cell trajectory prediction. These findings support the usefulness of data-informed path geometry, particularly when the intermediate trajectory is an important part of the task.
summary.tldr: Metric Flow Matching learns paths under data-induced geometry to produce more meaningful interpolations and improve trajectory-related tasks.

title: Metric Flow Matching for Smooth Interpolations on the Data Manifold

abstract: Biomolecular structure determination is essential to a mechanistic understanding of diseases and the development of novel therapeutics. Machine-learning-based structure prediction methods have made significant advancements by computationally predicting protein and bioassembly structures from sequences and molecular topology alone. Despite substantial progress in the field, challenges remain to deliver structure prediction models to real-world drug discovery. Here, we present NeuralPLexer3 -- a physics-inspired flow-based generative model that achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy on key biomolecular interaction types and improves training and sampling efficiency compared to its predecessors and alternative methodologies. Examined through existing and new benchmarks, NeuralPLexer3 excels in areas crucial to structure-based drug design, including blind docking, physical validity, and ligand-induced protein conformational changes.

Examined through existing and new benchmarks, NeuralPLexer3 excels in areas crucial to structure-based drug design, including blind docking, physical validity, and ligand-induced protein conformational changes.

paragraphs: NeuralPLexer3 is a generative model for predicting the structures of biomolecular complexes. Such structures help explain how biological molecules interact, making them relevant to understanding disease mechanisms and developing therapeutics. The paper addresses the continuing challenge of making computational structure prediction useful for real-world drug discovery.

The proposed model uses a physics-inspired, flow-based approach. The authors report state-of-the-art prediction accuracy for key biomolecular interaction types, together with improved training and sampling efficiency compared with predecessors and alternative methods. Both accuracy and efficiency matter to the stated goal of moving structure prediction toward practical discovery workflows.

Evaluation uses existing and new benchmarks and emphasizes blind docking, physical validity, and protein shape changes induced by ligands. These focus areas connect predicted structures with the interaction questions that arise in structure-based drug design. The reported findings therefore concern several aspects of useful complex prediction, including where molecules bind and how binding relates to protein conformation, alongside the efficiency of producing predictions.
summary.tldr: NeuralPLexer3 reports accurate, efficient biomolecular complex prediction using a physics-inspired flow model, with strengths relevant to drug design.

title: NeuralPLexer3: Accurate Biomolecular Complex Structure Prediction with Flow Models

abstract: Fast adversarial training (FAT) has been considered as one of the most effective alternatives to the computationally-intensive adversarial training. Generally, FAT methods pay equal attention to each sample of the target task. However, the distance between each sample and the decision boundary is different, learning samples which are far from the decision boundary (i.e., less important to adversarial robustness) brings additional training cost and leads to sub-optimal results. To tackle this issue, we present vulnerable data-aware adversarial training (VDAT) in this study. Specifically, we first propose a margin-based vulnerability calculation method to measure the vulnerability of data samples. Moreover, we propose a vulnerability-aware data filtering method to reduce the training data for adversarial training thus improve the training efficiency. The experiments are conducted in terms of adversarial training and robust neural architecture search on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K. The results demonstrate that VDAT is up to 76% more efficient than state-of-the-art FAT methods, while achieving improvements regarding the natural accuracy and adversarial accuracy in both scenarios. Furthermore, the visualizations and ablation studies show the effectiveness of both core components designed in VDAT.

paragraphs: Fast adversarial training reduces the cost of learning models that resist adversarial perturbations, but commonly treats all training examples equally. This paper argues that their value differs with their distance from the decision boundary. Examples farther from that boundary are less important to adversarial robustness, so spending equal effort on them can add cost and hurt results.

Vulnerable Data-Aware Adversarial Training first estimates each sample's vulnerability with a margin-based calculation. It then filters the training data according to those estimates, reducing the set used for adversarial training. The method connects an assessment of vulnerability directly to the allocation of training computation.

Experiments cover adversarial training and robust neural architecture search on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K. VDAT is reported to be up to 76% more efficient than state-of-the-art fast adversarial training methods, while improving both natural and adversarial accuracy in both scenarios. Visualizations and ablations support the effectiveness of the vulnerability calculation and filtering components, showing benefits from directing effort toward more vulnerable examples.
summary.tldr: VDAT filters training examples using margin-based vulnerability estimates to improve adversarial-training efficiency and accuracy.

title: Vulnerable Data-Aware Adversarial Training

abstract: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), they are increasingly deployed as autonomous computer-use agents capable of accomplishing complex computer tasks. However, a pressing issue arises: Can the safety risk principles designed and aligned for general MLLMs in dialogue scenarios be effectively transferred to real-world computer-use scenarios? Existing research on evaluating the safety risks of MLLM-based computer-use agents suffers from several limitations: it either lacks realistic interactive environments, or narrowly focuses on one or a few specific risk types. These limitations ignore the complexity, variability, and diversity of real-world environments, thereby restricting comprehensive risk evaluation for computer-use agents. To this end, we introduce **RiOSWorld**, a benchmark designed to evaluate the potential risks of MLLM-based agents during real-world computer manipulations. Our benchmark includes 492 risky tasks spanning various computer applications, involving web, social media, multimedia, os, email, and office software. We categorize these risks into two major classes based on their risk source: (i) User-originated risks and (ii) Environmental risks. For the evaluation, we evaluate safety risks from two perspectives: (i) Risk goal intention and (ii) Risk goal completion. Extensive experiments with multimodal agents on **RiOSWorld** demonstrate that current computer-use agents confront significant safety risks in real-world scenarios. Our findings highlight the necessity and urgency of safety alignment for computer-use agents in real-world computer manipulation, providing valuable insights for developing trustworthy computer-use agents.

paragraphs: RiOSWorld examines whether safety principles developed for conversational multimodal models carry over when those models operate computers. Acting through applications creates an interactive setting in which risky intentions and completed actions can differ. The findings support the need for safety alignment specifically suited to agents that manipulate computers and provide an evaluation resource for studying that problem in realistic interactive environments.
summary.tldr: RiOSWorld evaluates risky intentions and actions across 492 computer-use tasks, revealing substantial risks in current multimodal agents.

title: RiOSWorld: Benchmarking the Risk of Multimodal Computer-Use Agents

abstract: We propose a novel enhancement to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by incorporating learnable higher-order convolutions inspired by nonlinear biological visual processing. Our model extends the classical convolution operator using a Volterra-like expansion to capture multiplicative interactions observed in biological vision. Through extensive evaluation on standard benchmarks and synthetic datasets, we demonstrate that our architecture consistently outperforms traditional CNN baselines, achieving optimal performance with 3rd/4th order expansions. Systematic perturbation analysis and Representational Similarity Analysis reveal that different orders of convolution process distinct aspects of visual information, aligning with the statistical properties of natural images. This biologically-inspired approach offers both improved performance and deeper insights into visual information processing.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks build image representations through repeated local processing. This paper changes the convolution operation itself, drawing inspiration from nonlinear processing in biological vision. Its goal is to give the network a richer way to capture relationships within visual input, while investigating what different forms of that processing contribute.

The proposed operation uses a Volterra-like expansion with learnable higher-order terms. These terms capture multiplicative interactions, allowing the representation to depend on combinations of inputs. The order of the expansion controls which interactions are included. This makes interaction order an explicit architectural choice that the authors can vary and study.

Across standard benchmarks and synthetic datasets, the architecture consistently improves on the traditional CNN baselines evaluated. Third- and fourth-order expansions give the best performance in those experiments. Perturbation studies and comparisons of internal representations further suggest that different orders capture distinct aspects of visual information, consistent with natural-image statistics. The findings therefore support both a practical architectural improvement and an interpretation of how interaction order changes the information a network processes.
summary.tldr: Learnable higher-order convolutions improve tested image classifiers while revealing how different interaction orders capture different visual information.

title: Convolution Goes Higher-Order: A Biologically Inspired Mechanism Empowers Image Classification

abstract: Although Federated Learning (FL) is promising in privacy-preserving collaborative model training, it faces low inference performance due to heterogeneous data among clients. Due to heterogeneous data in each client, FL training easily learns the specific overfitting features. Existing FL methods adopt the coarse-grained average aggregation strategy, which causes the global model to easily get stuck in local optima, resulting in low generalization of the global model. Specifically, this paper presents a novel FL framework named FedPhoenix to address this issue, which stochastically resets partial parameters to destroy some features of the global model in each round to guide the FL training to learn multiple generalized features for inference rather than specific overfitting features. Experimental results on various well-known datasets demonstrate that compared to SOTA FL methods, FedPhoenix can achieve up to 20.73\% accuracy improvement.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model across clients whose data can differ substantially. The paper argues that this heterogeneity encourages features that overfit particular clients. When updates are combined through coarse averaging, the global model can become trapped in local optima and generalize poorly at inference time.

FedPhoenix introduces random partial parameter resets into each training round. Resetting some parameters deliberately disrupts part of the global model's learned features. The intended effect is to steer subsequent training toward a broader collection of generalizable features instead of repeatedly reinforcing features tied too closely to individual clients' data.

Experiments on several well-known datasets compare FedPhoenix with state-of-the-art federated learning methods and report accuracy improvements of up to 20.73%. This figure is the largest reported improvement, rather than a uniform gain across settings. The results support selective disruption as a useful component of collaborative training: partially removing learned structure can help the global model move beyond overfitted solutions in the heterogeneous settings studied.
summary.tldr: FedPhoenix randomly resets part of a federated model each round to improve generalization, reporting accuracy gains of up to 20.73%.

title: Rising from Ashes: Generalized Federated Learning via Dynamic Parameter Reset

abstract: Estimating hidden states in dynamical systems, also known as optimal filtering, is a long-standing problem in various fields of science and engineering. In this paper, we introduce a general filtering framework, $\textbf{LLM-Filter}$, which leverages large language models (LLMs) for state estimation by embedding noisy observations with text prototypes. In a number of experiments for classical dynamical systems, we find that first, state estimation can significantly benefit from the knowledge embedded in pre-trained LLMs. By achieving proper modality alignment with the frozen LLM, LLM-Filter outperforms the state-of-the-art learning-based approaches. Second, we carefully design the prompt structure, System-as-Prompt (SaP), incorporating task instructions that enable LLMs to understand tasks and adapt to specific systems. Guided by these prompts, LLM-Filter exhibits exceptional generalization, capable of performing filtering tasks accurately in changed or even unseen environments. We further observe a scaling-law behavior in LLM-Filter, where accuracy improves with larger model sizes and longer training times. These findings make LLM-Filter a promising foundation model of filtering.

The combination matters because the model must both receive observations in a compatible form and understand the estimation task those observations are meant to support.

In experiments on classical dynamical systems, proper modality alignment enables LLM-Filter to outperform state-of-the-art learning-based approaches. The authors also report accurate filtering in changed and previously unseen environments, together with a scaling pattern in which larger models and longer training improve accuracy. These findings motivate its proposed role as a foundation model for filtering, with the evidence coming from the systems and conditions evaluated.
summary.tldr: LLM-Filter aligns noisy observations with a frozen language model and uses system-specific prompts to estimate hidden dynamical states.

title: One Filters All: A Generalist Filter For State Estimation

abstract: Vision foundation models achieve remarkable performance but are only available in a limited set of pre-determined sizes, forcing sub-optimal deployment choices under real-world constraints. We introduce SnapViT: single-shot network approximation for pruned Vision Transformers, a new post-pretraining structured pruning method that enables elastic inference across a continuum of compute budgets. Our approach efficiently combines gradient information with cross-network structure correlations, approximated via an evolutionary algorithm, does not require labeled data, generalizes to models without a classification head, and is retraining-free. Experiments on DINO, SigLIPv2, DeIT, and AugReg models demonstrate superior performance over state-of-the-art methods across various sparsities, requiring less than five minutes on a single A100 GPU to generate elastic models that can be adjusted to any computational budget. Our key contributions include an efficient pruning strategy for pretrained Vision Transformers, a novel evolutionary approximation of Hessian off-diagonal structures, and a self-supervised importance scoring mechanism that maintains strong performance without requiring retraining or labels. Code and pruned models are available at: https://elastic.ashita.nl/

paragraphs: SnapViT addresses the mismatch between a few available sizes of pretrained vision models and the many compute budgets encountered in deployment. It creates pruned Vision Transformers whose inference cost can be adjusted across a continuum of budgets. This adaptation takes place after pretraining and requires neither model retraining nor labeled examples.

The pruning strategy combines gradient information with correlations among structures throughout the network. An evolutionary algorithm approximates off-diagonal Hessian structure, allowing the method to account for relationships between components when deciding their importance. A self-supervised scoring mechanism also lets it operate on models that lack a classification head, broadening the range of pretrained models it can adapt.

Experiments on DINO, SigLIPv2, DeIT, and AugReg report stronger performance than state-of-the-art pruning methods across different sparsity levels. Generating the elastic models takes less than five minutes on one A100 GPU in the reported evaluation. The practical contribution is a relatively quick conversion from a fixed pretrained model into one adjustable to deployment compute constraints.
summary.tldr: SnapViT converts pretrained Vision Transformers into adjustable-compute models through structured pruning without labels or retraining.

title: Elastic ViTs from Pretrained Models without Retraining

abstract: Pseudo-labeling is a commonly used paradigm in semi-supervised learning, yet its application to semi-supervised regression (SSR) remains relatively under-explored. Unlike classification, where pseudo-labels are discrete and confidence-based filtering is effective, SSR involves continuous outputs with heteroscedastic noise, making it challenging to assess pseudo-label reliability. As a result, naive pseudo-labeling can lead to error accumulation and overfitting to incorrect labels. To address this, we propose an uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling framework that dynamically adjusts pseudo-label influence from a bi-level optimization perspective. By jointly minimizing empirical risk over all data and optimizing uncertainty estimates to enhance generalization on labeled data, our method effectively mitigates the impact of unreliable pseudo-labels. We provide theoretical insights and extensive experiments to validate our approach across various benchmark SSR datasets, and the results demonstrate superior robustness and performance compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Pseudo-labeling uses a model’s predictions as training targets for unlabeled examples. In regression, those predictions are continuous, and their noise can vary from example to example. This heteroscedastic uncertainty makes reliability harder to judge than in classification. Treating unreliable predictions as trustworthy targets can accumulate errors and encourage overfitting.

The proposed framework adjusts the influence of pseudo-labels using learned uncertainty. It formulates the process as a bi-level optimization problem: one level minimizes empirical error across the available data, while another optimizes uncertainty estimates to improve generalization on labeled data. This ties the weight assigned to predicted labels to their usefulness for learning from known targets.

The paper provides theoretical insights and evaluates the approach on several semi-supervised regression benchmarks. Results show improved robustness and performance compared with existing methods. The main contribution is a principled way to control how much a learner trusts its own predictions when label quality varies, allowing unlabeled examples to contribute without giving unreliable pseudo-labels equal influence.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware bi-level optimization adjusts pseudo-label influence to improve semi-supervised regression when prediction noise varies across examples.

title: Semi-Supervised Regression with Heteroscedastic Pseudo-Labels

abstract: Time series forecasting plays a pivotal role in various real-world applications and has attracted significant attention in recent decades. While recent methods have achieved remarkable accuracy by incorporating advanced inductive biases and training strategies, we observe that instance-level variations remain a significant challenge. These variations—stemming from distribution shifts, missing data, and long-tail patterns—often lead to suboptimal forecasts for specific instances, even when overall performance appears strong. To address this issue, we propose a model-agnostic framework, PIR, designed to enhance forecasting performance through Post-forecasting Identification and Revision. Specifically, PIR first identifies biased forecast instances by estimating their predictive accuracy. Based on this, the framework revises the forecasts using contextual information, including covariates and historical time series, from both local and global perspectives in a post-processing fashion. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets with mainstream forecasting models demonstrate that PIR effectively mitigates instance-level errors and significantly improves forecasting reliability.

paragraphs: A forecasting model can have strong average accuracy while failing badly on particular sequences affected by missing values, distribution shifts, or rare patterns. PIR targets those instance-level errors after the original forecasting model has already produced its predictions.

The model-agnostic framework first estimates predictive accuracy to identify biased forecast instances. It then revises selected outputs using covariates and historical series from local and global perspectives. This creates a separate correction stage that can be applied across different underlying forecasting models.

Experiments with mainstream forecasters on real-world datasets show improved reliability and reduced instance-level error. The contribution focuses attention on which individual predictions need intervention, rather than uniformly changing every output. Its post-processing design makes contextual revision a complementary component that can improve existing forecasting systems without replacing their primary prediction architecture.
summary.tldr: PIR detects unreliable individual forecasts and revises them using local and global context.

title: Improving Time Series Forecasting via Instance-aware Post-hoc Revision

abstract: Linear recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba have become promising alternatives to softmax-attention as sequence mixing layers in Transformer architectures. Current models, however, do not exhibit the full state-tracking expressivity of RNNs because they rely on channel-wise (i.e. diagonal) sequence mixing. In this paper, we investigate parameterizations of a large class of dense linear RNNs as fixed-points of parallelizable diagonal linear RNNs. The resulting models can naturally trade expressivity for efficiency at a fixed number of parameters and achieve state-of-the-art results on the state-tracking benchmarks $A_5$ and $S_5$, while matching performance on copying and other tasks.

paragraphs: Linear recurrent networks and state-space models offer alternatives to attention for combining information across a sequence. The paper focuses on a restriction in current designs: sequence mixing happens separately within channels. This diagonal structure supports efficient computation, but the authors argue that it lacks the full state-tracking expressivity available to recurrent networks.

Their approach represents a large class of dense linear recurrent networks as fixed points of diagonal linear recurrent networks that can be parallelized. A fixed point is a state that remains unchanged when the defining update is applied. This connects a computationally convenient diagonal formulation to denser interactions between channels.

The resulting models can trade expressivity against efficiency while keeping the parameter count fixed. That makes the tradeoff about how computation is organized, rather than simply adding more learned weights. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on the A5 and S5 state-tracking benchmarks and matching performance on copying and other tasks. These results support the usefulness of recovering richer state tracking without abandoning the diagonal computation underlying the construction.
summary.tldr: Fixed-point formulations connect parallelizable diagonal RNNs to dense recurrence, enabling an efficiency–expressivity tradeoff at fixed parameter count.

title: Fixed-Point RNNs: Interpolating from Diagonal to Dense

abstract: Many confounding-resistant domain generalization methods for image classification have been developed based on causal interventions. However, their reliance on strong assumptions limits their effectiveness in handling unobserved confounders. Although recent work introduces instrumental variables (IVs) to overcome this limitation, the reliance on manually predefined instruments, particularly in the context of visual data, may result in severe bias or invalidity when IV conditions are violated. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach to automatically learning Visual Instrumental Variables for confounding-resistant Domain Generalization (VIV-DG). We observe that certain non-causal visual attributes in image data naturally satisfy the basic conditions required for valid IVs. Motivated by this insight, we propose the visual instrumental variable, a novel concept that extends classical IV theory to the visual domain. Furthermore, we develop an automatic visual instrumental variable learner that enforces IV conditions on learned representations, enabling the automatic learning of valid visual instrumental variables from image data. Ultimately, VIV-DG inherits the strengths of classical IVs to mitigate unobserved confounding and avoids the significant bias caused by violations of IV conditions in predefined IVs. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks verify that VIV-DG achieves superior generalization ability.

paragraphs: An image classifier can learn relationships that work in its training environment but fail elsewhere because hidden factors influence those relationships. Causal approaches try to address this confounding, but their assumptions can be restrictive. Instrumental variables offer another route, although manually choosing suitable instruments for images risks introducing bias when the required conditions do not hold.

VIV-DG proposes learning visual instrumental variables automatically. Its starting observation is that certain non-causal visual attributes naturally meet the basic requirements for an instrument. The method extends instrumental-variable reasoning to visual representations and trains a learner that explicitly enforces the relevant conditions, rather than depending on a predefined choice of visual instrument.

The intended benefit is to reduce the influence of unobserved confounders while avoiding bias from invalid predefined instruments. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report stronger generalization. These findings support learning instruments as part of the image-classification system, with validity conditions playing a central role in how those representations are constructed.
summary.tldr: VIV-DG automatically learns visual instrumental variables to reduce hidden confounding and improve image-classification generalization.

title: Automatic Visual Instrumental Variable Learning for Confounding-Resistant Domain Generalization

abstract: Adapting large-scale foundation models in multi-task scenarios often suffers from task conflict and oblivion. To mitigate such issues, we propose a novel "model MoE-ization" strategy that leads to a conflict- and oblivion-resistant multi-task adaptation method. Given a weight matrix of a pre-trained model, our method applies SVD to it and introduces a learnable router to adjust its singular values based on tasks and samples. Accordingly, the weight matrix becomes a Mixture of Orthogonal Rank-one Experts (MoORE), in which each expert corresponds to the outer product of a left singular vector and the corresponding right one. We can improve the model capacity by imposing a learnable orthogonal transform on the right singular vectors. Unlike low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and its MoE-driven variants, MoORE guarantees the experts' orthogonality and maintains the column space of the original weight matrix. These two properties make the adapted model resistant to the conflicts among the new tasks and the oblivion of its original tasks, respectively. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate that MoORE outperforms existing multi-task adaptation methods consistently, showing its superiority in terms of conflict- and oblivion-resistance. The code is available at https://github.com/DaShenZi721/MoORE.

paragraphs: Adapting a foundation model to several tasks can create interference between new tasks and weaken its original capabilities. MoORE addresses both problems by changing how pretrained weight matrices are adapted. It turns each matrix into a collection of orthogonal rank-one experts, with their contributions adjusted for particular tasks and samples.

The construction starts with singular value decomposition. Each paired left and right singular vector defines an expert, and a learned router adjusts the corresponding singular values. A learnable orthogonal transformation of the right singular vectors can increase capacity. The method guarantees expert orthogonality while preserving the original matrix's column space.

The paper connects these two structural properties to different goals: orthogonality supports resistance to conflicts among new tasks, while column-space preservation supports resistance to forgetting original tasks. Across the reported datasets, MoORE consistently outperforms existing multi-task adaptation methods. The contribution is a structured adaptation mechanism with guarantees about its representation, accompanied by empirical evidence of resistance to interference and forgetting.
summary.tldr: MoORE routes among orthogonal components of pretrained weights to improve multi-task adaptation while resisting interference and forgetting.

title: MoORE: SVD-based Model MoE-ization for Conflict- and Oblivion-Resistant Multi-Task Adaptation

abstract: Many emerging applications—such as adversarial training, AI alignment, and robust optimization—can be framed as zero-sum games between neural nets, with von Neumann–Nash equilibria (NE) capturing the desirable system behavior. While such games often involve non-convex non-concave objectives, empirical evidence shows that simple gradient methods frequently converge, suggesting a hidden geometric structure. In this paper, we provide a theoretical framework that explains this phenomenon through the lens of \emph{hidden convexity} and \emph{overparameterization}. We identify sufficient conditions spanning initialization, training dynamics, and network width—that guarantee global convergence to a NE in a broad class of non-convex min-max games. To our knowledge, this is the first such result for games that involve two-layer neural networks. Technically, our approach is twofold: (a) we derive a novel path-length bound for alternating gradient-descent-ascent scheme in min-max games; and (b) we show that games with hidden convex–concave geometry reduce to settings satisfying two-sided Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) and smoothness conditions, which hold with high probability under overparameterization, using tools from random matrix theory.

Although these objectives can be non-convex and non-concave, simple gradient methods often converge empirically. This paper develops a theoretical explanation based on hidden convexity and overparameterization, seeking conditions under which the dynamics reach a desirable Nash equilibrium.

The authors identify sufficient conditions involving initialization, training dynamics, and network width that guarantee global convergence for a broad class of these games. Their analysis includes games involving two-layer neural networks. A second ingredient connects hidden convex-concave geometry to two-sided Polyak–Łojasiewicz and smoothness conditions. Using random matrix theory, the authors show that the relevant conditions hold with high probability under overparameterization. The result explains how architecture and initialization can support successful gradient dynamics. Its guarantee depends on the identified sufficient conditions; it does not assert that arbitrary neural games or training setups converge.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions on width, initialization, and training dynamics for global convergence in a class of neural min-max games.

title: Solving Neural Min-Max Games: The Role of Architecture, Initialization & Dynamics

abstract: Many computational tasks benefit from being formulated as the composition of neural networks followed by a discrete symbolic program. The goal of neurosymbolic learning is to train the neural networks using end-to-end input-output labels of the composite. We introduce CTSketch, a novel, scalable neurosymbolic learning algorithm. CTSketch uses two techniques to improve the scalability of neurosymbolic inference: decompose the symbolic program into sub-programs and summarize each sub-program with a sketched tensor. This strategy allows us to approximate the output distribution of the program with simple tensor operations over the input distributions and the sketches. We provide theoretical insight into the maximum approximation error. Furthermore, we evaluate CTSketch on benchmarks from the neurosymbolic learning literature, including some designed for evaluating scalability. Our results show that CTSketch pushes neurosymbolic learning to new scales that were previously unattainable, with neural predictors obtaining high accuracy on tasks with one thousand inputs, despite supervision only on the final output.

paragraphs: CTSketch addresses learning systems in which neural networks feed their predictions into a discrete symbolic program. Training uses labels for the final combined output, so the neural components must learn from supervision that arrives after symbolic processing. The paper focuses on making this arrangement scale when the symbolic computation involves many inputs.

The method divides the symbolic program into smaller subprograms and represents each with a compact tensor sketch. It then combines those sketches with distributions over the neural predictions using simple tensor operations. This approximates the program's output distribution while preserving a compositional structure: summaries of smaller computations become building blocks for the larger computation. The authors also provide theoretical insight into the maximum approximation error.

Evaluations include established neurosymbolic benchmarks and tasks designed to test scalability. The reported neural predictors achieve high accuracy on tasks involving one thousand inputs despite receiving supervision only on the final output. The results show that approximating symbolic inference through compositional sketches can extend the practical scale of this learning setup.
summary.tldr: CTSketch compresses symbolic subprograms into tensor sketches, enabling accurate neurosymbolic learning on evaluated tasks with one thousand inputs.

title: CTSketch: Compositional Tensor Sketching for Scalable Neurosymbolic Learning

abstract: Transformer architectures can solve unseen tasks based on input-output pairs in a given prompt due to in-context learning (ICL). Existing theoretical studies on ICL have mainly focused on linear regression tasks, often with i.i.d. inputs. To understand how transformers express in-context learning when modeling dynamics-driven functions, we investigate Markovian function learning through a structured ICL setup, where we characterize the loss landscape to reveal underlying optimization behaviors. Specifically, we (1) provide the closed-form expression of the global minimizer (in an enlarged parameter space) for a single-layer linear self-attention (LSA) model; (2) prove that recovering transformer parameters that realize the optimal solution is NP-hard in general, revealing a fundamental limitation of one-layer LSA in representing structured dynamical functions; and (3) supply a novel interpretation of a multilayer LSA as performing preconditioned gradient descent to optimize multiple objectives beyond the square loss. These theoretical results are numerically validated using simplified transformers.

These theoretical results are numerically validated using simplified transformers.

paragraphs: This paper studies how Transformers learn from examples in a prompt when those examples describe Markovian dynamics. Such structured problems extend beyond the independent inputs and linear regression tasks emphasized by earlier theory. The authors analyze the optimization landscape of linear self-attention models to understand both their optimal solutions and the difficulty of realizing them.

For a single attention layer, they derive a closed-form global minimizer in an enlarged parameter space. However, recovering Transformer parameters that implement that solution is NP-hard in general. The distinction is consequential: expressing an optimum in a broader mathematical space does not make obtaining corresponding model parameters computationally straightforward.

The paper also interprets multilayer linear self-attention as carrying out preconditioned gradient descent across multiple objectives, extending beyond squared error. Numerical experiments with simplified Transformers validate the theoretical results. These findings give a more detailed account of in-context learning for dynamical functions, while keeping the hardness claim tied to the analyzed one-layer setting rather than asserting that every Transformer learning problem is intractable.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal linear-attention learning of Markovian functions and proves that recovering parameters for the one-layer optimum is NP-hard in general.

title: Optimality and NP-Hardness of Transformers in Learning Markovian Dynamical Functions

abstract: Adafactor is an early memory-efficient optimization algorithm proposed as an alternative to Adam. By eliminating first-order momentum and employing a rank-$1$ matrix factorization to approximate the second-moment matrix, Adafactor achieves near-zero memory overhead compared to traditional gradient descent methods. Despite its practical suitability for large-scale training tasks where memory efficiency is critical, its theoretical convergence analysis remains unexplored, largely due to the challenges posed by its matrix factorization and update clipping mechanisms. In this work, we provide a convergence analysis of Adafactor for non-convex smooth optimization. We establish optimal convergence rates (up to logarithmic factors) for finding stationary points in both deterministic and stochastic settings, the latter under sub-Gaussian noises. Central to our analysis involves viewing Adafactor as an approximation of Adam, and the use of a new proxy step-size to approximate the unique adaptive step-size induced by Adafactor's matrix factorization and update clipping, along with an induction argument to control the gradient magnitude. Our finding may theoretically suggest that involving rank-$1$ matrix approximation of the second-moment matrix in Adam does not fundamentally hinder the convergence.

paragraphs: Adafactor is a memory-efficient optimizer that approximates second-moment information with a rank-one matrix factorization and removes first-order momentum. This greatly reduces auxiliary storage compared with maintaining full optimizer statistics. The paper addresses a theoretical gap: understanding convergence when these compressed statistics interact with the algorithm's update-clipping mechanism.

The guarantee concerns stationary points rather than a claim of finding a global optimum.

The analysis treats Adafactor as an approximation to Adam. A new proxy step size captures the adaptive behavior arising from factorization and clipping, while an induction argument controls gradient magnitudes. The results suggest that rank-one approximation of Adam's second-moment matrix need not fundamentally impair convergence. This supplies theoretical support for a memory-saving design already motivated by large-scale training.
summary.tldr: Adafactor attains near-optimal stationary-point convergence rates for smooth non-convex optimization, including stochastic settings with sub-Gaussian noise.

title: Theoretical Investigation of Adafactor for Non-Convex Smooth Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of sampling distributions stemming from non-convex potentials with Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA). We prove the stability of the discrete-time ULA to drift approximations under the assumption that the potential is strongly convex at infinity. In many context, e.g. imaging inverse problems, potentials are non-convex and non-smooth. Proximal Stochastic Gradient Langevin Algorithm (PSGLA) is a popular algorithm to handle such potentials. It combines the forward-backward optimization algorithm with a ULA step. Our main stability result combined with properties of the Moreau envelope allows us to derive the first proof of convergence of the PSGLA for non-convex potentials. We empirically validate our methodology on synthetic data and in the context of imaging inverse problems. In particular, we observe that PSGLA exhibits faster convergence rates than Stochastic Gradient Langevin Algorithm for posterior sampling while preserving its restoration properties.

title: From stability of Langevin diffusion to convergence of proximal MCMC for non-log-concave sampling

abstract: Recent advancements in foundation models for 2D vision have substantially improved the analysis of dynamic scenes from monocular videos. However, despite their strong generalization capabilities, these models often lack 3D consistency, a fundamental requirement for understanding scene geometry and motion, thereby causing severe spatial misalignment and temporal flickering in complex 3D environments. In this paper, we present Motion4D, a novel framework that addresses these challenges by integrating 2D priors from foundation models into a unified 4D Gaussian Splatting representation. Our method features a two-part iterative optimization framework: 1) Sequential optimization, which updates motion and semantic fields in consecutive stages to maintain local consistency, and 2) Global optimization, which jointly refines all attributes for long-term coherence. To enhance motion accuracy, we introduce a 3D confidence map that dynamically adjusts the motion priors, and an adaptive resampling process that inserts new Gaussians into under-represented regions based on per-pixel RGB and semantic errors. Furthermore, we enhance semantic coherence through an iterative refinement process that resolves semantic inconsistencies by alternately optimizing the semantic fields and updating prompts of SAM2. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our Motion4D significantly outperforms both 2D foundation models and existing 3D-based approaches across diverse scene understanding tasks, including point-based tracking, video object segmentation, and novel view synthesis. Our code is available at https://hrzhou2.github.io/motion4d-web/.

Evaluations report significant improvements over both 2D foundation models and existing 3D approaches on point tracking, video object segmentation, and novel-view synthesis. title: Motion4D: Learning 3D-Consistent Motion and Semantics for 4D Scene Understanding

abstract: Humans naturally understand moments in a video by integrating visual and auditory cues. For example, localizing a scene in the video like “A scientist passionately speaks on wildlife conservation as dramatic orchestral music plays, with the audience nodding and applauding” requires simultaneous processing of visual, audio, and speech signals. However, existing models often struggle to effectively fuse and interpret audio information, limiting their capacity for comprehensive video temporal understanding. To address this, we present TriSense, a triple-modality large language model designed for holistic video temporal understanding through the integration of visual, audio, and speech modalities. Central to TriSense is a Query-Based Connector that adaptively reweights modality contributions based on the input query, enabling robust performance under modality dropout and allowing flexible combinations of available inputs. To support TriSense's multimodal capabilities, we introduce TriSense-2M, a high-quality dataset of over 2 million curated samples generated via an automated pipeline powered by fine-tuned LLMs. TriSense-2M includes long-form videos and diverse modality combinations, facilitating broad generalization. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of TriSense and its potential to advance multimodal video analysis.

Its Query-Based Connector adjusts the contribution of each modality according to the question. This makes the fusion responsive to what information the user seeks. The connector also supports different combinations of available inputs and robust performance when a modality is missing, rather than requiring the same inputs for every example.

title: Watch and Listen: Understanding Audio-Visual-Speech Moments with Multimodal LLM

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the necessity of traceability for accurate learning in stochastic convex optimization (SCO) under $\ell_p$ geometries. Informally, we say a learning algorithm is \emph{$m$-traceable} if, by analyzing its output, it is possible to identify at least $m$ of its training samples. Our main results uncover a fundamental tradeoff between traceability and excess risk in SCO. For every $p\in [1,\infty)$, we establish the existence of an excess risk threshold below which every sample-efficient learner is traceable with the number of samples which is a \emph{constant fraction} of its training sample. For $p\in [1,2]$, this threshold coincides with the best excess risk of differentially private (DP) algorithms, i.e., above this threshold, there exist algorithms that are not traceable, which corresponds to a sharp phase transition. For $p \in (2,\infty)$, this threshold instead gives novel lower bounds for DP learning, partially closing an open problem in this setup. En route to establishing these results, we prove a sparse variant of the fingerprinting lemma, which is of independent interest to the community.

For every finite p at least one, the authors establish an excess-risk threshold below which every sample-efficient learner is traceable to a constant fraction of its training set. title: On Traceability in $\ell_p$ Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: Dynamic GNNs, which integrate temporal and spatial features in Electroencephalography (EEG) data, have shown great potential in automating seizure detection. However, fully capturing the underlying dynamics necessary to represent brain states, such as seizure and non-seizure, remains a non-trivial task and presents two fundamental challenges. First, most existing dynamic GNN methods are built on temporally fixed static graphs, which fail to reflect the evolving nature of brain connectivity during seizure progression. Second, current efforts to jointly model temporal signals and graph structures and, more importantly, their interactions remain nascent, often resulting in inconsistent performance. To address these challenges, we present the first theoretical analysis of these two problems, demonstrating the effectiveness and necessity of explicit dynamic modeling and time-then-graph dynamic GNN method. Building on these insights, we propose EvoBrain, a novel seizure detection model that integrates a two-stream Mamba architecture with a GCN enhanced by Laplacian Positional Encoding, following neurological insights. Moreover, EvoBrain incorporates explicitly dynamic graph structures, allowing both nodes and edges to evolve over time. Our contributions include (a) a theoretical analysis proving the expressivity advantage of explicit dynamic modeling and time-then-graph over other approaches, (b) a novel and efficient model that significantly improves AUROC by 23\% and F1 score by 30\%, compared with the dynamic GNN baseline, and (c) broad evaluation of our method on the challenging early seizure prediction task.

It also examines how temporal signal processing and graph structure should interact to represent seizure and non-seizure states.

title: EvoBrain: Dynamic Multi-Channel EEG Graph Modeling for Time-Evolving Brain Networks

abstract: Probabilistic time series forecasting, essential in domains like healthcare and neuroscience, requires models capable of capturing uncertainty and intricate temporal dependencies. While deep learning has advanced forecasting, generating calibrated probability distributions over continuous future values remains challenging. We introduce Temporal Generative Flow Networks (Temporal GFNs), adapting Generative Flow Networks (GFNs) – a powerful framework for generating compositional objects – to this sequential prediction task. GFNs learn policies to construct objects (eg. forecast trajectories) step-by-step, sampling final objects proportionally to a reward signal. However, applying GFNs directly to continuous time series necessitates addressing their inherently discrete action spaces and ensuring differentiability. Our framework tackles this by representing time series segments as states and sequentially generating future values via quantized actions chosen by a forward policy. We introduce two key innovations: (1) An adaptive, curriculum-based quantization strategy that dynamically adjusts the number of discretization bins based on reward improvement and policy entropy, balancing precision and exploration throughout training. (2) A straight-through estimator mechanism enabling the forward policy to output both discrete (hard) samples for trajectory construction and continuous (soft) samples for stable gradient propagation. Training utilizes a trajectory balance loss objective, ensuring flow consistency, augmented by an entropy regularizer. We provide rigorous theoretical bounds on the quantization error's impact and the adaptive factor's range. We demonstrate how Temporal GFNs offer a principled way to leverage the structured generation capabilities of GFNs for probabilistic forecasting in continuous domains.

title: Adaptive Quantization in Generative Flow Networks for Probabilistic Sequential Prediction

abstract: Decoding natural language text from non-invasive brain signals, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), remains a central challenge in brain-computer interface research. While recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled open-vocabulary fMRI-to-text decoding, existing frameworks typically process the entire fMRI sequence in a single step, leading to performance degradation when handling long input sequences due to memory overload and semantic drift. To address this limitation, we propose a brain-inspired sequential fMRI-to-text decoding framework that mimics the human cognitive strategy of segmented and inductive language processing. Specifically, we divide long fMRI time series into consecutive segments aligned with optimal language comprehension length. Each segment is decoded incrementally, followed by a wrap-up mechanism that summarizes the semantic content and incorporates it as prior knowledge into subsequent decoding steps. This sequence-wise approach alleviates memory burden and ensures semantic continuity across segments. In addition, we introduce a text-guided masking strategy integrated with a masked autoencoder (MAE) framework for fMRI representation learning. This method leverages attention distributions over key semantic tokens to selectively mask the corresponding fMRI time points, and employs MAE to guide the model toward focusing on neural activity at semantically salient moments, thereby enhancing the capability of fMRI embeddings to represent textual information. Experimental results on the two datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, with performance gains increasing as decoding length grows.

title: Brain-Inspired fMRI-to-Text Decoding via Incremental and Wrap-Up Language Modeling

abstract: Foundational world models must be both interactive and preserve spatialtemporal coherence to enable effective future planning with different action choices. However, present models for long video generation have limited inherent world modeling capabilities due to two main challenges: compounding errors and insufficient memory mechanisms. We enhance image-to-video models with interactive capabilities through additional action conditioning and autoregressive framework, and reveal that compounding error is inherently irreducible in autoregressive video generation, while insufficient memory mechanism leads to incoherence of world models. We propose video retrieval augmented generation (VRAG) with explicit global state conditioning, which significantly reduces long-term compounding errors and increases spatialtemporal consistency of video world models. In contrast, naive autoregressive generation with extended context windows and retrieval-augmented generation prove less effective for video generation, primarily due to the limited in-context learning capabilities of current video models. Our work illuminates the fundamental challenges in video world models and establishes a comprehensive benchmark for improving video generation models with internal world modeling capabilities.

paragraphs: A video world model must respond to actions while keeping the depicted environment coherent over time. This paper adds action conditioning and autoregressive generation to image-to-video models, then examines why long sequences lose consistency. It identifies compounding prediction errors and insufficient memory as central challenges for interactive world modeling.

This gives generation a representation of the broader world state and significantly reduces long-term error accumulation while improving spatial and temporal consistency.

The distinction matters because additional history alone does not ensure useful memory. The paper contributes a benchmark alongside its method, providing a setting for evaluating progress toward interactive generation with stronger internal world modeling.
summary.tldr: VRAG uses explicit global-state conditioning to reduce long-term errors and improve coherence in action-conditioned video world models.

title: Learning World Models for Interactive Video Generation

abstract: The construction of confidence intervals for the mean of a bounded random variable is a classical problem in statistics with numerous applications in machine learning and virtually all scientific fields. In particular, obtaining the tightest possible confidence intervals is vital every time the sampling of the random variables is expensive. The current state-of-the-art method to construct confidence intervals is by using betting algorithms. This is a very successful approach for deriving optimal confidence sequences, even matching the rate of law of iterated logarithms. However, in the fixed horizon setting, these approaches are either sub-optimal or based on heuristic solutions with strong empirical performance but without a finite-time guarantee. Hence, no betting-based algorithm guaranteeing the optimal $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2\log\frac1\delta}{n}})$ width of the confidence intervals are known. This work bridges this gap. We propose a betting-based algorithm to compute confidence intervals that empirically outperforms the competitors. Our betting strategy uses the optimal strategy in every step (in a certain sense), whereas the standard betting methods choose a constant strategy in advance. Leveraging this fact results in strict improvements even for classical concentration inequalities, such as the ones of Hoeffding or Bernstein. Moreover, we also prove that the width of our confidence intervals is optimal up to an $1+o(1)$ factor diminishing with $n$.

summary.tldr: STAR-Bets adapts its betting strategy at each step to produce tighter fixed-horizon confidence intervals with asymptotically optimal width.

title: STAR-Bets: Sequential TArget-Recalculating Bets for Tighter Confidence Intervals

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved significant success, yet their application to time series data, particularly with regard to efficient sampling, remains an active area of research. We describe an operator-learning approach for conditioned time-series diffusion models that gives efficient single-step generation by leveraging insights from the frequency-domain characteristics of both the time-series data and the diffusion process itself. The forward diffusion process induces a structured, frequency-dependent smoothing of the data's probability density function. However, this frequency smoothing is related (e.g., via likelihood function) to easily accessible frequency components of time-series data. This suggests that a module operating in the frequency space of the time-series can, potentially, more effectively learn to reverse the frequency-dependent smoothing of the data distribution induced by the diffusion process. We set up an operator learning task, based on frequency-aware building blocks, which satisfies semi-group properties, while exploiting the structure of time-series data. Evaluations on multiple datasets show that our single-step generation proposal achieves forecasting/imputation results comparable (or superior) to many multi-step diffusion schemes while significantly reducing inference costs.

However, this frequency smoothing is related (e.g., via likelihood function) to easily accessible frequency components of time-series data. We set up an operator learning task, based on frequency-aware building blocks, which satisfies semi-group properties, while exploiting the structure of time-series data. Evaluations on multiple datasets show that our single-step generation proposal achieves forecasting/imputation results comparable (or superior) to many multi-step diffusion schemes while significantly reducing inference costs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can perform time-series forecasting and fill in missing observations, but repeated sampling steps add inference cost. This paper develops an operator-learning approach for conditioned time-series diffusion that generates an output in a single step. Its design draws on frequency structure in both the data and the diffusion process.

The authors describe forward diffusion as imposing frequency-dependent smoothing on the data's probability density. That smoothing is related to accessible frequency components of the time series. This relationship suggests that frequency-space modules may learn the reversal more effectively. The proposed learning task uses frequency-aware building blocks and satisfies semigroup properties, incorporating structure from the time series into the learned operator.

Across multiple datasets, single-step generation achieves forecasting and imputation results comparable to, or better than, many multistep diffusion schemes while substantially reducing inference costs. The evidence supports the proposed frequency-aware design as an efficient sampling approach. The motivation remains appropriately conditional: frequency structure suggests a useful route to learning the reversal, while the experiments establish its observed benefits.
summary.tldr: Frequency-aware operator learning enables single-step time-series diffusion with competitive forecasting and imputation quality at lower inference cost.

title: Single-Step Operator Learning for Conditioned Time-Series Diffusion Models

abstract: Much work in optimal control and inverse control has assumed that the controller has perfect knowledge of plant dynamics. However, if the controller is a human or animal subject, the subject’s internal dynamics model may differ from the true plant dynamics. Here, we consider the problem of learning the subject’s internal model from demonstrations of control and knowledge of task goals. Due to sensory feedback delay, the subject uses an internal model to generate an internal prediction of the current plant state, which may differ from the actual plant state. We develop a probabilistic framework and exact EM algorithm to jointly estimate the internal model, internal state trajectories, and feedback delay. We applied this framework to demonstrations by a nonhuman primate of brain-machine interface (BMI) control. We discovered that the subject’s internal model deviated from the true BMI plant dynamics and provided significantly better explanation of the recorded neural control signals than did the true plant dynamics.
