paragraphs: A person or animal controlling a system may act using an internal understanding that differs from the system's true dynamics. This paper seeks to recover that internal model from control demonstrations and known task goals. The distinction matters because behavior can reflect what the subject believes the system will do, rather than its actual behavior.

Sensory feedback delay is central to the framework. Because current feedback is unavailable immediately, the subject uses an internal model to predict the present state, and that prediction may differ from reality. The authors develop a probabilistic framework and an exact expectation-maximization algorithm that jointly estimate the internal dynamics, internal state trajectories, and feedback delay.

They apply the method to brain-machine interface control demonstrated by a nonhuman primate. The inferred internal model differs from the actual interface dynamics and explains recorded neural control signals significantly better than the true dynamics do. This finding supports explicitly modeling the subject's internal prediction process when interpreting the observed control signals.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic method infers a subject's internal dynamics and feedback delay, better explaining neural control signals in the reported brain-machine interface application.

title: Learning an Internal Dynamics Model from Control Demonstration

abstract: Active learning and transfer learning are two different methodologies that address the common problem of insufficient labels. Transfer learning addresses this problem by using the knowledge gained from a related and already labeled data source, whereas active learning focuses on selecting a small set of informative samples for manual annotation. Recently, there has been much interest in developing frameworks that combine both transfer and active learning methodologies. A few such frameworks reported in literature perform transfer and active learning in two separate stages. In this work, we present an integrated framework that performs transfer and active learning simultaneously by solving a single convex optimization problem. The proposed framework computes the weights of source domain data and selects the samples from the target domain data simultaneously, by minimizing a common objective of reducing distribution difference between the data set consisting of reweighted source and the queried target domain data and the set of unlabeled target domain data. Comprehensive experiments on three real world data sets demonstrate that the proposed method improves the classification accuracy by 5% to 10% over the existing two-stage approach

paragraphs: Transfer learning and active learning address limited labels in complementary ways. Transfer learning borrows information from a related labeled source, while active learning selects examples for people to label. The paper brings these decisions together, arguing through its formulation that the usefulness of source data and the choice of target examples can be assessed jointly.

The proposed framework solves one convex optimization problem that simultaneously weights source-domain examples and selects a batch of target-domain examples for annotation. Both decisions serve a common objective: reduce the distribution difference between the combined reweighted source and queried target data, and the remaining unlabeled target data. Thus annotation choices and source weighting are coordinated through the same distribution-matching goal.

Experiments on three real-world datasets report classification accuracy improvements of 5% to 10% over an existing two-stage approach. The findings support the value of integrating the two learning procedures in the evaluated settings. The methodological contribution is a single optimization framework that decides which existing labels to emphasize while also deciding which new labels to request.
summary.tldr: A single convex objective jointly weights labeled source data and selects target examples for annotation.

title: Joint Transfer and Batch-mode Active Learning

abstract: Topic models have become increasingly prominent text-analytic machine learning tools for research in the social sciences and the humanities. In particular, custom topic models can be developed to answer specific research questions. The design of these models requires a non-trivial amount of effort and expertise, motivating general-purpose topic modeling frameworks. In this paper we introduce latent topic networks, a flexible class of richly structured topic models designed to facilitate applied research. Custom models can straightforwardly be developed in our framework with an intuitive first-order logical probabilistic programming language. Latent topic networks admit scalable training via a parallelizable EM algorithm which leverages ADMM in the M-step. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the models with case studies on modeling influence in citation networks, and U.S. Presidential State of the Union addresses.

paragraphs: Researchers often need topic models tailored to a particular question, especially in the social sciences and humanities. Building those models individually requires substantial design effort and technical expertise. This paper introduces latent topic networks as a flexible family of structured topic models intended to make such customization more accessible within a common framework.

Users express custom models through a probabilistic programming language based on first-order logic. This provides a way to specify richer topic-model structure without designing a wholly separate framework for each application. Training uses a parallelizable expectation-maximization algorithm, with ADMM handling the maximization step, connecting modeling flexibility to a scalable computational procedure.

The paper demonstrates the framework through case studies involving influence in citation networks and presidential State of the Union addresses. These applications illustrate its ability to accommodate different research questions and text collections. The central contribution is a reusable route from structured model specification to training, with the case studies supporting broad applicability rather than establishing a single predictive advantage across all topic-modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: Latent topic networks combine logical probabilistic programming with parallelizable training to support customized, richly structured topic models.

title: Latent Topic Networks: A Versatile Probabilistic Programming Framework for Topic Models

abstract: We show that parametric models trained by a stochastic gradient method (SGM) with few iterations have vanishing generalization error. We prove our results by arguing that SGM is algorithmically stable in the sense of Bousquet and Elisseeff. Our analysis only employs elementary tools from convex and continuous optimization. We derive stability bounds for both convex and non-convex optimization under standard Lipschitz and smoothness assumptions. Applying our results to the convex case, we provide new insights for why multiple epochs of stochastic gradient methods generalize well in practice. In the non-convex case, we give a new interpretation of common practices in neural networks, and formally show that popular techniques for training large deep models are indeed stability-promoting. Our findings conceptually underscore the importance of reducing training time beyond its obvious benefit.

paragraphs: The paper connects the generalization of stochastic gradient methods to algorithmic stability: how sensitive training is to changes in the data. It shows that parametric models trained with sufficiently few iterations have vanishing generalization error under the analysis. This makes training duration relevant to statistical behavior as well as computational expense.

The authors derive stability bounds for both convex and nonconvex optimization using elementary tools from convex and continuous optimization. Their results rely on standard Lipschitz and smoothness assumptions. These conditions and the role of iteration count are part of the claim, so the result does not say that every short training run automatically produces an accurate model.

For convex problems, the analysis offers insight into why multiple training epochs can still generalize well. For nonconvex problems, it provides a stability-based interpretation of common neural-network practices and formally identifies popular training techniques as stability-promoting. The contribution explains one route by which optimization choices influence the gap between training behavior and performance beyond the training data.
summary.tldr: Stability analysis explains how stochastic gradient training duration and common training practices can support generalization.

title: Train faster, generalize better: Stability of stochastic gradient descent

abstract: We propose an Online Learning with Local Permutations (OLLP) setting, in which the learner is allowed to slightly permute the order of the loss functions generated by an adversary. On one hand, this models natural situations where the exact order of the learner’s responses is not crucial, and on the other hand, might allow better learning and regret performance, by mitigating highly adversarial loss sequences. Also, with random permutations, this can be seen as a setting interpolating between adversarial and stochastic losses. In this paper, we consider the applicability of this setting to convex online learning with delayed feedback, in which the feedback on the prediction made in round $t$ arrives with some delay $\tau$. With such delayed feedback, the best possible regret bound is well-known to be $O(\sqrt{\tau T})$. We prove that by being able to permute losses by a distance of at most $M$ (for $M\geq \tau$), the regret can be improved to $O(\sqrt{T}(1+\sqrt{\tau^2/M}))$, using a Mirror-Descent based algorithm which can be applied for both Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries. We also prove a lower bound, showing that for $M<\tau/3$, it is impossible to improve the standard $O(\sqrt{\tau T})$ regret bound by more than constant factors. Finally, we provide some experiments validating the performance of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Online learning usually requires responding to losses in the order they arrive. This paper introduces a setting where the learner may slightly rearrange that order. Such flexibility models situations where precise response ordering is unimportant and may soften highly adversarial sequences. Random rearrangements also provide a connection between adversarial and stochastic loss settings.

The analysis focuses on convex online learning with feedback delayed by tau rounds. Without rearrangement, the standard optimal regret scales as O(sqrt(tau T)). If losses can move at most M positions and M is at least tau, a mirror-descent-based algorithm obtains O(sqrt(T)(1 + sqrt(tau²/M))) regret. The algorithm accommodates both Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries.

The benefit depends on how much reordering is allowed. When M is smaller than tau/3, the authors prove that the standard regret rate cannot improve beyond constant factors. Experiments support the algorithm's performance. The upper and lower bounds jointly explain when limited scheduling flexibility can meaningfully reduce the learning cost of delayed feedback.
summary.tldr: Limited reordering can reduce regret with delayed feedback, provided the allowed movement is sufficiently large relative to the delay.

title: Online Learning with Local Permutations and Delayed Feedback

abstract: While simulated game environments have greatly accelerated research in reinforcement learning, existing environments lack the open-domain realism of tasks in computer vision or natural language processing, which operate on artifacts created by humans in natural, organic settings. To foster reinforcement learning research in such settings, we introduce the World of Bits (WoB), a platform in which agents complete tasks on the Internet by performing low-level keyboard and mouse actions. The two main challenges are: (i) to curate a large, diverse set of interesting web-based tasks, and (ii) to ensure that these tasks have a well-defined reward structure and are reproducible despite the transience of the web. To do this, we develop a methodology in which crowdworkers create tasks defined by natural language questions and provide demonstrations of how to answer the question on real websites using keyboard and mouse; HTTP traffic is cached to create a reproducible offline approximation of the web site. Finally, we show that agents trained via behavioral cloning and reinforcement learning can successfully complete a range of our web-based tasks.

paragraphs: World of Bits is a platform for studying agents that complete web tasks through keyboard and mouse actions. Its motivation is to bring reinforcement-learning research into environments built organically by people. Websites provide such settings, but assembling diverse tasks with clear rewards and repeatable conditions presents practical challenges.

The authors develop a process in which crowdworkers create tasks expressed as natural-language questions and demonstrate how to answer them on real websites. The demonstrations record interaction through keyboard and mouse. To address the changing nature of websites, the platform caches HTTP traffic, creating an offline approximation that can be used reproducibly.

Agents trained through behavioral cloning and reinforcement learning successfully complete a range of the platform's tasks. This demonstrates that the collected tasks and interaction format can support learning, while the cached environments make repeated evaluation possible. The contribution combines a research platform, a method for gathering tasks and demonstrations, and evidence that learned agents can operate within this web-based setting.
summary.tldr: World of Bits turns demonstrated web tasks into reproducible environments for training agents that use keyboards and mice.

title: World of Bits: An Open-Domain Platform for Web-Based Agents

abstract: The Cox process is a stochastic process which generalises the Poisson process by letting the underlying intensity function itself be a stochastic process. In this paper we present a fast Bayesian inference scheme for the permanental process, a Cox process under which the square root of the intensity is a Gaussian process. In particular we exploit connections with reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, to derive efficient approximate Bayesian inference algorithms based on the Laplace approximation to the predictive distribution and marginal likelihood. We obtain a simple algorithm which we apply to toy and real-world problems, obtaining orders of magnitude speed improvements over previous work.

We obtain a simple algorithm which we apply to toy and real-world problems, obtaining orders of magnitude speed improvements over previous work.

paragraphs: An intensity function describes how frequently events occur across a domain. A Cox process makes that intensity random, extending the Poisson process to include uncertainty in the event-generating rate itself. This paper develops fast Bayesian inference for the permanental process, where the square root of the intensity is modeled as a Gaussian process.

The approach uses connections with reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces to derive efficient approximate inference algorithms. It applies a Laplace approximation to the predictive distribution and marginal likelihood. These are central quantities for describing predictions and assessing the model through observed data, so computing them efficiently directly addresses the cost of Bayesian intensity estimation.

The authors obtain a simple algorithm and apply it to both toy examples and real-world problems. They report speed improvements of orders of magnitude over previous work. The result supports the computational value of this approximation scheme for the studied problems while retaining the permanental process as the underlying probabilistic model.
summary.tldr: Kernel-space connections and Laplace approximations make Bayesian permanental-process inference orders of magnitude faster in the reported applications.

title: Fast Bayesian Intensity Estimation for the Permanental Process

abstract: One of the main challenges in reinforcement learning is solving tasks with sparse reward. We show that the difficulty of discovering a distant rewarding state in an MDP is bounded by the expected cover time of a random walk over the graph induced by the MDP’s transition dynamics. We therefore propose to accelerate exploration by constructing options that minimize cover time. We introduce a new option discovery algorithm that diminishes the expected cover time by connecting the most distant states in the state-space graph with options. We show empirically that the proposed algorithm improves learning in several domains with sparse rewards.
originalAbstract: One of the main challenges in reinforcement learning is solving tasks with sparse reward. We show that the difficulty of discovering a distant rewarding state in an MDP is bounded by the expected cover time of a random walk over the graph induced by the MDP’s transition dynamics. We therefore propose to accelerate exploration by constructing options that minimize cover time. We introduce a new option discovery algorithm that diminishes the expected cover time by connecting the most distant states in the state-space graph with options. We show empirically that the proposed algorithm improves learning in several domains with sparse rewards.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because an agent may need to travel far before receiving useful feedback. This paper connects that discovery problem to the graph defined by an environment's transition dynamics. It shows that the difficulty of reaching a distant rewarding state is bounded by the expected cover time of a random walk on that graph.

Cover time describes how long a walk is expected to take to visit all states. The authors use it as a target for discovering options, which are actions extending over multiple steps. Their algorithm connects the most distant states in the state-space graph with options, reducing expected cover time and giving exploration additional ways to traverse the environment.

This approach links option construction to a mathematical quantity associated with reward discovery. Instead of treating exploration improvements solely as a matter of immediate feedback, it considers the connectivity of the entire state space. Experiments show improved learning in several sparse-reward domains, supporting the usefulness of the proposed options in those settings.
summary.tldr: Options connecting distant states reduce graph cover time and empirically improve learning in sparse-reward environments.

title: Discovering Options for Exploration by Minimizing Cover Time

abstract: The prosodic aspects of speech signals produced by current text-to-speech systems are typically averaged over training material, and as such lack the variety and liveliness found in natural speech. To avoid monotony and averaged prosody contours, it is desirable to have a way of modeling the variation in the prosodic aspects of speech, so audio signals can be synthesized in multiple ways for a given text. We present a new, hierarchically structured conditional variational auto-encoder to generate prosodic features (fundamental frequency, energy and duration) suitable for use with a vocoder or a generative model like WaveNet. At inference time, an embedding representing the prosody of a sentence may be sampled from the variational layer to allow for prosodic variation. To efficiently capture the hierarchical nature of the linguistic input (words, syllables and phones), both the encoder and decoder parts of the auto-encoder are hierarchical, in line with the linguistic structure, with layers being clocked dynamically at the respective rates. We show in our experiments that our dynamic hierarchical network outperforms a non-hierarchical state-of-the-art baseline, and, additionally, that prosody transfer across sentences is possible by employing the prosody embedding of one sentence to generate the speech signal of another.

paragraphs: The same text can be spoken with different pitch patterns, energy, and timing. Speech synthesis that averages these properties across training examples can produce monotonous delivery. CHiVE models their variation so that a fixed sentence can support multiple synthesized renditions, rather than being associated with a single averaged prosodic pattern.

The model is a conditional variational autoencoder whose encoder and decoder follow the linguistic hierarchy of words, syllables, and phones. Different layers update at rates corresponding to those units. A sentence-level prosody embedding can be sampled during inference, and the resulting fundamental frequency, energy, and duration features can feed a vocoder or a generative speech model such as WaveNet.

Experiments show the dynamic hierarchical network outperforming a state-of-the-art non-hierarchical baseline. They also demonstrate that an embedding from one sentence can guide the prosody of another. These findings support both the hierarchical architecture and the possibility of transferring prosodic information across sentences, alongside generating variation by sampling the learned representation.
summary.tldr: CHiVE uses a linguistic hierarchy and sampled sentence embeddings to generate varied prosody and enable prosody transfer between sentences.

title: CHiVE: Varying Prosody in Speech Synthesis with a Linguistically Driven Dynamic Hierarchical Conditional Variational Network

abstract: Many machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks; for example, adding adversarial perturbations that are imperceptible to humans can often make machine learning models produce wrong predictions with high confidence; moreover, although we may obtain robust models on the training dataset via adversarial training, in some problems the learned models cannot generalize well to the test data. In this paper, we focus on $\ell_\infty$ attacks, and study the adversarially robust generalization problem through the lens of Rademacher complexity. For binary linear classifiers, we prove tight bounds for the adversarial Rademacher complexity, and show that the adversarial Rademacher complexity is never smaller than its natural counterpart, and it has an unavoidable dimension dependence, unless the weight vector has bounded $\ell_1$ norm, and our results also extend to multi-class linear classifiers; in addition, for (nonlinear) neural networks, we show that the dimension dependence in the adversarial Rademacher complexity also exists. We further consider a surrogate adversarial loss for one-hidden layer ReLU network and prove margin bounds for this setting. Our results indicate that having $\ell_1$ norm constraints on the weight matrices might be a potential way to improve generalization in the adversarial setting. We demonstrate experimental results that validate our theoretical findings.

In this paper, we focus on $\ell_\infty$ attacks, and study the adversarially robust generalization problem through the lens of Rademacher complexity. For binary linear classifiers, we prove tight bounds for the adversarial Rademacher complexity, and show that the adversarial Rademacher complexity is never smaller than its natural counterpart, and it has an unavoidable dimension dependence, unless the weight vector has bounded $\ell_1$ norm, and our results also extend to multi-class linear classifiers; in addition, for (nonlinear) neural networks, we show that the dimension dependence in the adversarial Rademacher complexity also exists. paragraphs: A model can resist adversarial perturbations on its training examples yet remain vulnerable on new data. This paper studies that generalization problem for attacks constrained in the infinity norm. It uses Rademacher complexity to analyze how the difficulty of robust generalization depends on the classifier family and the input dimension.

For binary linear classifiers, the authors prove tight bounds and show that adversarial Rademacher complexity is at least as large as its ordinary counterpart. They also identify unavoidable dimension dependence unless the weight vector has bounded one-norm. The results extend to multiclass linear classification, and dimension dependence also appears in their analysis of nonlinear neural networks.

For a one-hidden-layer ReLU network, the paper studies a surrogate adversarial loss and proves margin bounds. Together, the findings suggest that one-norm constraints on weight matrices might improve adversarial generalization. This is presented as a potential direction, rather than a universal prescription. Experiments validate the theoretical findings, connecting the complexity analysis to observed behavior under adversarial evaluation.
summary.tldr: The analysis reveals dimension dependence in adversarial generalization complexity and suggests one-norm weight constraints as a possible way to improve it.

title: Rademacher Complexity for Adversarially Robust Generalization

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) has proven to be a data efficient approach for learning control tasks but is difficult to utilize in domains with complex observations such as images. In this paper, we present a method for learning representations that are suitable for iterative model-based policy improvement, even when the underlying dynamical system has complex dynamics and image observations, in that these representations are optimized for inferring simple dynamics and cost models given data from the current policy. This enables a model-based RL method based on the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) to be used for systems with image observations. We evaluate our approach on a range of robotics tasks, including manipulation with a real-world robotic arm directly from images. We find that our method produces substantially better final performance than other model-based RL methods while being significantly more efficient than model-free RL.

In this paper, we present a method for learning representations that are suitable for iterative model-based policy improvement, even when the underlying dynamical system has complex dynamics and image observations, in that these representations are optimized for inferring simple dynamics and cost models given data from the current policy. This enables a model-based RL method based on the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) to be used for systems with image observations. We evaluate our approach on a range of robotics tasks, including manipulation with a real-world robotic arm directly from images. We find that our method produces substantially better final performance than other model-based RL methods while being significantly more efficient than model-free RL.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can use data efficiently, but image observations make it difficult to construct a useful model for control. SOLAR addresses this by learning representations suited to repeated model-based policy improvement, including when the underlying system has complex dynamics. The representation is shaped by what the control procedure needs to infer.

Specifically, the learned representation supports simple dynamics and cost models fitted from data collected by the current policy. This allows a method based on the linear-quadratic regulator to operate on systems observed through images. The key connection is between representation learning and control: the representation is optimized to make the models used for policy improvement tractable.

The authors evaluate the approach on several robotics tasks, including manipulation by a real robotic arm controlled directly from images. They report substantially better final performance than other model-based methods and significantly greater efficiency than model-free reinforcement learning. These findings support the usefulness of learning a representation around the requirements of iterative control, even when the raw observations and physical dynamics are complicated.
summary.tldr: SOLAR learns image representations that support simple control models, enabling efficient model-based learning on robotic tasks.

title: SOLAR: Deep Structured Representations for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new randomized second-order optimization algorithm—Stochastic Subspace Cubic Newton (SSCN)—for minimizing a high dimensional convex function $f$. Our method can be seen both as a \emph{stochastic} extension of the cubically-regularized Newton method of Nesterov and Polyak (2006), and a \emph{second-order} enhancement of stochastic subspace descent of Kozak et al. (2019). We prove that as we vary the minibatch size, the global convergence rate of SSCN interpolates between the rate of stochastic coordinate descent (CD) and the rate of cubic regularized Newton, thus giving new insights into the connection between first and second-order methods. Remarkably, the local convergence rate of SSCN matches the rate of stochastic subspace descent applied to the problem of minimizing the quadratic function $\frac12 (x-x^*)^\top \nabla^2f(x^*)(x-x^*)$, where $x^*$ is the minimizer of $f$, and hence depends on the properties of $f$ at the optimum only. Our numerical experiments show that SSCN outperforms non-accelerated first-order CD algorithms while being competitive to their accelerated variants.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a new randomized second-order optimization algorithm—Stochastic Subspace Cubic Newton (SSCN)—for minimizing a high dimensional convex function $f$. Our method can be seen both as a \emph{stochastic} extension of the cubically-regularized Newton method of Nesterov and Polyak (2006), and a \emph{second-order} enhancement of stochastic subspace descent of Kozak et al. (2019). We prove that as we vary the minibatch size, the global convergence rate of SSCN interpolates between the rate of stochastic coordinate descent (CD) and the rate of cubic regularized Newton, thus giving new insights into the connection between first and second-order methods. Remarkably, the local convergence rate of SSCN matches the rate of stochastic subspace descent applied to the problem of minimizing the quadratic function $\frac12 (x-x^*)^\top \nabla^2f(x^*)(x-x^*)$, where $x^*$ is the minimizer of $f$, and hence depends on the properties of $f$ at the optimum only. Our numerical experiments show that SSCN outperforms non-accelerated first-order CD algorithms while being competitive to their accelerated variants.

paragraphs: Stochastic Subspace Cubic Newton, or SSCN, is a randomized second-order method for minimizing high-dimensional convex functions. It connects two approaches: Newton-style updates with cubic regularization and stochastic descent within subspaces. This makes it both a stochastic extension of cubic Newton optimization and a curvature-aware enhancement of stochastic subspace descent.

The authors prove that changing the minibatch size moves the global convergence rate between those of stochastic coordinate descent and cubic regularized Newton. This gives a theoretical connection between first-order and second-order methods within one algorithm. The batch size controls where the method sits along that spectrum of convergence behavior.

Near the minimizer, SSCN’s convergence rate matches stochastic subspace descent on the quadratic defined by the objective’s curvature at that minimizer. Consequently, this local rate depends only on properties of the objective at the optimum. Numerical experiments show better performance than non-accelerated first-order coordinate descent and competitive performance with accelerated variants, supporting the practical promise of the theoretical connection.
summary.tldr: SSCN combines randomized subspace updates with cubic Newton optimization, with convergence rates that bridge coordinate descent and second-order methods.

title: Stochastic Subspace Cubic Newton Method

abstract: The goal of neural-symbolic computation is to integrate the connectionist and symbolist paradigms. Prior methods learn the neural-symbolic models using reinforcement learning (RL) approaches, which ignore the error propagation in the symbolic reasoning module and thus converge slowly with sparse rewards. In this paper, we address these issues and close the loop of neural-symbolic learning by (1) introducing the grammar model as a symbolic prior to bridge neural perception and symbolic reasoning, and (2) proposing a novel back-search algorithm which mimics the top-down human-like learning procedure to propagate the error through the symbolic reasoning module efficiently. We further interpret the proposed learning framework as maximum likelihood estimation using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling and the back-search algorithm as a Metropolis-Hastings sampler. The experiments are conducted on two weakly-supervised neural-symbolic tasks: (1) handwritten formula recognition on the newly introduced HWF dataset; (2) visual question answering on the CLEVR dataset. The results show that our approach significantly outperforms the RL methods in terms of performance, converging speed, and data efficiency. Our code and data are released at https://liqing-ustc.github.io/NGS.

title: Closed Loop Neural-Symbolic Learning via Integrating Neural Perception, Grammar Parsing, and Symbolic Reasoning

abstract: Graphical modeling has been broadly useful for exploring the dependence structure among features in a dataset. However, the strength of graphical modeling hinges on our ability to encode and estimate conditional dependencies. In particular, commonly used measures such as partial correlation are only meaningful under strongly parametric (in this case, multivariate Gaussian) assumptions. These assumptions are unverifiable, and there is often little reason to believe they hold in practice. In this paper, we instead consider 3 non-parametric measures of conditional dependence. These measures are meaningful without structural assumptions on the multivariate distribution of the data. In addition, we show that for 2 of these measures there are simple, strong plug-in estimators that require only the estimation of a conditional mean. These plug-in estimators (1) are asymptotically linear and non-parametrically efficient, (2) allow incorporation of flexible machine learning techniques for conditional mean estimation, and (3) enable the construction of valid Wald-type confidence intervals. In addition, by leveraging the influence function of these estimators, one can obtain intervals with simultaneous coverage guarantees for all pairs of features.

paragraphs: Graphical modeling describes how features depend on one another after accounting for other features. Common tools such as partial correlation rely on strong distributional assumptions for this interpretation. This paper develops alternatives that remain meaningful without imposing structural assumptions on the joint distribution of the data.

The authors consider three nonparametric measures of conditional dependence. For two, they construct plug-in estimators whose main estimation task is learning a conditional mean. This creates a practical connection to machine learning: flexible prediction methods can supply that conditional mean while the surrounding statistical framework targets a dependence measure.

The estimators are shown to be asymptotically linear and nonparametrically efficient, and they support valid Wald-type confidence intervals. The authors also use influence functions to construct intervals with simultaneous coverage across all feature pairs. That distinction matters when exploring an entire graph, where many relationships are assessed together. The contribution combines flexible modeling of relationships with formal uncertainty statements, with the stated efficiency properties applying asymptotically.
summary.tldr: Nonparametric dependence measures let graphical models incorporate machine learning while supporting statistically justified confidence intervals.

title: A Flexible Framework for Nonparametric Graphical Modeling that Accommodates Machine Learning

abstract: Modern machine learning models with high accuracy are often miscalibrated—the predicted top probability does not reflect the actual accuracy, and tends to be \emph{over-confident}. It is commonly believed that such over-confidence is mainly due to \emph{over-parametrization}, in particular when the model is large enough to memorize the training data and maximize the confidence. In this paper, we show theoretically that over-parametrization is not the only reason for over-confidence. We prove that \emph{logistic regression is inherently over-confident}, in the realizable, under-parametrized setting where the data is generated from the logistic model, and the sample size is much larger than the number of parameters. Further, this over-confidence happens for general well-specified binary classification problems as long as the activation is symmetric and concave on the positive part. Perhaps surprisingly, we also show that over-confidence is not always the case—there exists another activation function (and a suitable loss function) under which the learned classifier is \emph{under-confident} at some probability values. Overall, our theory provides a precise characterization of calibration in realizable binary classification, which we verify on simulations and real data experiments.

paragraphs: A classifier can make accurate predictions while assigning probabilities that exaggerate how often it is correct. This paper examines the common explanation that such over-confidence mainly arises because a model has enough parameters to memorize its training data. Its theory shows that over-parametrization is not required for the problem to occur.

The authors prove over-confidence for logistic regression in a realizable, under-parametrized setting: the data follows the assumed logistic model, and there are many more samples than parameters. They extend the finding to well-specified binary classification problems whose activation function is symmetric and concave on its positive part. These conditions identify a broader setting in which confidence can still be systematically too high.

The analysis also demonstrates that over-confidence is not inevitable across activation choices. Another activation, paired with a suitable loss, yields under-confidence at some probability values. Simulations and real-data experiments verify the theory, showing that calibration depends on the learning formulation even when the assumed model correctly describes the data.
summary.tldr: Even correctly specified, under-parametrized classifiers can be over-confident, and activation choices can also produce under-confidence.

title: Don’t Just Blame Over-parametrization for Over-confidence: Theoretical Analysis of Calibration in Binary Classification

abstract: Low-dimensional node embeddings play a key role in analyzing graph datasets. However, little work studies exactly what information is encoded by popular embedding methods, and how this information correlates with performance in downstream learning tasks. We tackle this question by studying whether embeddings can be inverted to (approximately) recover the graph used to generate them. Focusing on a variant of the popular DeepWalk method \cite{PerozziAl-RfouSkiena:2014, QiuDongMa:2018}, we present algorithms for accurate embedding inversion – i.e., from the low-dimensional embedding of a graph $G$, we can find a graph $\tilde G$ with a very similar embedding. We perform numerous experiments on real-world networks, observing that significant information about $G$, such as specific edges and bulk properties like triangle density, is often lost in $\tilde G$. However, community structure is often preserved or even enhanced. Our findings are a step towards a more rigorous understanding of exactly what information embeddings encode about the input graph, and why this information is useful for learning tasks.

paragraphs: Node embeddings compress a graph into low-dimensional representations, but successful downstream use does not explain exactly which graph properties survive that compression. This paper investigates the question by reversing the process. Starting from embeddings produced by a variant of DeepWalk, it asks whether a graph can be reconstructed that produces a similar representation.

The authors develop algorithms for accurate embedding inversion. The reconstruction target is a graph with embeddings close to the supplied ones, so matching the representation does not itself establish that the original graph has been recovered. Comparing the reconstructed graph with the original provides a way to examine which structural details the embedding retains or loses.

Experiments on real networks find that individual edges and broader properties such as triangle density are often lost, while community structure is often preserved or strengthened. These observations suggest that this embedding method can emphasize groups of related nodes without retaining detailed connectivity. The results help clarify what information may support learning tasks that use these representations.
summary.tldr: Inverting a DeepWalk variant reveals that similar embeddings can preserve communities while losing edges and other graph properties.

title: DeepWalking Backwards: From Embeddings Back to Graphs

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is an emerging learning scheme that allows different distributed clients to train deep neural networks together without data sharing. Neural networks have become popular due to their unprecedented success. To the best of our knowledge, the theoretical guarantees of FL concerning neural networks with explicit forms and multi-step updates are unexplored. Nevertheless, training analysis of neural networks in FL is non-trivial for two reasons: first, the objective loss function we are optimizing is non-smooth and non-convex, and second, we are even not updating in the gradient direction. Existing convergence results for gradient descent-based methods heavily rely on the fact that the gradient direction is used for updating. The current paper presents a new class of convergence analysis for FL, Federated Neural Tangent Kernel (FL-NTK), which corresponds to overparamterized ReLU neural networks trained by gradient descent in FL and is inspired by the analysis in Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). Theoretically, FL-NTK converges to a global-optimal solution at a linear rate with properly tuned learning parameters. Furthermore, with proper distributional assumptions, FL-NTK can also achieve good generalization. The proposed theoretical analysis scheme can be generalized to more complex neural networks.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets distributed clients train a shared neural network without sharing their data. Analyzing this training process is difficult because neural-network losses are nonconvex and nonsmooth, and multiple client updates do not generally produce an update in the global gradient direction. Consequently, standard gradient-descent convergence arguments do not transfer directly.

The paper introduces Federated Neural Tangent Kernel, or FL-NTK, as a framework for analyzing overparameterized ReLU networks trained by gradient descent in the federated setting. It adapts ideas from neural tangent kernel analysis to account for the structure of federated updates. The contribution is a theoretical treatment of explicit neural networks with multiple update steps.

With appropriately tuned learning parameters, the analysis establishes convergence to a globally optimal solution at a linear rate. Good generalization additionally requires suitable distributional assumptions. The authors also state that the framework can extend to more complex networks. These qualifications matter: the guarantees concern the analyzed network and training setting, with tuning and distributional conditions playing explicit roles.
summary.tldr: FL-NTK provides conditional convergence and generalization guarantees for federated training of overparameterized ReLU networks.

title: FL-NTK: A Neural Tangent Kernel-based Framework for Federated Learning Analysis

abstract: Given an inverse problem with a normalizing flow prior, we wish to estimate the distribution of the underlying signal conditioned on the observations. We approach this problem as a task of conditional inference on the pre-trained unconditional flow model. We first establish that this is computationally hard for a large class of flow models. Motivated by this, we propose a framework for approximate inference that estimates the target conditional as a composition of two flow models. This formulation leads to a stable variational inference training procedure that avoids adversarial training. Our method is evaluated on a variety of inverse problems and is shown to produce high-quality samples with uncertainty quantification. We further demonstrate that our approach can be amortized for zero-shot inference.

Motivated by this, we propose a framework for approximate inference that estimates the target conditional as a composition of two flow models. This formulation leads to a stable variational inference training procedure that avoids adversarial training. Our method is evaluated on a variety of inverse problems and is shown to produce high-quality samples with uncertainty quantification. We further demonstrate that our approach can be amortized for zero-shot inference.

paragraphs: An inverse problem asks what underlying signal could have produced a set of observations. This paper seeks a distribution over possible signals conditioned on those observations. It starts with a pretrained normalizing flow that models signals without conditioning, then treats reconstruction as conditional inference within that existing model.

The authors first establish that this inference problem is computationally hard for a large class of flow models. They respond with an approximate method that represents the desired conditional distribution by composing two flows. The resulting formulation supports a stable variational inference training procedure and does not require adversarial training.

Evaluations across several inverse problems produce high-quality samples together with uncertainty quantification. This matters because a distribution can represent multiple plausible reconstructions and the uncertainty associated with them. The paper also demonstrates amortization for zero-shot inference: the learned inference procedure can be reused to obtain conditional results. The contribution connects an expressive pretrained signal model with a practical approximation to its difficult conditional inference problem.
summary.tldr: Composing two normalizing flows enables approximate conditional inference for inverse problems, producing plausible reconstructions with uncertainty estimates.

title: Composing Normalizing Flows for Inverse Problems

abstract: The knowledge gradient (KG) algorithm is a popular and effective algorithm for the best arm identification (BAI) problem. Due to the complex calculation of KG, theoretical analysis of this algorithm is difficult, and existing results are mostly about the asymptotic performance of it, e.g., consistency, asymptotic sample allocation, etc. In this research, we present new theoretical results about the finite-time performance of the KG algorithm. Under independent and normally distributed rewards, we derive lower bounds and upper bounds for the probability of error and simple regret of the algorithm. With these bounds, existing asymptotic results become simple corollaries. We also show the performance of the algorithm for the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem. These developments not only extend the existing analysis of the KG algorithm, but can also be used to analyze other improvement-based algorithms. Last, we use numerical experiments to further demonstrate the finite-time behavior of the KG algorithm.

paragraphs: The knowledge gradient algorithm is used to identify the best option among alternatives whose rewards must be learned through sampling. Although it is widely used, its complicated calculations make theoretical analysis difficult. Earlier results mostly described what happens as sampling continues indefinitely, leaving its behavior after a finite amount of sampling less understood.

Under independent, normally distributed rewards, this paper derives both upper and lower bounds on error probability and simple regret. These quantities capture the chance of selecting the wrong option and the loss associated with the final selection. Bounding them from both directions characterizes finite-time performance more fully than an eventual-convergence statement alone.

The resulting bounds also recover existing asymptotic findings as direct consequences. The authors examine knowledge gradient performance for the multi-armed bandit problem and describe how the analytical developments can support other improvement-based algorithms. Numerical experiments further illustrate finite-time behavior. The contribution makes the theory more relevant to decisions made with a limited sampling budget.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds knowledge gradient’s finite-time error and simple regret under independent Gaussian rewards, extending its largely asymptotic theory.

title: On the Finite-Time Performance of the Knowledge Gradient Algorithm

abstract: We consider unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), where labeled data from a source domain (e.g., photos) and unlabeled data from a target domain (e.g., sketches) are used to learn a classifier for the target domain. Conventional UDA methods (e.g., domain adversarial training) learn domain-invariant features to generalize from the source domain to the target domain. In this paper, we show that contrastive pre-training, which learns features on unlabeled source and target data and then fine-tunes on labeled source data, is competitive with strong UDA methods. However, we find that contrastive pre-training does not learn domain-invariant features, diverging from conventional UDA intuitions. We show theoretically that contrastive pre-training can learn features that vary subtantially across domains but still generalize to the target domain, by disentangling domain and class information. We empirically validate our theory on benchmark vision datasets.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation aims to classify data in a target domain using labeled examples from a different source domain and unlabeled target examples. A common approach seeks features that hide the distinction between domains. This paper examines an alternative: contrastive pretraining on unlabeled data from both domains, followed by fine-tuning on labeled source data.

The authors find that this procedure is competitive with strong domain-adaptation methods even though its learned features retain substantial domain information. That observation challenges the idea that successful transfer must work by making representations domain-invariant. Features can remain sensitive to the domain while still supporting classification in the target domain.

The paper supplies a theoretical explanation based on separating domain information from class information within the representation. It shows that contrastive pretraining can learn features with substantial cross-domain variation and nevertheless generalize to the target. Experiments on vision benchmarks support this explanation, suggesting that organizing the two kinds of information can be sufficient without eliminating domain variation.
summary.tldr: Contrastive pretraining can support domain adaptation by separating class and domain information while retaining domain-sensitive features.

title: Connect, Not Collapse: Explaining Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) encode a lot of information about a particular distribution in their structure. However, compute required to infer these structures is typically super-exponential in the number of variables, as inference requires a sweep of a combinatorially large space of potential structures. That is, until recent advances made it possible to search this space using a differentiable metric, drastically reducing search time. While this technique— named NOTEARS —is widely considered a seminal work in DAG-discovery, it concedes an important property in favour of differentiability: transportability. To be transportable, the structures discovered on one dataset must apply to another dataset from the same domain. We introduce D-Struct which recovers transportability in the discovered structures through a novel architecture and loss function while remaining fully differentiable. Because D-Struct remains differentiable, our method can be easily adopted in existing differentiable architectures, as was previously done with NOTEARS. In our experiments, we empirically validate D-Struct with respect to edge accuracy and structural Hamming distance in a variety of settings.

paragraphs: Directed acyclic graphs represent information about a distribution through relationships among variables. Searching for the graph can be computationally demanding because the number of possible structures grows rapidly. Differentiable structure learning, exemplified by NOTEARS, makes this search more manageable by allowing it to use continuous optimization rather than sweeping through the full combinatorial space.

The paper focuses on transportability: whether a graph learned from one dataset also applies to another dataset from the same domain. The authors argue that NOTEARS gives up this property in obtaining differentiability. They introduce D-Struct, which uses a new architecture and loss function to recover transportability while keeping the learning procedure fully differentiable.

Maintaining differentiability matters because D-Struct can be incorporated into existing differentiable architectures in a manner similar to NOTEARS. The authors empirically validate the method in several settings using edge accuracy and structural Hamming distance, measures concerned with agreement between graph structures. The central aim is therefore to make learned structures applicable across datasets from the same domain while retaining the computational advantages of differentiable search.
summary.tldr: D-Struct adds an architecture and loss for transportable graph discovery while retaining fully differentiable structure learning.

title: Differentiable and Transportable Structure Learning

abstract: We present a framework for using transformer networks as universal computers by programming them with specific weights and placing them in a loop. Our input sequence acts as a punchcard, consisting of instructions and memory for data read/writes. We demonstrate that a constant number of encoder layers can emulate basic computing blocks, including lexicographic operations, non-linear functions, function calls, program counters, and conditional branches. Using this framework, we emulate a computer using a simple instruction-set architecture, which allows us to map iterative algorithms to programs that can be executed by a constant depth looped transformer network. We show how a single frozen transformer, instructed by its input, can emulate a basic calculator, a basic linear algebra library, and even a full backpropagation, in-context learning algorithm. Our findings reveal the potential of transformer networks as programmable compute units and offer insight into the mechanics of attention.

Using this framework, we emulate a computer using a simple instruction-set architecture, which allows us to map iterative algorithms to programs that can be executed by a constant depth looped transformer network. paragraphs: This paper constructs transformers that act as programmable computers by setting specific weights and repeatedly running the network in a loop. The input sequence serves as a program and memory, containing instructions together with locations for reading and writing data. Computation is organized through repeated execution of a fixed network.

The authors show that a constant number of encoder layers can emulate computing components such as nonlinear functions, function calls, program counters, conditional branches, and lexicographic operations. They combine these components into a simple instruction-set architecture. Iterative algorithms can then be expressed as programs executed by a transformer whose depth remains constant across loop iterations.

A single frozen transformer can, when given suitable input instructions, emulate a basic calculator, a linear algebra library, and an in-context learning algorithm that performs full backpropagation. These are constructive demonstrations of what specifically programmed looped transformers can compute. They illustrate how attention can support programmable operations and how input instructions can change the computation performed without changing the transformer's weights.
summary.tldr: Specifically programmed transformers can execute input-defined programs through looping, including calculations, linear algebra, and backpropagation.

title: Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers

abstract: Matrix manifolds, such as manifolds of Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) matrices and Grassmann manifolds, appear in many applications. Recently, by applying the theory of gyrogroups and gyrovector spaces that is a powerful framework for studying hyperbolic geometry, some works have attempted to build principled generalizations of Euclidean neural networks on matrix manifolds. However, due to the lack of many concepts in gyrovector spaces for the considered manifolds, e.g., the inner product and gyroangles, techniques and mathematical tools provided by these works are still limited compared to those developed for studying hyperbolic geometry. In this paper, we generalize some notions in gyrovector spaces for SPD and Grassmann manifolds, and propose new models and layers for building neural networks on these manifolds. We show the effectiveness of our approach in two applications, i.e., human action recognition and knowledge graph completion.
originalAbstract: Matrix manifolds, such as manifolds of Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) matrices and Grassmann manifolds, appear in many applications. Recently, by applying the theory of gyrogroups and gyrovector spaces that is a powerful framework for studying hyperbolic geometry, some works have attempted to build principled generalizations of Euclidean neural networks on matrix manifolds. However, due to the lack of many concepts in gyrovector spaces for the considered manifolds, e.g., the inner product and gyroangles, techniques and mathematical tools provided by these works are still limited compared to those developed for studying hyperbolic geometry. In this paper, we generalize some notions in gyrovector spaces for SPD and Grassmann manifolds, and propose new models and layers for building neural networks on these manifolds. We show the effectiveness of our approach in two applications, i.e., human action recognition and knowledge graph completion.

paragraphs: Some learning problems represent information using matrices that belong to a structured geometric space. Symmetric positive definite matrices and points on Grassmann manifolds are examples considered here. Building neural networks for these spaces calls for mathematical operations that respect their geometry, rather than assuming that ordinary Euclidean constructions transfer directly.

Earlier work approached this problem through gyrogroups and gyrovector spaces, a framework used to study hyperbolic geometry. However, the corresponding tools for these matrix manifolds remained incomplete, including concepts such as inner products and gyroangles. The authors generalize several gyrovector-space notions for symmetric positive definite and Grassmann manifolds, expanding the mathematical vocabulary available for network design.

They then use these developments to propose new neural network models and layers on the two kinds of manifolds. Applications to human action recognition and knowledge graph completion demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The paper's central contribution links mathematical foundations to usable architectures: extending the available geometric operations creates additional ways to construct networks for structured matrix representations.
summary.tldr: The paper extends gyrovector-space mathematics to build new neural network layers on symmetric positive definite and Grassmann manifolds.

title: Building Neural Networks on Matrix Manifolds: A Gyrovector Space Approach

abstract: We investigate how pair-wise data augmentation techniques like Mixup affect the sample complexity of finding optimal decision boundaries in a binary linear classification problem. For a family of data distributions with a separability constant $\kappa$, we analyze how well the optimal classifier in terms of training loss aligns with the optimal one in test accuracy (i.e., Bayes optimal classifier). For vanilla training without augmentation, we uncover an interesting phenomenon named the curse of separability. As we increase $\kappa$ to make the data distribution more separable, the sample complexity of vanilla training increases exponentially in $\kappa$; perhaps surprisingly, the task of finding optimal decision boundaries becomes harder for more separable distributions. For Mixup training, we show that Mixup mitigates this problem by significantly reducing the sample complexity. To this end, we develop new concentration results applicable to $n^2$ pair-wise augmented data points constructed from $n$ independent data, by carefully dealing with dependencies between overlapping pairs. Lastly, we study other masking-based Mixup-style techniques and show that they can distort the training loss and make its minimizer converge to a suboptimal classifier in terms of test accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how pairwise augmentation affects the amount of data needed to learn an optimal decision boundary in binary linear classification. For a particular family of distributions, it compares the classifier minimizing training loss with the classifier achieving the best test accuracy. A separability parameter controls how distinctly the two classes are distributed.

The authors find that, without augmentation, increasing separability makes the sample requirement grow exponentially in that parameter. Thus, in this setting, more separable data can make identifying the optimal boundary harder. They prove that Mixup substantially reduces this sample complexity, mitigating what they call the curse of separability.

The analysis requires new concentration results because the many augmented pairs constructed from a dataset share original examples and are therefore dependent. The paper also examines masking-based Mixup variants and shows that they can distort the training objective, causing its minimizer to approach a classifier with suboptimal test accuracy. These results establish a benefit for Mixup in the analyzed setting while showing that related augmentation procedures need not preserve that benefit.
summary.tldr: For a studied binary linear classification family, Mixup reduces the sample burden of finding optimal boundaries as class separability increases.

title: Provable Benefit of Mixup for Finding Optimal Decision Boundaries

abstract: Generating desirable molecular structures in 3D is a fundamental problem for drug discovery. Despite the considerable progress we have achieved, existing methods usually generate molecules in atom resolution and ignore intrinsic local structures such as rings, which leads to poor quality in generated structures, especially when generating large molecules. Fragment-based molecule generation is a promising strategy, however, it is nontrivial to be adapted for 3D non-autoregressive generations because of the combinational optimization problems. In this paper, we utilize a coarse-to-fine strategy to tackle this problem, in which a Hierarchical Diffusion-based model (i.e. HierDiff) is proposed to preserve the validity of local segments without relying on autoregressive modeling. Specifically, HierDiff first generates coarse-grained molecule geometries via an equivariant diffusion process, where each coarse-grained node reflects a fragment in a molecule. Then the coarse-grained nodes are decoded into fine-grained fragments by a message-passing process and a newly designed iterative refined sampling module. Lastly, the fine-grained fragments are then assembled to derive a complete atomic molecular structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HierDiff consistently improves the quality of molecule generation over existing methods.

paragraphs: Generating molecules atom by atom in a three-dimensional representation can overlook meaningful local structures such as rings. The paper identifies this as a source of poor structural quality, especially for larger molecules. Working with molecular fragments offers a way to preserve these local structures, but arranging fragments in a non-autoregressive generator creates difficult combinatorial choices.

HierDiff addresses this problem through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. An equivariant diffusion process first generates a rough molecular geometry whose nodes represent fragments. A message-passing process and an iterative sampling refinement module then turn those coarse nodes into detailed fragments. Finally, the fragments are assembled into a complete molecular structure at atomic resolution.

The hierarchy separates the broad arrangement of a molecule from the detailed construction of its local pieces. This provides a mechanism for preserving valid local segments without requiring autoregressive generation. Across the reported experiments, HierDiff consistently improves molecular generation quality over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of building three-dimensional structures through coordinated coarse and fine stages.
summary.tldr: HierDiff generates coarse molecular geometry, refines it into fragments, and assembles them to improve three-dimensional molecule generation.

title: Coarse-to-Fine: a Hierarchical Diffusion Model for Molecule Generation in 3D

abstract: Novel Class Discovery (NCD) aims at inferring novel classes in an unlabeled set by leveraging prior knowledge from a labeled set with known classes. Despite its importance, there is a lack of theoretical foundations for NCD. This paper bridges the gap by providing an analytical framework to formalize and investigate when and how known classes can help discover novel classes. Tailored to the NCD problem, we introduce a graph-theoretic representation that can be learned by a novel NCD Spectral Contrastive Loss (NSCL). Minimizing this objective is equivalent to factorizing the graph’s adjacency matrix, which allows us to derive a provable error bound and provide the sufficient and necessary condition for NCD. Empirically, NSCL can match or outperform several strong baselines on common benchmark datasets, which is appealing for practical usage while enjoying theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Novel class discovery uses a labeled dataset of known categories to help identify previously unseen categories in unlabeled data. The paper asks when that prior knowledge helps and how the benefit can be understood formally. Its contribution is an analytical framework for a task whose practical importance had outpaced its theoretical foundations.

The authors introduce a graph representation tailored to novel class discovery and a training objective called NCD Spectral Contrastive Loss. Minimizing this loss is equivalent to factorizing the graph's adjacency matrix. That equivalence connects representation learning to a mathematical object that can be analyzed to obtain an error bound and a necessary-and-sufficient condition for discovery within the framework.

Experiments show that NSCL can match or outperform several strong baselines on common benchmark datasets. The result combines a practically competitive learning objective with an explanation of when known-class information supports the discovery task. Its theoretical conditions and error bound provide a structured account of that transfer, alongside the empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: A spectral graph framework explains when known classes help discover novel ones and yields a theoretically supported, competitive learning objective.

title: When and How Does Known Class Help Discover Unknown Ones? Provable Understanding Through Spectral Analysis

abstract: Calibrating deep learning models to yield uncertainty-aware predictions is crucial as deep neural networks get increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications. While existing post-hoc calibration methods achieve impressive results on in-domain test datasets, they are limited by their inability to yield reliable uncertainty estimates in domain-shift and out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios. We aim to bridge this gap by proposing DAC, an accuracy-preserving as well as Density-Aware Calibration method based on k-nearest-neighbors (KNN). In contrast to existing post-hoc methods, we utilize hidden layers of classifiers as a source for uncertainty-related information and study their importance. We show that DAC is a generic method that can readily be combined with state-of-the-art post-hoc methods. DAC boosts the robustness of calibration performance in domain-shift and OOD, while maintaining excellent in-domain predictive uncertainty estimates. We demonstrate that DAC leads to consistently better calibration across a large number of model architectures, datasets, and metrics. Additionally, we show that DAC improves calibration substantially on recent large-scale neural networks pre-trained on vast amounts of data.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence should help users judge how much to trust its predictions. Calibration methods adjust that confidence, but methods that work well on familiar test data can become unreliable when the data distribution changes. This paper introduces Density-Aware Calibration, or DAC, to improve uncertainty estimates across those different conditions while preserving prediction accuracy.

DAC uses nearest-neighbor information and the classifier’s hidden representations as sources of information about uncertainty. Its central move is to look inside the network for information useful to calibration, rather than relying only on the information used by existing post-processing methods. The authors also examine the importance of hidden layers and make DAC compatible with existing calibration approaches.

Experiments report consistently improved calibration across multiple architectures, datasets, and evaluation measures. The improvements extend to shifted and out-of-domain data while retaining strong calibration on familiar data. The authors also report substantial improvements for large networks pretrained on extensive datasets. These findings support hidden representations as a useful resource for making confidence estimates more robust under the evaluated distribution changes.
summary.tldr: DAC uses nearest-neighbor information from hidden representations to improve calibration under distribution shifts while preserving accuracy.

title: Beyond In-Domain Scenarios: Robust Density-Aware Calibration

abstract: Adversarial poisoning attacks pose huge threats to various machine learning applications. Especially, the recent accumulative poisoning attacks show that it is possible to achieve irreparable harm on models via a sequence of imperceptible attacks followed by a trigger batch. Due to the limited data-level discrepancy in real-time data streaming, current defensive methods are indiscriminate in handling the poison and clean samples. In this paper, we dive into the perspective of model dynamics and propose a novel information measure, namely, Memorization Discrepancy, to explore the defense via the model-level information. By implicitly transferring the changes in the data manipulation to that in the model outputs, Memorization Discrepancy can discover the imperceptible poison samples based on their distinct dynamics from the clean samples. We thoroughly explore its properties and propose Discrepancy-aware Sample Correction (DSC) to defend against accumulative poisoning attacks. Extensive experiments comprehensively characterized Memorization Discrepancy and verified its effectiveness. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Memorization-Discrepancy.

paragraphs: Accumulative poisoning attacks can build damage through a sequence of subtle manipulations followed by a trigger batch. In streaming data, poisoned examples may differ so little from clean ones that defenses based on those visible differences struggle to separate them. This paper investigates whether the model’s behavior can provide a more useful signal.

The authors introduce Memorization Discrepancy, an information measure that examines differences in model dynamics. Its purpose is to expose manipulation through changes in model outputs: examples that appear nearly indistinguishable at the data level can produce different learning dynamics. The method therefore uses information about how the model responds to samples to help discover poisoning.

Building on this measure, the paper proposes Discrepancy-aware Sample Correction as a defense against accumulative attacks. The authors study the measure’s properties and report extensive experiments characterizing it and verifying its effectiveness. The contribution is a model-level basis for detecting subtle poisoning and using that signal in a corrective defense, supported by the reported empirical investigation.
summary.tldr: Memorization Discrepancy uses differences in model dynamics to detect subtle accumulative poisoning and support a sample-correction defense.

title: Exploring Model Dynamics for Accumulative Poisoning Discovery

abstract: Quantization techniques commonly reduce the inference costs of neural networks by restricting the precision of weights and activations. Recent studies show that also reducing the precision of the accumulator can further improve hardware efficiency at the risk of numerical overflow, which introduces arithmetic errors that can degrade model accuracy. To avoid numerical overflow while maintaining accuracy, recent work proposed accumulator-aware quantization (A2Q)—a quantization-aware training method that constrains model weights during training to safely use a target accumulator bit width during inference. Although this shows promise, we demonstrate that A2Q relies on an overly restrictive constraint and a sub-optimal weight initialization strategy that each introduce superfluous quantization error. To address these shortcomings, we introduce: (1) an improved bound that alleviates accumulator constraints without compromising overflow avoidance; and (2) a new strategy for initializing quantized weights from pre-trained floating-point checkpoints. We combine these contributions with weight normalization to introduce A2Q+. We identify and characterize the various tradeoffs that arise as a consequence of accumulator constraints and support our analysis with experiments that show A2Q+ significantly improves these trade-offs when compared to prior methods.

paragraphs: Neural network quantization usually reduces the precision of weights and activations to lower inference costs. Reducing the precision of the accumulator, which holds intermediate sums, can improve hardware efficiency further. However, values exceeding its numerical range cause overflow and arithmetic errors that can damage model accuracy.

Accumulator-aware quantization addresses this by constraining weights during training so inference can safely use a chosen accumulator width. The authors identify two sources of unnecessary error in the existing A2Q method: an overly restrictive constraint and a suboptimal initialization procedure. They introduce a less restrictive bound that still avoids overflow, together with a new way to initialize quantized weights from pretrained floating-point models.

A2Q+ combines those improvements with weight normalization. The paper analyzes the tradeoffs introduced by accumulator constraints and reports experiments showing substantially better tradeoffs than prior methods. Its contribution is to make more effective use of the available numerical range while preserving overflow avoidance, improving the balance between reduced precision and model accuracy.
summary.tldr: A2Q+ improves low-precision neural networks through looser overflow-safe weight constraints and better quantized-weight initialization.

title: A2Q+: Improving Accumulator-Aware Weight Quantization

abstract: Event-based vision has drawn increasing attention due to its unique characteristics, such as high temporal resolution and high dynamic range. It has been used in video super-resolution (VSR) recently to enhance the flow estimation and temporal alignment. Rather than for motion learning, we propose in this paper the first VSR method that utilizes event signals for texture enhancement. Our method, called EvTexture, leverages high-frequency details of events to better recover texture regions in VSR. In our EvTexture, a new texture enhancement branch is presented. We further introduce an iterative texture enhancement module to progressively explore the high-temporal-resolution event information for texture restoration. This allows for gradual refinement of texture regions across multiple iterations, leading to more accurate and rich high-resolution details. Experimental results show that our EvTexture achieves state-of-the-art performance on four datasets. For the Vid4 dataset with rich textures, our method can get up to 4.67dB gain compared with recent event-based methods. Code: https://github.com/DachunKai/EvTexture.
