paragraphs: Video super-resolution aims to recover detailed, higher-resolution video from lower-resolution inputs. Event signals offer finely timed information that has previously been used to improve motion estimation and alignment between frames. EvTexture explores another use for this information: recovering the fine textures that make image regions look detailed.

The method adds a dedicated texture enhancement branch that draws on high-frequency details in the events. An iterative module progressively uses their high temporal resolution to restore texture. Instead of obtaining all of the refinement in a single step, the model revisits texture regions across multiple iterations, gradually improving the reconstructed details.

The authors report leading performance on four datasets. On Vid4, which contains rich textures, the improvement over recent event-based methods reaches up to 4.67 dB. That maximum is specific to the stated comparison, rather than an improvement promised for every video. The results support treating events as a source of appearance detail as well as a tool for tracking movement, broadening their role in video reconstruction.
summary.tldr: EvTexture progressively uses event signals to restore fine textures, achieving leading video super-resolution results on four datasets.

title: EvTexture: Event-driven Texture Enhancement for Video Super-Resolution

abstract: Recently, various pre-training methods have been introduced in vision-based Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, their generalization ability remains unclear due to evaluations being limited to in-distribution environments and non-unified experimental setups. To address this, we introduce the Atari Pre-training Benchmark (Atari-PB), which pre-trains a ResNet-50 model on 10 million transitions from 50 Atari games and evaluates it across diverse environment distributions. Our experiments show that pre-training objectives focused on learning task-agnostic features (e.g., identifying objects and understanding temporal dynamics) enhance generalization across different environments. In contrast, objectives focused on learning task-specific knowledge (e.g., identifying agents and fitting reward functions) improve performance in environments similar to the pre-training dataset but not in varied ones. We publicize our codes, datasets, and model checkpoints at https://github.com/dojeon-ai/Atari-PB.

paragraphs: Pretraining can help reinforcement-learning agents interpret visual observations, but success in familiar environments does not establish that the learned representation transfers elsewhere. This paper investigates which pretraining objectives support generalization, addressing earlier evaluations that used different setups or focused mainly on environments resembling the training data.

The authors introduce Atari-PB, a benchmark that pretrains a ResNet-50 on 10 million transitions from 50 Atari games. They then evaluate across diverse environment distributions. This shared experimental framework allows them to compare objectives according to whether their benefits persist as the evaluation environment changes.

The experiments find that objectives emphasizing task-agnostic features, such as recognizing objects and understanding temporal dynamics, improve generalization across environments. Objectives emphasizing task-specific knowledge, such as identifying agents or fitting reward functions, help in similar environments but not varied ones. The distinction matters for choosing what pretraining should teach: knowledge useful for the original tasks can have a different transfer profile from more broadly applicable visual and temporal features.
summary.tldr: Atari-PB finds that task-agnostic pretraining objectives generalize across environments better than objectives focused on task-specific knowledge.

title: Investigating Pre-Training Objectives for Generalization in Vision-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A wide range of empirical and theoretical works have shown that overparameterisation can amplify the performance of neural networks. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, overparameterised networks have an increased chance of containing a sub-network that is well-initialised to solve the task at hand. A more parsimonious approach, inspired by animal learning, consists in guiding the learner towards solving the task by curating the order of the examples, ie. providing a curriculum. However, this learning strategy seems to be hardly beneficial in deep learning applications. In this work, we propose a theoretical analysis that connects curriculum learning and overparameterisation. In particular, we investigate their interplay in the online learning setting for a 2-layer network in the XOR-like Gaussian Mixture problem. Our results show that a high degree of overparameterisation—while simplifying the problem—can limit the benefit from curricula, providing a theoretical account of the ineffectiveness of curricula in deep learning.

paragraphs: Two approaches can make neural-network learning easier: increasing the network’s size and arranging training examples into a curriculum. The lottery ticket hypothesis motivates the first by suggesting that larger networks are more likely to contain a favorably initialized subnetwork. Curriculum learning instead tries to guide progress through the order in which examples appear.

This paper connects these ideas through a theoretical analysis of a two-layer network learning an XOR-like Gaussian mixture problem. The analysis uses an online learning setting and examines how the amount of overparameterization changes the benefits available from a curriculum. This makes network size and example ordering parts of the same learning question.

The results show that substantial overparameterization can simplify the task while reducing the additional benefit of a curriculum. This offers a theoretical explanation for why curricula may provide little improvement in deep learning. The conclusion is grounded in the analyzed network and problem setting: it identifies a mechanism by which larger models can diminish curriculum gains, rather than establishing that curricula never help.
summary.tldr: A theoretical two-layer-network analysis shows that strong overparameterization can reduce the additional benefit of curriculum learning.

title: Tilting the Odds at the Lottery: the Interplay of Overparameterisation and Curricula in Neural Networks

abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing have relied heavily on using Transformer-based language models. However, Transformers often require large parameter sizes and model depth. Existing Transformer-free approaches using state-space models demonstrate superiority over Transformers, yet they still lack a neuro-biologically connection to the human brain. This paper proposes ${\it LasF}$, representing ${\bf L}$anguage tokens ${\bf as}$ ${\bf F}$unctionals of semantic fields, to simulate the neuronal behaviors for better language modeling. The ${\it LasF}$ module is equivalent to a nonlinear approximator tailored for sequential data. By replacing the final layers of pre-trained language models with the ${\it LasF}$ module, we obtain ${\it LasF}$-based models. Experiments conducted for standard reading comprehension and question-answering tasks demonstrate that the ${\it LasF}$-based models consistently improve accuracy with fewer parameters. Besides, we use CommonsenseQA’s blind test set to evaluate a full-parameter tuned ${\it LasF}$-based model, which outperforms the prior best ensemble and single models by $0.4%$ and $3.1%$, respectively. Furthermore, our ${\it LasF}$-only language model trained from scratch outperforms existing parameter-efficient language models on standard datasets such as WikiText103 and PennTreebank.

paragraphs: LasF explores a language-modeling module inspired by neuronal behavior. It represents language tokens as functionals of semantic fields: token representations are formulated in relation to those fields. The paper describes the module as a nonlinear approximator designed for sequential data, motivated by the size and depth often required by Transformer models.

The authors first replace the final layers of pre-trained language models with LasF modules. On standard reading-comprehension and question-answering tasks, these modified models consistently achieve higher accuracy with fewer parameters. This evaluates whether the proposed representation can improve an existing model while reducing its parameter requirements.

A fully tuned LasF-based model also exceeds the previous best ensemble and single-model results on the CommonsenseQA blind test set by the reported margins of 0.4% and 3.1%, respectively. Separately, a LasF-only model trained from scratch outperforms existing parameter-efficient language models on datasets including WikiText103 and PennTreebank. The findings support both replacing portions of pre-trained models and using the module as the basis of a language model trained independently.
summary.tldr: LasF models tokens through semantic fields, improving reported language-task accuracy with fewer parameters and supporting models trained from scratch.

title: Modeling Language Tokens as Functionals of Semantic Fields

abstract: The fine-tuning paradigm in addressing long-tail learning tasks has sparked significant interest since the emergence of foundation models. Nonetheless, how fine-tuning impacts performance in long-tail learning was not explicitly quantified. In this paper, we disclose that heavy fine-tuning may even lead to non-negligible performance deterioration on tail classes, and lightweight fine-tuning is more effective. The reason is attributed to inconsistent class conditions caused by heavy fine-tuning. With the observation above, we develop a low-complexity and accurate long-tail learning algorithms LIFT with the goal of facilitating fast prediction and compact models by adaptive lightweight fine-tuning. Experiments clearly verify that both the training time and the learned parameters are significantly reduced with more accurate predictive performance compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/shijxcs/LIFT.

The reason is attributed to inconsistent class conditions caused by heavy fine-tuning. paragraphs: Long-tail learning deals with data in which some classes are common while others have few examples. Foundation models offer a starting point for these tasks, but the amount of adaptation can affect rare classes differently. This paper examines that effect and finds that heavy fine-tuning may substantially reduce performance on tail classes.

The authors attribute this deterioration to inconsistent class conditions introduced by heavy fine-tuning. Their findings favor lighter adaptation and motivate LIFT, an algorithm based on adaptive lightweight fine-tuning. Its design aims to combine accurate prediction with low complexity, compact models, and fast prediction, making the amount of model adaptation a central design choice.

In the reported experiments, LIFT reduces training time and the number of learned parameters while improving predictive accuracy relative to state-of-the-art approaches. These results suggest that more extensive fine-tuning is not automatically beneficial for imbalanced tasks. The stated finding is that heavy adaptation can hurt rare classes, while the proposed lighter approach provides a favorable accuracy and efficiency balance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Heavy fine-tuning can harm rare classes, while LIFT's adaptive lightweight tuning improves reported accuracy with less training and fewer learned parameters.

title: Long-Tail Learning with Foundation Model: Heavy Fine-Tuning Hurts

abstract: Recent advancements in solving large-scale traveling salesman problems (TSP) utilize the heatmap-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) paradigm, where machine learning (ML) models generate heatmaps, indicating the probability distribution of each edge being part of the optimal solution, to guide MCTS in solution finding. However, our theoretical and experimental analysis raises doubts about the effectiveness of ML-based heatmap generation. In support of this, we demonstrate that a simple baseline method can outperform complex ML approaches in heatmap generation. Furthermore, we question the practical value of the heatmap-guided MCTS paradigm. To substantiate this, our findings show its inferiority to the LKH-3 heuristic despite the paradigm's reliance on problem-specific, hand-crafted strategies. For the future, we suggest research directions focused on developing more theoretically sound heatmap generation methods and exploring autonomous, generalizable ML approaches for combinatorial problems. The code is available for review: https://github.com/xyfffff/rethink_mcts_for_tsp.

paragraphs: Some approaches to large traveling salesman problems use a learned heatmap to guide Monte Carlo tree search. The heatmap estimates which edges belong in an optimal tour, and search uses those estimates to construct solutions. This position paper examines whether the learned component and the combined search paradigm deliver the value attributed to them.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental analysis questioning machine-learning-based heatmap generation. They demonstrate that a simple baseline can outperform complex learned approaches at this stage. They also compare the broader heatmap-guided search paradigm with LKH-3 and find it inferior, despite its use of problem-specific, handcrafted strategies.

These findings challenge both the contribution of learned heatmaps and the practical competitiveness of the surrounding pipeline in the studied setting. The paper proposes two directions: stronger theoretical foundations for heatmap generation and more autonomous, generalizable machine-learning approaches to combinatorial problems. Its argument encourages separating gains from the learned guidance from those supplied by search and handcrafted components.
summary.tldr: The paper challenges learned heatmap-guided TSP search, finding a simple heatmap baseline competitive and the overall paradigm inferior to LKH-3.

title: Position: Rethinking Post-Hoc Search-Based Neural Approaches for Solving Large-Scale Traveling Salesman Problems

abstract: Decision tree optimization is fundamental to interpretable machine learning. The most popular approach is to greedily search for the best feature at every decision point, which is fast but provably suboptimal. Recent approaches find the global optimum using branch and bound with dynamic programming, showing substantial improvements in accuracy and sparsity at great cost to scalability. An ideal solution would have the accuracy of an optimal method and the scalability of a greedy method. We introduce a family of algorithms called SPLIT (SParse Lookahead for Interpretable Trees) that moves us significantly forward in achieving this ideal balance. We demonstrate that not all sub-problems need to be solved to optimality to find high quality trees; greediness suffices near the leaves. Since each depth adds an exponential number of possible trees, this change makes our algorithms orders of magnitude faster than existing optimal methods, with negligible loss in performance. We extend this algorithm to allow scalable computation of sets of near-optimal trees (i.e., the Rashomon set).

paragraphs: Decision trees are attractive because their branching decisions can be inspected, but finding a high-quality tree involves a difficult computational tradeoff. Greedy methods choose the best immediate split quickly, while global optimization considers how choices affect the entire tree. Optimal methods can improve accuracy and sparsity, but the search becomes expensive as the space of possible trees grows.

SPLIT combines these approaches by using sparse lookahead while allowing greedy decisions near the leaves. The paper’s central observation is that producing a high-quality whole tree does not require solving every smaller problem optimally. Since additional depth greatly expands the search space, simplifying decisions near the bottom can remove substantial computation.

The authors report speedups of orders of magnitude over existing optimal methods with negligible performance loss. They also extend the approach to compute sets of near-optimal trees, known as Rashomon sets, at greater scale. This makes the contribution relevant both to finding a strong individual tree and to examining multiple similarly performing alternatives.
summary.tldr: SPLIT uses greedy decisions near tree leaves to achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups with negligible reported performance loss.

title: Near-Optimal Decision Trees in a SPLIT Second

abstract: Split Conformal Prediction (SCP) provides a computationally efficient way to construct confidence intervals in prediction problems. Notably, most of the theory built around SCP is focused on the single test point setting. In real-life, inference sets consist of multiple points, which raises the question of coverage guarantees for many points simultaneously. While on average, the False Coverage Proportion (FCP) remains controlled, it can fluctuate strongly around its mean, the False Coverage Rate (FCR). We observe that when a dataset is split multiple times, classical SCP may not control the FCP in a majority of the splits. We propose CoJER, a novel method that achieves sharp FCP control in probability for conformal prediction, based on a recent characterization of the distribution of conformal $p$-values in a transductive setting. This procedure incorporates an aggregation scheme which provides robustness with respect to modeling choices. We show through extensive real data experiments that CoJER provides FCP control while standard SCP does not. Furthermore, CoJER yields shorter intervals than the state-of-the-art method for FCP control and only slightly larger intervals than standard SCP.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals can have acceptable coverage on average while behaving unevenly across batches of predictions. This paper studies that distinction for split conformal prediction. The false coverage proportion is the fraction of intervals that miss their targets in a particular inference set; its average can remain controlled even when individual realizations fluctuate substantially.

The authors observe that ordinary split conformal prediction may fail to control this proportion for a majority of repeated dataset splits. They propose CoJER, which controls false coverage proportion in probability. Its construction uses a characterization of conformal p-values in a transductive setting and includes an aggregation scheme designed to make the result more robust to modeling choices.

Real-data experiments show the intended proportion control for CoJER where standard split conformal prediction does not provide it. CoJER also produces shorter intervals than the compared state-of-the-art method for this stronger coverage objective, with intervals only slightly wider than ordinary split conformal prediction. This makes the distinction between average reliability and batch-level reliability practically consequential.
summary.tldr: CoJER controls the proportion of missed targets across prediction intervals in probability, with modest interval widening relative to standard split conformal prediction.

title: False Coverage Proportion Control for Conformal Prediction

abstract: Graphical models have been widely used as parsimonious encoders of constraints of the underlying probability models. When organized in a structured way, these models can facilitate the derivation of non-trivial constraints, the inference of quantities of interest, and the optimization of their estimands. In particular, causal diagrams allow for the efficient representation of structural constraints of the underlying causal system. In this paper, we introduce an efficient graphical construction called Ancestral Multi-world Networks that is sound and complete for reading counterfactual independences from a causal diagram using d-separation. Moreover, we introduce the counterfactual (ctf-) calculus, which can be used to transform counterfactual quantities using three rules licensed by the constraints encoded in the diagram. This result generalizes Pearl’s celebrated do-calculus from interventional to counterfactual reasoning.

paragraphs: Causal diagrams compactly represent assumptions about how variables influence one another. This paper develops tools for using those diagrams to reason about counterfactual quantities: questions involving what would happen under alternative circumstances. The central challenge is extracting the relationships and constraints that the underlying causal structure imposes on those quantities.

The authors introduce Ancestral Multi-world Networks, an efficient graphical construction for reading counterfactual independences through d-separation. The construction is sound and complete for this purpose. In plain terms, the graphical procedure correctly identifies the relevant independences implied by the causal diagram and captures all such independences within the stated framework. This gives counterfactual reasoning a structured graphical basis.

The paper also introduces a counterfactual calculus consisting of three transformation rules justified by constraints encoded in the diagram. These rules extend Pearl’s do-calculus from intervention questions to counterfactual reasoning. Together, the network construction and calculus provide complementary tools: one exposes independence relationships, while the other uses diagram-supported constraints to transform quantities of interest.
summary.tldr: Ancestral Multi-world Networks and a three-rule counterfactual calculus extend graphical causal reasoning to counterfactual independences and quantities.

title: Counterfactual Graphical Models: Constraints and Inference

abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) generate guarantees for treatment effects. However, RCTs often spend unnecessary resources exploring sub-optimal treatments, which can reduce the power of treatment guarantees. To address this, we propose a two-stage RCT design. In the first stage, a data-driven screening procedure prunes low-impact treatments, while the second stage focuses on developing high-probability lower bounds for the best-performing treatment effect. Unlike existing adaptive RCT frameworks, our method is simple enough to be implemented in scenarios with limited adaptivity. We derive optimal designs for two-stage RCTs and demonstrate how such designs can be implemented through sample splitting. Empirically, we demonstrate that two-stage designs improve upon single-stage approaches, especially for scenarios where domain knowledge is available through a prior. Our work is thus, a simple yet effective design for RCTs, optimizing for the ability to certify with high probability the largest possible treatment effect for at least one of the arms studied.

paragraphs: A randomized controlled trial can spend substantial resources testing treatments that have little impact. This paper asks how to allocate a trial so that it can certify a strong effect for at least one treatment. Its objective is specifically to obtain a high-probability lower bound on the best-performing treatment effect.

The proposed design has two stages. First, a data-driven screening procedure removes low-impact treatments. Second, the trial focuses on establishing lower bounds for the strongest remaining treatment effect. The authors derive optimal designs for this two-stage formulation and show how to implement them through sample splitting. This structure is intended for settings where repeatedly adapting a trial is difficult.

Empirical results favor the two-stage designs over single-stage approaches, especially when prior knowledge about the treatments is available. The significance is that screening can improve how trial resources support a treatment-effect guarantee. The claimed benefit concerns the strength of a probabilistic certificate for at least one studied arm, rather than a promise that every treatment will be well estimated.
summary.tldr: A two-stage trial screens out weak treatments before concentrating resources on certifying a strong treatment effect with high probability.

title: Data-driven Design of Randomized Control Trials with Guaranteed Treatment Effects

abstract: In this work, we argue that large language models (LLMs), though trained to predict only the next token, exhibit emergent planning behaviors: $\textbf{their hidden representations encode future outputs beyond the next token}$. Through simple probing, we demonstrate that LLM prompt representations encode global attributes of their entire responses, including $\textit{structure attributes}$ (e.g., response length, reasoning steps), $\textit{content attributes}$ (e.g., character choices in storywriting, multiple-choice answers at the end of response), and $\textit{behavior attributes}$ (e.g., answer confidence, factual consistency). In addition to identifying response planning, we explore how it scales with model size across tasks and how it evolves during generation. The findings that LLMs plan ahead for the future in their hidden representations suggest potential applications for improving transparency and generation control.

paragraphs: Language models are trained to predict the next token, yet this paper argues that their internal representations contain information about much later parts of a response. The researchers use simple probes to investigate what can be recovered from the model’s representation of a prompt. Their focus is on properties of the response as a whole.

The probes reveal information about several kinds of future attributes. Structural attributes include response length and the number of reasoning steps. Content attributes include characters chosen for a story and a multiple-choice answer appearing at the end. Behavioral attributes include answer confidence and factual consistency. These findings indicate that prompt representations can carry information extending beyond the immediate next token.

The study also examines how this response planning varies with model size across tasks and how it changes during generation. The authors interpret the evidence as emergent planning in hidden representations. They suggest that these signals could support greater transparency and control over generation, presenting those applications as potential uses of the findings.
summary.tldr: Probes reveal that LLM prompt representations encode attributes of future responses, providing evidence of emergent response planning.

title: Emergent Response Planning in LLMs

abstract: We present MFRNet, a novel network for multi-modal object re-identification that integrates multi-modal data features to effectively retrieve specific objects across different modalities. Current methods suffer from two principal limitations: (1) insufficient interaction between pixel-level semantic features across modalities, and (2) difficulty in balancing modality-shared and modality-specific features within a unified architecture. To address these challenges, our network introduces two core components. First, the Feature Fusion Module (FFM) enables fine-grained pixel-level feature generation and flexible cross-modal interaction. Second, the Feature Representation Module (FRM) efficiently extracts and combines modality-specific and modality-shared features, achieving strong discriminative ability with minimal parameter overhead. Extensive experiments on three challenging public datasets (RGBNT201, RGBNT100, and MSVR310) demonstrate the superiority of our approach in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, with 8.4% mAP and 6.9% accuracy improved in RGBNT201 with negligible additional parameters.

paragraphs: Multimodal object re-identification aims to retrieve a particular object using information from different modalities. MFRNet addresses two difficulties in combining that information: limited interaction among fine-grained features across modalities, and the challenge of preserving both shared information and features specific to each modality. Both matter for distinguishing the target object from other candidates.

The network separates these responsibilities into two components. Its Feature Fusion Module creates pixel-level features and enables flexible interaction across modalities. Its Feature Representation Module extracts and combines modality-specific and modality-shared features. Together, they aim to retain useful distinctions while making information from the different inputs work together, with little additional parameter overhead.

Experiments on RGBNT201, RGBNT100, and MSVR310 support improvements in accuracy and efficiency. On RGBNT201, the abstract reports improvements of 8.4% in mean average precision and 6.9% in accuracy, with negligible extra parameters. The findings suggest that better organization of feature fusion and representation can improve retrieval without requiring a large increase in model size.
summary.tldr: MFRNet improves multimodal object retrieval by combining fine-grained cross-modal fusion with shared and modality-specific feature representations.

title: Multi-Modal Object Re-identification via Sparse Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Fake images, created by recently advanced generative models, have become increasingly indistinguishable from real ones, making their detection crucial, urgent, and challenging. This paper introduces PiD (Pixelwise Decomposition Residuals), a novel detection method that focuses on residual signals within images. Generative models are designed to optimize high-level semantic content (principal components), often overlooking low-level signals (residual components). PiD leverages this observation by disentangling residual components from images, encouraging the model to uncover more underlying and general forgery clues independent of semantic content. Compared to prior approaches that rely on reconstruction techniques or high-frequency information, PiD is computationally efficient and does not rely on any generative models for reconstruction. Specifically, PiD operates at the pixel level, mapping the pixel vector to another color space (e.g., YUV) and then quantizing the vector. The pixel vector is mapped back to the RGB space and the quantization loss is taken as the residual for AIGC detection. Our experiment results are striking and highly surprising: PiD achieves 98% accuracy on the widely used GenImage benchmark, highlighting the effectiveness and generalization performance.

paragraphs: PiD detects generated images by focusing on low-level residual signals rather than their visible semantic content. The motivating observation is that generative models prioritize high-level content and can overlook lower-level components. Separating those components aims to expose forgery clues that depend less on what an image depicts and can therefore be useful across different image content.

The extraction procedure operates on individual pixel vectors. It transforms a pixel from RGB into another color space, such as YUV, quantizes the transformed vector, and maps it back into RGB. The loss introduced by quantization becomes the residual used for detection. This provides a direct way to obtain a detection signal without reconstructing the image through a generative model.

The authors describe PiD as computationally efficient relative to prior approaches based on reconstruction or high-frequency information. They report 98% accuracy on the GenImage benchmark, supporting its effectiveness and generalization in that evaluation. The distinctive contribution is a simple pixel-level decomposition designed to make less semantic, more general forgery evidence available to the detector.
summary.tldr: PiD extracts pixelwise quantization residuals to detect generated images, achieving reported accuracy of 98% on GenImage.

title: PiD: Generalized AI-Generated Images Detection with Pixelwise Decomposition Residuals

abstract: We consider learning underlying laws of dynamical systems governed by ordinary differential equations (ODE). A key challenge is how to discover intrinsic dynamics across multiple environments while circumventing environment-specific mechanisms. Unlike prior work, we tackle more complex environments where changes extend beyond function coefficients to entirely different function forms. For example, we demonstrate the discovery of ideal pendulum’s natural motion $\alpha^2 \sin{\theta_t}$ by observing pendulum dynamics in different environments, such as the damped environment $\alpha^2 \sin(\theta_t) - \rho \omega_t$ and powered environment $\alpha^2 \sin(\theta_t) + \rho \frac{\omega_t}{\left|\omega_t\right|}$. Here, we formulate this problem as an invariant function learning task and propose a new method, known as Disentanglement of Invariant Functions (DIF), that is grounded in causal analysis. We propose a causal graph and design an encoder-decoder hypernetwork that explicitly disentangles invariant functions from environment-specific dynamics. The discovery of invariant functions is guaranteed by our information-based principle that enforces the independence between extracted invariant functions and environments. Quantitative comparisons with meta-learning and invariant learning baselines on three ODE systems demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method. Furthermore, symbolic regression explanation results highlight the ability of our framework to uncover intrinsic laws.

paragraphs: Observations of a physical system mix its underlying dynamics with effects specific to its environment. This paper aims to recover the common law across environments described by ordinary differential equations. It considers changes that alter entire functional forms, extending beyond changes to coefficients in an otherwise fixed equation.

The proposed method, Disentanglement of Invariant Functions, uses a causal graph and an encoder-decoder hypernetwork to separate shared dynamics from environmental effects. Symbolic regression results further show its ability to express recovered intrinsic laws. The contribution concerns isolating the common dynamics underlying several environments, so that changes in surrounding mechanisms do not become confused with the system's invariant behavior.
summary.tldr: DIF separates shared physical dynamics from environment-specific effects, recovering invariant laws across systems with changing functional forms.

title: Discovering Physics Laws of Dynamical Systems via Invariant Function Learning

abstract: Contrastive Representation Learning (CRL) has achieved impressive success in various domains in recent years. Nevertheless, the theoretical understanding of the generalization behavior of CRL has remained limited. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, the current literature only analyzes generalization bounds under the assumption that the data tuples used for contrastive learning are independently and identically distributed. However, in practice, we are often limited to a fixed pool of reusable labeled data points, making it inevitable to recycle data across tuples to create sufficiently large datasets. Therefore, the tuple-wise independence condition imposed by previous works is invalidated. In this paper, we provide a generalization analysis for the CRL framework under non-$i.i.d.$ settings that adheres to practice more realistically. Drawing inspiration from the literature on U-statistics, we derive generalization bounds which indicate that the required number of samples in each class scales as the logarithm of the covering number of the class of learnable feature representations associated to that class. Next, we apply our main results to derive excess risk bounds for common function classes such as linear maps and neural networks.

paragraphs: Contrastive representation learning constructs training tuples from examples, but practical datasets often reuse the same labeled points in many tuples. This reuse makes the tuples dependent. The paper addresses a mismatch with earlier generalization analyses that assume tuples are independently and identically distributed, even though that assumption fails under this common construction.

The authors derive bounds for supervised contrastive learning in a setting that accounts for these dependencies. Their analysis draws on U-statistics, providing a way to reason about combinations built from a shared pool of observations. The resulting bounds relate the required number of examples in each class to the logarithm of a covering number for that class's learnable representations.

A covering number describes the size of a collection needed to approximate a function class, so the result connects sample needs with representation complexity. The authors then derive excess-risk bounds for linear maps and neural networks. The contribution is a theoretical account of generalization that better reflects reuse of labeled data when constructing contrastive training tuples.
summary.tldr: The paper derives contrastive-learning generalization bounds that account for dependent tuples formed by reusing labeled examples.

title: Generalization Analysis for Supervised Contrastive Representation Learning under Non-IID Settings

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generative tasks but suffer from high computational costs due to their iterative sampling process and quadratic-attention costs. Existing training-free acceleration strategies that reduce per-step computation cost, while effectively reducing sampling time, demonstrate low faithfulness compared to the original baseline. We hypothesize that this fidelity gap arises because (a) different prompts correspond to varying denoising trajectory, and (b) such methods do not consider the underlying ODE formulation and its numerical solution. In this paper, we propose Stability-guided Adaptive Diffusion Acceleration (SADA), a novel paradigm that unifies step-wise and token-wise sparsity decisions via a single stability criterion to accelerate sampling of ODE-based generative models (Diffusion and Flow-matching). Moreover, SADA adapts seamlessly to other pipelines and modalities: It accelerates ControlNet without any modifications and speeds up MusicLDM by $1.8\times$ with $\sim 0.01$ spectrogram LPIPS. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Ting-Justin-Jiang/sada-icml.

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at generating highly detailed captions but often produce hallucinations. Our analysis reveals that existing hallucination detection methods struggle with detailed captions. We attribute this to the increasing reliance of MLLMs on their generated text, rather than the input image, as the sequence length grows. To address this issue, we propose a multiagent approach that leverages LLM-MLLM collaboration to correct given captions. Additionally, we introduce an evaluation framework and a benchmark dataset to facilitate the systematic analysis of detailed captions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed evaluation method aligns better with human judgments of factuality than existing metrics. Moreover, we show that current approaches for enhancing MLLM factuality often fail in hyper-detailed image captioning tasks. In contrast, our approach significantly enhances the factual accuracy of captions, even improving those generated by GPT-4V. Finally, we highlight a limitation of VQA-centric benchmarking by demonstrating that an MLLM’s performance on VQA benchmarks may not correlate with its ability to generate detailed image captions.

paragraphs: Highly detailed image captions can include unsupported claims even when the model describes much of the image correctly. This paper finds that existing hallucination detectors struggle with such captions. The authors attribute the difficulty to multimodal models increasingly relying on their own generated text as captions grow longer, weakening the connection to the input image.

The proposed correction method uses collaboration between language models and multimodal language models to revise existing captions. The paper also introduces an evaluation framework and benchmark for detailed caption analysis, with factuality and coverage as evaluation concerns. This pairs a method for improving captions with tools for examining whether their claims are accurate and how thoroughly they describe the image.

Experiments show that the proposed evaluation aligns better with human factuality judgments than existing metrics. The correction approach significantly improves caption accuracy, including captions produced by GPT-4V, while current factuality-enhancement methods often fail in this setting. The paper also finds that visual question-answering performance may not correlate with detailed captioning ability, highlighting the need to evaluate this generation task directly.
summary.tldr: Collaborating language and multimodal models improve detailed captions, while a new evaluation framework better matches human factuality judgments.

title: Toward Robust Hyper-Detailed Image Captioning: A Multiagent Approach and Dual Evaluation Metrics for Factuality and Coverage

abstract: KV cache quantization can improve Large Language Models (LLMs) inference throughput and latency in long contexts and large batch-size scenarios while preserving LLMs effectiveness. However, current methods have three unsolved issues: overlooking layer-wise sensitivity to KV cache quantization, high overhead of online fine-grained decision-making, and low flexibility to different LLMs and constraints. Therefore, we theoretically analyze the inherent correlation of layer-wise transformer attention patterns to KV cache quantization errors and study why key cache is generally more important than value cache for quantization error reduction. We further propose a simple yet effective framework KVTuner to adaptively search for the optimal hardware-friendly layer-wise KV quantization precision pairs for coarse-grained KV cache with multi-objective optimization and directly utilize the offline searched configurations during online inference. To reduce the computational cost of offline calibration, we utilize the intra-layer KV precision pair pruning and inter-layer clustering to reduce the search space. Experimental results show that we can achieve nearly lossless 3.25-bit mixed precision KV cache quantization for LLMs like Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 4.0-bit for sensitive models like Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on mathematical reasoning tasks. The maximum inference throughput can be improved by 21.25% compared with KIVI-KV8 quantization over various context lengths. Our code and searched configurations are available at https://github.com/cmd2001/KVTuner.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model's key-value cache can improve inference efficiency, but different transformer layers respond differently to quantization. KVTuner investigates this variation through the relationship between attention patterns and quantization error. It also examines why preserving key-cache precision is generally more important than preserving value-cache precision for reducing error.

The framework searches offline for hardware-friendly pairs of key and value precisions for each layer, balancing multiple objectives. Those configurations are then used directly during inference, avoiding repeated online precision decisions. To reduce calibration cost, the search prunes candidate precision pairs within layers and clusters layers to shrink the overall search space.

On mathematical reasoning tasks, the authors report nearly lossless mixed-precision caches averaging 3.25 bits for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 4.0 bits for the more sensitive Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The maximum reported throughput improvement over KIVI-KV8 is 21.25% across the evaluated context lengths. These results illustrate how allocating precision according to layer sensitivity can preserve task performance while improving inference efficiency.
summary.tldr: KVTuner searches offline for layer-specific KV-cache precisions that improve inference efficiency while nearly preserving evaluated reasoning performance.

title: KVTuner: Sensitivity-Aware Layer-Wise Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient and Nearly Lossless LLM Inference

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at capturing global token dependencies via self-attention but face prohibitive compute and memory costs on lengthy inputs. While sub-quadratic methods (e.g., linear attention) can reduce these costs, they often degrade accuracy due to overemphasizing recent tokens. In this work, we first propose dual-state linear attention (DSLA), a novel design that maintains two specialized hidden states—one for preserving historical context and one for tracking recency—thereby mitigating the short-range bias typical of linear-attention architectures. To further balance efficiency and accuracy under dynamic workload conditions, we introduce DSLA-Serve, an online adaptive distillation framework that progressively replaces Transformer layers with DSLA layers at inference time, guided by a sensitivity-based layer ordering. DSLA-Serve uses a chained fine-tuning strategy to ensure that each newly converted DSLA layer remains consistent with previously replaced layers, preserving the overall quality. Extensive evaluations on commonsense reasoning, long-context QA, and text summarization demonstrate that DSLA-Serve yields 2.3$\times$ faster inference than Llama2-7B and 3.0$\times$ faster than the hybrid Zamba-7B, while retaining comparable performance across downstream tasks. Our ablation studies show that DSLA’s dual states capture both global and local dependencies, addressing the historical-token underrepresentation seen in prior linear attentions.

paragraphs: Long inputs make Transformer attention expensive in both computation and memory. Linear attention can reduce these costs, but it often gives too much emphasis to recent tokens and loses useful earlier context. This paper introduces dual-state linear attention, or DSLA, with one hidden state dedicated to historical information and another dedicated to recency.

The authors combine this architecture with DSLA-Serve, an adaptive distillation framework that progressively converts Transformer layers into DSLA layers during serving. A sensitivity-based ordering guides which layers are replaced. Chained fine-tuning keeps each newly converted layer consistent with earlier conversions, helping preserve overall model quality as the architecture changes.

Evaluations on commonsense reasoning, long-context question answering, and summarization report 2.3 times faster inference than Llama2-7B and 3.0 times faster inference than Zamba-7B, with comparable downstream performance. Ablations indicate that the two states capture both global and local dependencies. The findings support separating historical context from recency as a way to reduce the short-range bias of linear attention while improving serving efficiency.
summary.tldr: DSLA-Serve progressively replaces Transformer layers with dual-state linear attention, reporting faster inference while retaining comparable task performance.

title: On-the-Fly Adaptive Distillation of Transformer to Dual-State Linear Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become indispensable in numerous real-world applications. However, fine-tuning these models at scale, especially in federated settings where data privacy and communication efficiency are critical, presents significant challenges. Existing approaches often resort to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to mitigate communication overhead, but this typically comes at the cost of model accuracy. To this end, we propose federated full-parameter tuning at scale for LLMs (Ferret), the first first-order method with shared randomness to enable scalable full-parameter tuning of LLMs across decentralized data sources while maintaining competitive model accuracy. Ferret accomplishes this through three aspects: (i) it employs widely used first-order methods for efficient local updates; (ii) it projects these updates into a low-dimensional space to considerably reduce communication overhead; and (iii) it reconstructs local updates from this low-dimensional space with shared randomness to facilitate effective full-parameter global aggregation, ensuring fast convergence and competitive final performance. Our rigorous theoretical analyses and insights along with extensive experiments, show that Ferret significantly enhances the scalability of existing federated full-parameter tuning approaches by achieving high computational efficiency, reduced communication overhead, and fast convergence, all while maintaining competitive model accuracy. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/allen4747/Ferret.

paragraphs: Ferret addresses the communication cost of updating all parameters of a language model across decentralized data sources. Federated approaches often reduce this burden through parameter-efficient tuning, which the authors note can sacrifice accuracy. Ferret instead retains full-parameter tuning and changes how participating clients communicate their local updates to support aggregation.

Clients use first-order optimization methods for local training, then project their updates into a low-dimensional space. Shared randomness allows updates to be reconstructed from those compact representations for full-parameter global aggregation. The important distinction is between the dimensionality of the communicated representation and the scope of the model update: a small message can still contribute to updating the full model.

The authors present theoretical analyses and extensive experiments supporting computational efficiency, lower communication overhead, fast convergence, and competitive final accuracy. They describe Ferret as the first first-order method using shared randomness for this purpose. Its contribution is a way to scale federated full-parameter training by compressing update communication while retaining an effective global training process.
summary.tldr: Ferret enables scalable federated full-parameter tuning by communicating compact projections of updates and reconstructing them with shared randomness.

title: Ferret: Federated Full-Parameter Tuning at Scale for Large Language Models

abstract: Bayesian phylogenetics is vital for understanding evolutionary dynamics, and requires accurate and efficient approximation of posterior distributions over trees. In this work, we develop a variational Bayesian approach for ultrametric phylogenetic trees. We present a novel variational family based on coalescent times of a single-linkage clustering and derive a closed-form density for the resulting distribution over trees. Unlike existing methods for ultrametric trees, our method performs inference over all of tree space, it does not require any Markov chain Monte Carlo subroutines, and our variational family is differentiable. Through experiments on benchmark genomic datasets and an application to the viral RNA of SARS-CoV-2, we demonstrate that our method achieves competitive accuracy while requiring significantly fewer gradient evaluations than existing state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: Bayesian phylogenetics represents uncertainty about evolutionary trees through a posterior distribution, rather than committing to one tree. Approximating that distribution accurately and efficiently is challenging. This paper develops a variational Bayesian method for ultrametric phylogenetic trees, introducing a new family of distributions that can be optimized to approximate the posterior.

The variational family is constructed from the coalescent times of single-linkage clustering. The authors derive a closed-form density for the resulting distribution over trees, and the family is differentiable. Their approach can perform inference across the full ultrametric tree space without Markov chain Monte Carlo subroutines. These properties provide a direct optimization route while avoiding restrictions to only part of the relevant tree space.

Experiments use benchmark genomic datasets and an application involving SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA. The method achieves competitive accuracy with significantly fewer gradient evaluations than existing state-of-the-art techniques. The findings support this distribution family as an efficient basis for evolutionary uncertainty estimation, with the reported computational benefit specifically measured through gradient evaluations.
summary.tldr: A differentiable variational distribution enables full-space ultrametric tree inference with competitive accuracy and fewer gradient evaluations.

title: Variational Phylogenetic Inference with Products over Bipartitions

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have proven effective in generating high-quality videos but are hindered by high computational costs. Existing video diffusion sampling acceleration methods often rely on costly fine-tuning or exhibit limited generalization capabilities. We propose Asymmetric Reduction and Restoration (AsymRnR), a training-free and model-agnostic method to accelerate video DiTs. It builds on the observation that redundancies of feature tokens in DiTs vary significantly across different model blocks, denoising steps, and feature types. Our AsymRnR asymmetrically reduces redundant tokens in the attention operation, achieving acceleration with negligible degradation in output quality and, in some cases, even improving it. We also tailored a reduction schedule to distribute the reduction across components adaptively. To further accelerate this process, we introduce a matching cache for more efficient reduction. Backed by theoretical foundations and extensive experimental validation, AsymRnR integrates into state-of-the-art video DiTs and offers substantial speedup.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers can produce high-quality videos, but their computation is expensive. AsymRnR targets that cost without additional training. Its starting observation is that feature-token redundancy varies across model blocks, denoising steps, and feature types. Consequently, different parts of the generation process offer different opportunities to reduce attention computation.

The method removes redundant tokens asymmetrically within attention rather than applying the same reduction everywhere. A tailored schedule distributes reduction adaptively across components, reflecting the uneven redundancy the authors observe. A matching cache further accelerates the reduction process, addressing the overhead involved in deciding which tokens can be reduced.

The authors describe the approach as model-agnostic and demonstrate integration into leading video diffusion transformers. Their theoretical treatment and experiments support substantial acceleration with negligible deterioration in output quality; some cases even show quality improvements. These findings suggest that selectively reducing attention work can make video generation faster while preserving the information needed for good outputs in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: AsymRnR accelerates video diffusion transformers without training by adaptively reducing redundant attention tokens.

title: AsymRnR: Video Diffusion Transformers Acceleration with Asymmetric Reduction and Restoration

abstract: Multi-view data involves various data forms, such as multi-feature, multi-sequence and multimodal data, providing rich semantic information for downstream tasks. The inherent challenge of incomplete multi-view missing multi-label learning lies in how to effectively utilize limited supervision and insufficient data to learn discriminative representation. Starting from the sufficiency of multi-view shared information for downstream tasks, we argue that the existing contrastive learning paradigms on missing multi-view data show limited consistency representation learning ability, leading to the bottleneck in extracting multi-view shared information. In response, we propose to minimize task-independent redundant information by pursuing the maximization of cross-view mutual information. Additionally, to alleviate the hindrance caused by missing labels, we develop a dual-branch soft pseudo-label cross-imputation strategy to improve classification performance. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks validate our advantages and demonstrate strong compatibility with both missing and complete data.

paragraphs: Multi-view classification uses different forms of information about the same examples, such as multiple feature sets, sequences, or modalities. This paper tackles the harder setting where some views and some labels are missing. The central challenge is learning representations that distinguish classes despite having incomplete inputs and limited supervision.

The authors start from the sufficiency of shared information across views for downstream tasks. They argue that existing contrastive approaches to missing-view data have limited ability to learn consistent representations. Their method pursues greater mutual information across views while aiming to reduce redundant information unrelated to the task, concentrating representation learning on useful shared semantics.

To address missing labels, the method adds a two-branch strategy that uses soft pseudo-labels for cross-imputation. This supplies estimated label information within the learning process alongside the shared-representation objective. Experiments on multiple benchmarks report advantages over compared methods and compatibility with both incomplete and complete data. The contribution combines handling missing input views with handling missing supervision, treating both as obstacles to learning discriminative representations.
summary.tldr: The method combines shared-information learning across views with soft pseudo-label cross-imputation to improve classification when inputs and labels are incomplete.

title: Learning Compact Semantic Information for Incomplete Multi-View Missing Multi-Label Classification

abstract: While existing benchmarks probe the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) across diverse domains, they predominantly assess passive reasoning, providing models with all the information needed to reach a solution. By contrast, active reasoning—where an LLM must interact with external systems to acquire missing evidence or data—has received little systematic attention. To address this shortfall, we present AR-Bench, a novel benchmark designed explicitly to evaluate an LLM’s active reasoning skills. AR-Bench comprises three task families—detective cases, situation puzzles, and guessing numbers—that together simulate real-world, agentic scenarios and measure performance across commonsense, logical, and symbolic reasoning challenges. Empirical evaluation on AR-Bench demonstrates that contemporary LLMs exhibit pronounced difficulties with active reasoning: they frequently fail to acquire or leverage the information needed to solve tasks. This gap highlights a stark divergence between their passive and active reasoning abilities. Moreover, ablation studies indicate that even advanced strategies, such as tree-based searching or post-training approaches, yield only modest gains and fall short of the levels required for real-world deployment. Collectively, these findings highlight the critical need to advance methodology for active reasoning, e.g., incorporating interactive learning, real-time feedback loops, and environment-aware objectives for training. The benchmark is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/AR-Bench.

paragraphs: Many reasoning benchmarks supply all the evidence needed to solve a problem. AR-Bench examines a different capability: recognizing that information is missing and interacting with an external system to obtain it. This separates reasoning over a complete prompt from active reasoning, where asking useful questions is part of solving the task.

The benchmark contains detective cases, situation puzzles, and number-guessing tasks. Together, these task families cover commonsense, logical, and symbolic reasoning in interactive settings. Success depends on both acquiring relevant information and making effective use of it, so the benchmark can expose failures that ordinary question-answering evaluations may overlook.

Evaluations find pronounced difficulties among contemporary language models, including failures to collect or use necessary evidence. Ablations show that tree-based search and post-training approaches provide only modest improvements, which the authors judge insufficient for real-world deployment. The results motivate further work on interactive learning, real-time feedback, and objectives that account for the environment; these are proposed directions rather than demonstrated solutions in the abstract.
summary.tldr: AR-Bench reveals that language models struggle to ask for and use missing information, even when stronger search or post-training strategies are applied.

title: From Passive to Active Reasoning: Can Large Language Models Ask the Right Questions under Incomplete Information?

abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have achieved remarkable progress in text-to-image generation, yet they frequently suffer from concept omission, where specified objects or attributes fail to emerge in the generated image. By performing linear probing on text tokens, we demonstrate that text embeddings can distinguish a characteristic ‘omission signal’ representing the absence of target concepts. Leveraging this insight, we propose Omission Signal Intervention (OSI), which amplifies the omission signal to actively catalyze the generation of missing concepts. Comprehensive experiments on FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Medium demonstrate that OSI significantly alleviates concept omission even in extreme scenarios.

By performing linear probing on text tokens, we demonstrate that text embeddings can distinguish a characteristic ‘omission signal’ representing the absence of target concepts. Leveraging this insight, we propose Omission Signal Intervention (OSI), which amplifies the omission signal to actively catalyze the generation of missing concepts. Comprehensive experiments on FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Medium demonstrate that OSI significantly alleviates concept omission even in extreme scenarios.

paragraphs: A text-to-image model can produce an image while leaving out an object or attribute explicitly requested in the prompt. This paper studies that problem, called concept omission, in multimodal diffusion Transformers. Its central question is whether the model’s text representations contain a detectable sign that a requested concept will be absent.

The authors apply linear probing to text tokens and find an identifiable omission signal in their embeddings. This means the representations carry information that distinguishes the absence of target concepts. They use that observation to develop Omission Signal Intervention, or OSI, which amplifies the identified signal to encourage the missing concept to appear during generation.

The intervention is noteworthy because it turns an internal diagnostic signal into a means of correction. Experiments on FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Medium show significant reductions in concept omission, including under scenarios the authors describe as extreme. The stated result is improved inclusion of requested content; the abstract supports alleviating this failure mode rather than claiming that every prompt detail is always rendered.
summary.tldr: OSI detects an internal signal associated with missing image concepts and amplifies it to improve their inclusion.

title: Diagnosing and Correcting Concept Omission in Multimodal Diffusion Transformers

abstract: Human vision is foveated, with variable resolution peaking at the center of a large field of view; this reflects an efficient trade-off for active sensing, allowing eye-movements to bring different parts of the world into focus with other parts of the world in context. In contrast, most computer vision systems encode the visual world at a uniform resolution, raising challenges for processing full-field high-resolution images efficiently. We propose a foveated vision interface (FOVI) based on the human retina and primary visual cortex (V1), that reformats a variable-resolution retina-like sensor array into a uniformly dense, V1-like sensor manifold. We demonstrate two use cases: (1) an end-to-end kNN-convolutional architecture, and (2) a foveated adaptation of the DINOv3 ViT foundation model, leveraging low-rank adaptation (LoRA). These models provide competitive performance with a fraction of the pixels and computational cost of full resolution non-foveated baselines, opening pathways for efficient and scalable active sensing for high-resolution egocentric vision. Code (https://github.com/nblauch/fovi) and pre-trained models (https://huggingface.co/fovi-pytorch) are available.

title: FOVI: A biologically-inspired foveated interface for deep vision models

abstract: Generating physically consistent 3D tabletop scenes is a fundamental yet underexplored problem for interactive and generalist robotic learning. The challenge stems from dense object hierarchies and irregular affordances. Here, an interactive scene denotes a physically valid, collision-free environment directly loadable into physics simulators. Existing methods, ranging from decoupled symbolic solvers to end-to-end regression models, often suffer from error propagation or overfitting to noisy supervision containing widespread physical violations. To address these limitations, we introduce PhyScene3D, a framework that reformulates generation as a Human-Mimetic Constructive Process. The proposed Cognitive Topological Reasoning Chain (CTRC) factorizes scene synthesis into a sequential, anchor-conditioned process. It employs a 3D AABB-based placement scheme that imposes a strong structural inductive bias. To address imperfect supervision and physical infeasibility, we introduce Physics-Aware Denoising Alignment (PADA). It integrates a differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) with Test-Time Optimization (TTO) to project generated scenes onto a physics-feasible manifold while preserving semantic intent. Experiments demonstrate that PhyScene3D outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both semantic accuracy and physical validity, achieving a 40% reduction in scene-wise collision rate relative to the human-annotated training data.

paragraphs: PhyScene3D generates tabletop environments intended for direct use in physics simulators. These scenes must satisfy physical constraints while preserving meaningful object arrangements. Dense object hierarchies and irregular affordances make this difficult, and training examples themselves can contain physical violations that a generator may learn to reproduce.

The framework treats scene generation as a sequential constructive process. Its Cognitive Topological Reasoning Chain places objects conditionally on anchors, using three-dimensional axis-aligned bounding boxes to impose structural guidance. This breaks scene synthesis into ordered placement decisions rather than asking the model to resolve the entire arrangement at once.

A second component, Physics-Aware Denoising Alignment, combines a differentiable signed distance field with test-time optimization to move generated scenes toward physically feasible configurations while retaining their semantic intent. Experiments report better semantic accuracy and physical validity than state-of-the-art approaches. Scene-wise collision rate is reduced by 40% relative to the human-annotated training data. This result shows that the framework can improve physical consistency beyond the imperfect examples it learns from.
summary.tldr: PhyScene3D combines sequential object placement with physics-aware refinement to generate more semantically accurate and physically valid tabletop scenes.

title: PhyScene3D: Physically Consistent Interactive 3D Tabletop Scene Generation

abstract: Large-scale learning systems often face the challenge of balancing multiple, potentially competing objectives, such as fairness, accuracy, and latency. While recent work has formalized this as an optimization problem over binary states, many real-world control parameters—such as fairness thresholds, diversity mixing rates, or resource budgets—are continuous. In this work, we extend the framework to continuous state spaces. We model the problem as minimizing a sum of linear objectives subject to movement costs that penalize system instability. We capture the local structure of the objectives using a dependency graph (or factor graph), where each objective is determined by a subset of the state attributes. To address the tension between exploration and stability, we propose Lazy Graph-LinUCB, an algorithm that performs lazy updates to minimize switching costs while maintaining near-optimal regret. Beyond stability, we introduce three advanced mechanisms to exploit the underlying graph structure: (1) an asynchronous update schedule that eliminates synchronization overhead in sparse graphs; (2) an adaptive algorithm that learns the graph structure from data; and (3) a joint estimator that leverages data sharing among correlated objectives to significantly tighten regret bounds. Empirically, we demonstrate that these structural exploitations reduce movement costs by more than a factor of three in heterogeneous systems while maintaining similar cumulative losses.

paragraphs: Learning systems often adjust continuous controls while balancing objectives such as accuracy, fairness, and latency. Frequent changes can also destabilize the system. This paper models that tension through a sum of linear objectives and movement costs, extending an earlier binary-state formulation to continuous choices. A dependency graph records which state attributes affect each objective.

The proposed Lazy Graph-LinUCB algorithm delays updates to reduce switching costs while retaining near-optimal regret. The authors then develop three ways to exploit the graph further: asynchronous updates for sparse dependencies, adaptive learning of the graph itself, and a joint estimator that shares information across correlated objectives to tighten regret bounds.

These components address different costs of coordinating a system: unnecessary switching, synchronization, uncertainty about dependencies, and inefficient use of shared observations. In experiments on heterogeneous systems, exploiting this structure reduces movement costs by more than a factor of three while maintaining similar cumulative losses. The finding suggests that the dependency structure can help make continuous adaptation more stable without a comparable increase in the measured objective losses.
summary.tldr: Lazy Graph-LinUCB uses dependencies among objectives to optimize continuous controls while reducing costly changes.

title: Beyond Binary: Continuous State Optimization with Graph-Structured Objectives

abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a flexible family of amortized samplers trained to generate discrete and compositional objects with probability proportional to a reward function. To this end, they learn a policy function over an intractably large state graph by minimizing a stochastic objective over sampled trajectories. However, learning efficiency is constrained by the model’s ability to rapidly explore diverse high-probability regions during training. To mitigate this issue, recent works have focused on incentivizing the exploration of unvisited and valuable states via curiosity-driven search and self-supervised random network distillation, which tend to waste samples on already well-approximated regions of the state space. In this context, we propose Adaptive Complementary Exploration (ACE), a principled algorithm for the effective exploration of novel and high-probability regions when learning GFlowNets. To achieve this, ACE introduces an exploration GFlowNet explicitly trained to search for high-reward states in regions underexplored by the canonical GFlowNet, which learns to sample from the target distribution. Through extensive experiments, we show that ACE consistently and significantly improves upon prior work in terms of approximation accuracy to the target distribution and discovery rate of diverse high-reward states.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks learn to construct discrete objects so that higher-reward objects appear more often, in proportion to their rewards. Training requires exploring a potentially enormous graph of intermediate construction states. Learning can be slow if sampled trajectories repeatedly visit regions the model already represents well, even when other valuable regions remain insufficiently explored.

The paper proposes Adaptive Complementary Exploration, or ACE, which gives exploration its own GFlowNet. The canonical GFlowNet learns the desired reward-proportional distribution. A separate exploration GFlowNet searches for high-reward states in areas the canonical model has underexplored. This makes the exploration objective depend on what the main model still needs to discover, while retaining reward as a guide to worthwhile discoveries.

Across the reported experiments, ACE consistently and significantly improves approximation of the target distribution and the discovery rate of diverse high-reward states relative to prior work. These results connect two goals that can otherwise compete for training samples: accurately representing the desired distribution and finding valuable states beyond familiar regions. The approach makes exploration complementary to the main sampler’s current knowledge.
summary.tldr: ACE trains a separate exploration GFlowNet to find rewarding states that the main sampler has not adequately explored.

title: Avoid What You Know: Divergent Trajectory Balance for GFlowNets

abstract: Score-based diffusion models are a highly effective method for generating samples from a distribution of images. We consider scenarios where the training data comes from a noisy version of the target distribution, and present an efficiently implementable modification of the inference procedure to generate noiseless samples. Our approach is motivated by the manifold hypothesis, according to which meaningful data is concentrated around some low-dimensional manifold of a high-dimensional ambient space. The central idea is that noise manifests as low magnitude variation in off-manifold directions in contrast to the relevant variation of the desired distribution which is mostly confined to on-manifold directions. We introduce the notion of an extended score and show that, in a simplified setting, it can be used to reduce small variations to zero, while leaving large variations mostly unchanged. We describe how its approximation can be computed efficiently from an approximation to the standard score and demonstrate its efficacy on toy problems, synthetic data, and real data.

paragraphs: A diffusion model trained on noisy data learns from a distribution that differs from the clean distribution of interest. MAD modifies the sampling procedure to target noiseless samples in this setting. Its motivation comes from the manifold hypothesis: meaningful high-dimensional data is concentrated near a structure with fewer intrinsic dimensions.

The approach distinguishes small variations away from that structure from larger variations associated with meaningful data. It introduces an extended score designed to suppress the former while retaining the latter. In a simplified setting, the authors show that this score can reduce small variations to zero while leaving large variations mostly unchanged, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed behavior.

The extended score can be approximated efficiently from an approximation to the standard score, making the change implementable within inference. Demonstrations on toy problems, synthetic data, and real data show its effectiveness. The stated mechanism depends on the geometric distinction between noise and relevant variation, and the precise theoretical suppression result is established in the simplified setting.
summary.tldr: MAD modifies diffusion sampling to suppress small off-manifold variations and generate cleaner samples from models trained on noisy data.

title: MAD: Manifold Attracted Diffusion

abstract: Relational reasoning is the ability to infer relations that jointly bind multiple entities, attributes, or variables. While this capability is essential for scientific reasoning, most existing evaluations of relational reasoning in large language models focus on structured inputs such as tables, graphs, or synthetic relational tasks, and do not isolate the sources of difficulty that arise from higher-arity relational binding. We study this problem through the lens of Relational Complexity (RC), defined as the minimum number of independent entities or operands that must be simultaneously bound to apply a relation. RC provides a principled way to vary reasoning difficulty independently of confounders such as input size, vocabulary, and representational choices. Building on RC, we introduce REL, a generative benchmark framework spanning algebra, chemistry, and biology that varies RC within each domain. Evaluating frontier LLMs, we observe a consistent and monotonic degradation in performance as RC increases, even when the total number of entities is held fixed. This failure mode persists under increased test-time compute and with in-context learning, suggesting a limitation tied to the arity of the required relational binding rather than insufficient inference steps or exposure to examples. Our results identify a well-defined regime of higher-arity reasoning in which current models struggle and motivate revisiting reasoning benchmarks through the lens of relational complexity.

paragraphs: Reasoning can become harder because a relation requires several entities to be considered together, even when the input contains no additional entities overall. This paper isolates that difficulty using relational complexity: the minimum number of independent entities or operands that must be bound simultaneously to apply a relation. The goal is to distinguish this demand from input length, vocabulary, or presentation.
