summary.tldr: REL finds that language-model performance declines as more entities must be related simultaneously, even with fixed entity counts and added inference support.

title: Evaluating Relational Reasoning in LLMs with REL

abstract: Continual learning (CL) involves continual parameter updates, posing a significant challenge to backdoor persistence. In this paper, we reveal that the most advanced existing attack relies on an implicit assumption that task-critical neurons remain stable across task learning; however, this assumption does not hold in class-incremental learning (CIL). This exposes a critical research gap: backdoor persistence in CIL remains an open question. Inspired by functional stability, we discover that CIL models preserve task knowledge in shallow, structurally invariant subspaces. Motivated by these findings, we propose PBTO, the first persistent and targeted backdoor attack in CIL. PBTO trains a surrogate model on proxy tasks to obtain a parameter trajectory. It then optimizes a universal trigger that ensures misclassification to the target label across all model states and anchors trigger embeddings in shallow layers. Experimental results verify that PBTO maintains a high final attack success rate (ASR) across all benchmarks, while representative baselines degrade substantially after sequential learning. Code is available at https://github.com/hjhkkkc/PBTO.

paragraphs: A backdoor planted in a continually learning model may disappear as subsequent training changes its parameters. This paper examines that problem in class-incremental learning, where the model learns additional classes over time. It finds that an assumption behind an advanced existing attack—that task-critical neurons remain stable—does not hold in this setting.

The authors instead identify shallow, structurally invariant subspaces that preserve task knowledge. summary.tldr: PBTO anchors backdoor behavior in stable shallow representations, maintaining high attack success after class-incremental learning in the reported experiments.

title: Persistent Backdoor Attacks in Class-Incremental Learning via Structural Invariant Anchoring

abstract: In-context localization (ICL) seeks to localize a target object specified by a small set of support examples in a query image, operating on the fly without training or parameter updates. Despite rapid advances in vision–language models (VLMs), achieving category-agnostic and visually grounded ICL remains an open problem, even though it is essential for applications such as image editing, personalized visual search, and retrieval. Existing methods are fragile and rely on explicit category supervision, which not only limits applicability in realistic settings with unnamed or instance-specific objects but also introduces category bias that steers predictions toward semantic priors rather than visual evidence. We introduce a two-stage training framework that explicitly optimizes in-context attention between support bounding boxes and query images without category supervision. We further refine localization via reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to directly minimize localization error. This formulation enforces visual correspondence over semantic priors, yielding robust instance-level localization. Empirically, a 7B-parameter model trained with our objectives outperforms models up to 72B parameters, demonstrating that context-aware localization objectives can surpass scaling alone. Comprehensive ablations validate the contribution of each component.

paragraphs: In-context object localization asks a model to find an object in a query image using a few visual examples. The target may be unnamed or specific to a particular instance, making category labels an awkward guide. FOCUS trains models to rely more directly on correspondence between the supplied examples and the query.

Its two-stage framework optimizes attention between support bounding boxes and query images without category supervision. A reinforcement-learning refinement stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to directly reduce localization error. These objectives address the tendency for semantic category expectations to displace the visual evidence that actually specifies the requested object.

The training produces a model intended to perform localization on the fly without parameter updates for each new target. In the reported experiments, a 7-billion-parameter model trained with these objectives outperforms models as large as 72 billion parameters. Ablations support the contribution of each component. The result shows that, in the evaluated setting, training specifically for visual context use can provide greater localization gains than model scaling alone.
summary.tldr: FOCUS trains visual correspondence and directly optimizes localization error, enabling a 7B model to outperform evaluated models up to 72B.

title: FOCUS: Forcing In-Context Object Localization through Visual Support Constraints and Policy Optimization

abstract: Deep stochastic processes have recently become a central paradigm for image enhancement, with many methods explicitly conditioning the stochastic trajectory on the degraded input. However, the relationship between these conditional processes and standard diffusion models remains unclear. In this work, we introduce a unified perspective on stochastic image enhancement by classifying recent methods into three families of continuous-time processes: unconditional diffusion models, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes, and diffusion bridges. We show that all of these approaches arise from a common stochastic differential equation (SDE) formulation. This framework makes explicit that seemingly disparate methods differ primarily in their drift and diffusion terms, terminal distributions, and boundary conditions, while schedulers and samplers constitute orthogonal design choices. Leveraging this unification, we conduct a controlled empirical study across multiple image enhancement tasks using identical architectures and training protocols. Our results reveal no consistently dominant method; instead, we identify and disentangle the specific design choices that most strongly influence performance. Finally, we release ItoVision, a modular PyTorch library that implements the unified framework and enables rapid prototyping and fair comparison of stochastic image enhancement methods.

title: Unifying Deep Stochastic Processes for Image Enhancement

abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) have shown strong capabilities in audio-visual understanding by jointly reasoning over visual, auditory, and linguistic inputs. However, processing long-form audio-visual content often requires a large number of tokens, leading to substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing efficiency-oriented methods typically apply uniform compression or pruning strategies, which overlook modality-specific characteristics and instruction-dependent reasoning behaviors in multimodal models. In this work, we present PRIM, an inference framework for efficient multimodal reasoning that systematically compresses audio-visual representations based on attention dynamics and instruction relevance. Motivated by an attention-based analysis revealing modality imbalance and layer-wise redundancy in LMMs, PRIM introduces a cooperative compression pipeline that spans both multimodal encoders and the language model. Specifically, PRIM performs early text-conditioned audio-visual fusion to externalize cross-modal interactions, applies attention-guided and frequency-aware strategies to remove redundant audio and video tokens, and further adapts token retention inside the language model according to task demands. Extensive experiments on multiple audio-visual benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRIM consistently achieves stable and superior efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across diverse tasks and datasets. These results demonstrate that PRIM, a multimodal cooperative compression approach, provides an effective pathway toward scalable and efficient audio-visual reasoning.

paragraphs: Long audio-visual inputs produce many tokens, making multimodal inference expensive in computation and memory. Uniform compression can overlook differences between audio and video, as well as differences in what a particular instruction requires. PRIM uses those distinctions to decide how representations should be compressed throughout the model.

The framework follows an attention-based analysis that finds imbalance between modalities and redundancy across layers. It first performs text-conditioned audio-visual fusion, bringing interactions between modalities into an early stage. Attention-guided and frequency-aware mechanisms then remove redundant audio and video tokens. Within the language model, token retention adapts further according to the task’s demands.

Experiments across multiple audio-visual datasets report consistently stable and superior efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. The contribution is a coordinated compression process spanning both the multimodal encoders and the language model. This matters because the usefulness of an input token depends on its modality, its relationship to other inputs, and the instruction being answered. PRIM makes those factors part of the compression process instead of applying one retention rule everywhere.
summary.tldr: PRIM compresses audio-visual tokens across encoders and language-model layers according to attention, modality characteristics, and task relevance.

title: PRIM: Cooperative Dynamic Token Compression for Efficient Large Multimodal Models

abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have achieved remarkable success in generalizing across diverse domains. However, they mainly focus on Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs), leaving Multimodal-Attributed Graphs (MAGs) largely untapped. Although recent Multimodal Graph Foundation Models (MGFMs) attempt to bridge this gap by integrating diverse modality information, our empirical investigation reveals two fundamental limitations: (1)they fail to explicitly model modality interaction, essential for capturing intricate cross-modal semantics beyond simple aggregation, and (2)they exhibit sub-optimal modality alignment, which is critical for bridging the significant semantic disparity between distinct modal spaces. To address these challenges, we propose PLANET (graPh topoLogy-aware modAlity iNteraction and alignmEnT), a novel framework employing a Divide-and-Conquer strategy to decouple modality interaction and alignment across distinct granularities. At the embedding granularity, (1)Embedding-wise Domain Gating (EDG) performs local semantic enrichment by adaptively infusing topology-aware cross-modal context, achieving modality interaction. At the node granularity, (2)Node-wise Discretization Retrieval (NDR) ensures global modality alignment by constructing a Discretized Semantic Representation Space (DSRS) to bridge modality gaps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PLANET significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse graph-centric and multimodal generative tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sapnapnet/PLANET.

paragraphs: Graphs can carry multiple kinds of information, but combining those modalities requires more than aggregating their representations. This paper identifies two weaknesses in existing multimodal graph foundation models: insufficient modeling of interactions between modalities and imperfect alignment between their semantic spaces. PLANET addresses these as separate problems at different representation levels.

At the embedding level, Embedding-wise Domain Gating adaptively introduces context from other modalities while accounting for graph topology. This enriches local meaning through cross-modal interaction. At the node level, Node-wise Discretization Retrieval constructs a shared discretized semantic representation space to bridge modality gaps. The division gives interaction and alignment distinct mechanisms rather than asking one operation to accomplish both.

Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across graph-centered tasks and multimodal generation tasks. These findings support the framework’s strategy of separating local semantic enrichment from global alignment. The contribution is a way to combine graph structure and heterogeneous information while explicitly addressing both how modalities inform one another and how their meanings become comparable.
summary.tldr: PLANET separates cross-modal interaction from semantic alignment to improve multimodal graph understanding and generation.

title: Toward Effective Multimodal Graph Foundation Model: A Divide-and-Conquer Based Approach

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce hallucinated outputs, which limit their reliability in high-stakes applications. Conformal prediction can provide guarantees on the correctness and factuality of LLM outputs, but existing approaches rely on the exchangeability assumption, which rarely holds in online settings where user queries and interests change over time. To solve this problem, in this paper, we propose PACE (Proactive Adaptive Conformal InferencE), a novel framework that sequentially updates the time-varying target miscoverage parameter with a dynamic step size to maintain valid coverage under online distribution shifts. PACE is motivated by the theoretical connections between expected miscoverage error and key factors such as distribution shifts and instantaneous parameter error. It integrates two complementary signals: (1) a proactive shift detection to estimate the magnitude of distribution shifts, and (2) a reactive error that scales updates according to the local coverage gap. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that PACE consistently outperforms advanced adaptive baselines. It reduces the deviation from the target error rate by up to 60% in QA tasks and accelerates coverage recovery by over 2.5x during abrupt shifts, ensuring stable factuality guarantees without compromising utility and stability.

paragraphs: PACE addresses factuality control when the questions reaching a language model change over time. Existing conformal approaches rely on exchangeability, an assumption that often breaks in online use as users’ interests shift. The resulting challenge is to keep the observed error behavior close to a target while the incoming data changes.

The framework repeatedly updates a time-varying target miscoverage parameter using an adaptive step size. It combines a proactive signal estimating distribution shifts with a reactive signal measuring the local coverage gap. The first responds to evidence that the data has changed; the second responds to errors already observed. The design is motivated by theoretical relationships between expected miscoverage, distribution shifts, and parameter error.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improvements over advanced adaptive alternatives. In question answering, deviation from the target error rate falls by up to 60%, and coverage recovery after abrupt shifts accelerates by more than 2.5 times. These are findings about maintaining aggregate coverage behavior under change, rather than a claim that every individual answer becomes factual.
summary.tldr: PACE combines shift detection with observed coverage errors to adapt factuality control as online language-model queries change.

title: Beyond Reactivity: Proactive Adaptive Conformal Inference for Online LLM Factuality

abstract: Assisting non-expert users to develop complex interactive websites has become a popular task for LLM-powered code agents. However, existing code agents tend to only generate frontend web pages, masking the lack of real full-stack data processing and storage with fancy visual effects. Notably, constructing production-level full-stack web applications is far more challenging than only generating frontend web pages, demanding careful control of data flow, comprehensive understanding of constantly updating packages and dependencies, and accurate localization of obscure bugs in the codebase. To address these difficulties, we introduce FullStack-Agent, a unified agent system for full-stack agentic coding that consists of three parts: (1) FullStack-Dev, a multi-agent framework with strong planning, code editing, codebase navigation, and bug localization abilities. (2) FullStack-Learn, an innovative data-scaling and self-improving method that back-translates crawled and synthesized website repositories to improve the backbone LLM of FullStack-Dev. (3) FullStack-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark that systematically tests the frontend, backend and database functionalities of the generated website. Our FullStack-Dev outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method by 8.7%, 38.2%, and 15.9% on the frontend, backend, and database test cases respectively. Additionally, FullStack-Learn raises the performance of a 30B model by 9.7%, 9.5%, and 2.8% on the three sets of test cases through self-improvement, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: A convincing website interface can conceal missing backend behavior or data storage. This paper targets the broader challenge of generating functioning full-stack applications, where an agent must manage data flow, understand dependencies, and locate bugs across a repository. It combines an agent framework, a learning method, and a benchmark.

FullStack-Dev coordinates multiple agents for planning, editing, code navigation, and bug localization. FullStack-Learn improves the underlying language model by back-translating crawled and synthesized website repositories into learning material. FullStack-Bench evaluates frontend, backend, and database functionality separately, making success across the application’s layers visible rather than judging the interface alone.

FullStack-Dev improves over the previous state of the art by 8.7%, 38.2%, and 15.9% on those three groups of tests, respectively. Self-improvement through FullStack-Learn raises a 30B model’s performance by 9.7%, 9.5%, and 2.8%. Together, these results support both the development framework and repository-derived learning as ways to improve functional web application generation.
summary.tldr: FullStack-Agent combines coordinated coding agents, repository-derived learning, and functional testing to improve generated frontend, backend, and database behavior.

title: FullStack-Agent: Enhancing Agentic Full-Stack Web Coding via Development-Oriented Testing and Repository Back-Translation

abstract: Token-level adaptive computation seeks to reduce inference cost by allocating more computation to harder tokens and less to easier ones. However, prior work is primarily evaluated on natural-language benchmarks using task-level metrics, where token-level difficulty is unobservable and confounded with architectural factors, making it unclear whether compute allocation truly aligns with underlying complexity. We address this gap through three contributions. First, we introduce a complexity-controlled evaluation paradigm using existing algorithmic and synthetic language tasks with parameterized difficulty, enabling direct testing of token-level compute allocation. Second, we propose ANIRA, a unified recurrent Transformer framework that supports per-token variable-depth computation while isolating compute allocation decisions from other model factors. Third, we use this framework to conduct a systematic analysis of token-level adaptive computation across alignment with complexity, generalization, and decision timing. Our results show that compute allocation aligned with task complexity can emerge without explicit difficulty supervision, but such alignment does not imply algorithmic generalization: models fail to extrapolate to unseen input sizes despite allocating additional computation. We further find that early compute decisions rely on static structural cues, whereas online halting more closely tracks algorithmic execution state. Code: https://github.com/merlresearch/ANIRA

paragraphs: Adaptive computation aims to spend more inference effort on difficult tokens and less on easy ones. But natural-language task scores do not directly reveal each token’s difficulty, making it hard to tell whether extra computation follows genuine complexity. Architectural differences can further obscure what the allocation mechanism itself contributes.

The paper introduces a controlled evaluation using algorithmic and synthetic language tasks with adjustable difficulty. It also presents ANIRA, a recurrent Transformer framework that supports variable computation depth for each token while separating allocation decisions from other model factors. This setup lets the authors examine complexity alignment, generalization, and the timing of decisions within a common framework.

The experiments show that computation can align with task complexity without explicit difficulty supervision. However, that alignment does not establish algorithmic generalization: models still fail on unseen input sizes despite spending additional computation. The authors also find that early allocation decisions rely on static structural cues, while online stopping decisions track algorithmic execution state more closely. These results distinguish learning where to spend effort from learning procedures that extrapolate.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments show that recurrent Transformers can allocate compute according to difficulty without learning to generalize to larger unseen problems.

title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers

abstract: Consider a market of competing model providers selling query access to models with varying costs and capabilities. Customers submit problem instances and are willing to pay up to a budget for a verifiable solution. An arbitrageur efficiently allocates inference budget across providers to undercut the market, thus creating a competitive offering with no model-development risk. In this work, we initiate the study of arbitrage in AI model markets, empirically demonstrating the viability of arbitrage and illustrating its economic consequences. We conduct an in-depth case study of SWE-bench GitHub issue resolution using two representative models, GPT-5 mini and DeepSeek v3.2. In this verifiable domain, simple arbitrage strategies generate net profit margins of up to 40%. Robust arbitrage strategies that generalize across different domains remain profitable. Distillation further creates strong arbitrage opportunities, potentially at the expense of the teacher model’s revenue. Multiple competing arbitrageurs drive down consumer prices, reducing the marginal revenue of model providers. At the same time, arbitrage reduces market segmentation and facilitates market entry for smaller model providers by enabling earlier revenue capture. Our results suggest that arbitrage can be a powerful force in AI model markets with implications for model development, distillation, and deployment.

paragraphs: The paper considers a market where customers pay for verifiable solutions and competing model providers charge different amounts for different capabilities. An intermediary can allocate inference spending across providers and sell solutions below prevailing prices. This creates a possible business opportunity without requiring the intermediary to develop its own underlying model.

The authors investigate this computational arbitrage through a detailed SWE-bench issue-resolution study using GPT-5 mini and DeepSeek v3.2. In that verifiable setting, simple strategies achieve net profit margins of up to 40%. They also report profitable strategies that generalize across domains and identify distillation as another source of arbitrage, potentially reducing the teacher model's revenue.

The economic effects extend beyond intermediary profits. Multiple arbitrageurs push consumer prices down and reduce providers' marginal revenue. At the same time, arbitrage reduces market segmentation and can help smaller providers earn revenue earlier. The findings suggest that how inference is purchased and combined can influence competition and deployment, alongside the capabilities of individual models.
summary.tldr: Allocating inference across competing providers can generate arbitrage profits while lowering customer prices and changing model-market competition.

title: Computational Arbitrage in AI Model Markets

abstract: Offline cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces unique challenges due to the distribution shift between online and offline data collection. While online MARL typically converges to a single coordinated joint policy, offline datasets are often mixtures of diverse cooperative behaviors, resulting in highly multimodal joint behavior distributions. In such settings, independent policy regularization often misaligns joint policy constraints and leads to severe distribution shift. To address this, we propose OMSD, which sequentially decomposes the joint behavior policy into individual conditional distributions and leverages diffusion-based generative models to provide modality-coordinated regularization for each agent. Combined with centralized critic guidance, OMSD achieves coordinated exploration within high-value, in-distribution regions, and avoids out-of-distribution joint actions. Experiments across multiple datasets on various continuous control tasks demonstrate that OMSD consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, especially in challenging multimodal scenarios. Our results highlight the necessity of modality-aware coordination for robust offline MARL.

paragraphs: Offline cooperative learning can draw on datasets containing several distinct ways for agents to coordinate. This creates a joint behavior distribution with multiple modes. Keeping each agent individually close to the data may still produce an unfamiliar combination of actions, because individually plausible choices need not belong to the same coordinated behavior.

OMSD addresses this by sequentially decomposing the joint behavior policy into conditional distributions for individual agents. Diffusion-based generative models then provide regularization that coordinates agents around compatible behavior modes. A centralized critic guides the policy toward valuable regions while this conditional structure keeps joint actions aligned with the dataset.

The approach aims to explore high-value, in-distribution combinations and avoid joint actions outside the observed behavior distribution. Experiments across multiple datasets and continuous-control tasks report consistent state-of-the-art performance, with particular strength in difficult multimodal settings. The findings highlight why offline coordination must account for relationships among agents’ choices: matching each agent’s behavior separately can miss the structure that made the original joint behavior cooperative.
summary.tldr: OMSD uses conditional diffusion-based regularization to keep offline agents’ actions coordinated within valuable behavior modes represented in the data.

title: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Sequential Score Decomposition

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generative modeling, yet their application to time series forecasting remains suboptimal. Existing approaches apply uniform Gaussian noise across all time steps, assuming all frequency components should be corrupted at the same rate. However, energy distribution across frequencies in time series is highly non-uniform: when uniform noise is added, high-frequency components are disproportionately overwhelmed while low-frequency trends remain inadequately diffused. We propose EADiff, an energy-adaptive diffusion framework operating in the wavelet domain to address this frequency-energy imbalance. Our key insight is that high-energy components require stronger perturbation while low-energy details need gentler corruption to preserve informative structures. We introduce a learnable modulation mechanism that automatically adjusts noise levels for each frequency band on a per-instance basis. Built upon this adaptive scheduler, we design a conditional diffusion framework where low-frequency trends serve as generation conditions, and noise-level-aware loss weighting naturally emphasizes different frequency components according to their signal characteristics. This cohesive design enables the model to respect the intrinsic multi-scale structure throughout both forward and reverse processes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EADiff consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based and state-of-the-art deterministic methods.

paragraphs: Diffusion forecasting learns to generate future signals through a process of adding and removing noise. The paper argues that applying uniform Gaussian noise ignores how unevenly energy is distributed across time-series frequencies. The same corruption can overwhelm higher-frequency details while leaving stronger low-frequency trends insufficiently diffused.

EADiff moves the process into the wavelet domain, where components at different scales can receive different noise levels. Its guiding principle is to perturb high-energy components more strongly and low-energy details more gently. A learnable mechanism adjusts this balance separately for each frequency band and each input instance, making the schedule responsive to the signal being forecast.

The framework uses low-frequency trends as conditions for generation and weights the training loss according to noise levels and signal characteristics. These elements coordinate how multiscale information is treated during both corruption and reconstruction. Experiments report consistent improvements over existing diffusion-based forecasting approaches and state-of-the-art deterministic methods. The results support matching the noise process to the signal’s energy structure as a useful design choice for forecasting.
summary.tldr: EADiff improves time-series forecasting by adapting diffusion noise to the energy of each frequency band for each input.

title: Not All Frequencies Are Equal: Energy-Adaptive Diffusion for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that neural networks trained on different modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of the world. Recent work exploits this convergence by aligning frozen pretrained vision and language models with lightweight alignment layers, but typically relies on contrastive losses and millions of paired samples. In this work, we ask whether meaningful alignment can be achieved with substantially less supervision. We introduce a semi-supervised setting in which pretrained unimodal encoders are aligned using a small number of image-text pairs together with large amounts of unpaired data. To address this challenge, we propose SOTAlign, a two-stage framework that first recovers a coarse shared geometry from limited paired data using a linear teacher, and then refines the alignment on unpaired samples via an optimal-transport-based divergence that transfers relational structure without overconstraining the target space. Unlike existing semi-supervised methods, SOTAlign effectively leverages unpaired images and text, learning robust joint embeddings across datasets and encoder pairs, and significantly outperforming supervised and semi-supervised baselines.

paragraphs: SOTAlign studies how to connect pretrained vision and language models when only a small number of matched image-text examples is available. Its motivation is the hypothesis that separately trained models can develop related representations of the world. The paper asks whether this relationship can support alignment using abundant unpaired data and limited direct supervision.

The method has two stages. A linear teacher first uses the paired examples to recover a coarse shared geometry. An optimal-transport-based divergence then refines the alignment with unpaired images and text. This second stage transfers relationships among representations while avoiding excessive constraints on the target space.

The authors report robust joint embeddings across different datasets and encoder combinations, with significant improvements over supervised and semi-supervised baselines. These findings support the usefulness of unpaired data for alignment in the proposed setting. The approach makes limited image-text matches serve as an initial guide, then uses the structure of larger unpaired collections to improve the connection between the two modalities.
summary.tldr: SOTAlign combines a small paired dataset with optimal transport on unpaired data to align pretrained vision and language representations.

title: SOTAlign: Semi-Supervised Alignment of Unimodal Vision and Language Models via Optimal Transport

abstract: Most existing cultural evaluation frameworks for large language models (LLMs) focus on matching model outputs to ground-truth answers, primarily measuring factual cultural awareness. This overlooks whether models internalize broader cultural structure and pluralism. We introduce a spectral-analysis-based framework that captures large-scale macrostructural patterns in models’ cultural knowledge and evaluate eight LLMs across nine cultural domains spanning all five of Newmark’s cultural dimensions and 170 countries. Comparing with human data, we find that instruction-tuned models align more closely with human cultural structure than older models, while increased model size does not consistently improve performance. Finally, simulation-based experiments show that our proposed spectral metric better predicts a model’s ability to serve users from unfamiliar cultural backgrounds than existing ones.

paragraphs: Answering factual questions about a culture does not fully reveal whether a language model represents broader cultural differences and relationships. This paper proposes evaluating that larger organization of knowledge. Its focus is meta-cultural competency: whether a model captures cultural structure and pluralism beyond agreement with individual reference answers.

The authors introduce a framework based on spectral analysis to capture large-scale patterns in cultural knowledge. They evaluate eight language models across nine cultural domains, covering all five of Newmark’s cultural dimensions and 170 countries. Comparing the resulting structures with human data provides a way to assess organization across cultures rather than only counting correct responses.

Instruction-tuned models align more closely with human cultural structure than older models in the study, while larger model size does not consistently improve performance. In simulation-based experiments, the proposed metric predicts ability to serve users from unfamiliar cultural backgrounds better than existing metrics. The findings suggest that structural evaluation captures useful information missed by factual cultural tests, with the reported service-related evidence coming from simulations.
summary.tldr: A spectral metric evaluates cultural knowledge structure and better predicts simulated performance with unfamiliar cultural backgrounds than existing metrics.

title: Measuring Meta-Cultural Competency: A Spectral Framework for LLM Knowledge Structures

abstract: We introduce a testing-by-betting framework that leverages predictions on unlabeled data to enhance the power of sequential hypothesis testing. Given limited samples from the joint distribution of $(X,Y)$, and additional unlabeled samples from the marginal of $X$, we ask how unlabeled data can be used to hypothesize about the distribution of $Y$, and the conditional distribution of $Y\mid X$. We introduce an e-statistic and use it to construct a sequential test. Under standard distributional assumptions—label shift or concept shift—we establish that the test is anytime valid. Furthermore, we show that for binary data, the e-statistic has non-trivial power. Crucially, our approach retains these properties even when the underlying predictions are inaccurate. Through simulations and applications to large language models evaluation, we demonstrate power gains over baseline approaches, including prediction-powered inference. These gains persist even with relatively limited unlabeled data and when predictions have low accuracy due to weak correlation between $X$ and $Y$.

We introduce an e-statistic and use it to construct a sequential test. Under standard distributional assumptions—label shift or concept shift—we establish that the test is anytime valid. Through simulations and applications to large language models evaluation, we demonstrate power gains over baseline approaches, including prediction-powered inference. paragraphs: Statistical testing often has access to few labeled examples but many additional inputs without labels. This paper asks how predictions on those unlabeled inputs can improve tests about outcomes and their relationship to inputs. It develops a testing-by-betting framework that accumulates evidence sequentially using an e-statistic.

Under label-shift or concept-shift assumptions, the resulting test is anytime valid: its validity is preserved when the stopping time depends on the evidence observed so far. The authors also establish non-trivial power for binary data. These properties remain available even when the predictions are inaccurate, so predictive accuracy alone does not determine whether unlabeled examples can contribute useful statistical evidence.

Simulations and applications to language-model evaluation show power gains over comparison methods, including prediction-powered inference. The gains persist with relatively few unlabeled examples and with low prediction accuracy caused by weak relationships between inputs and outcomes. The contribution combines conditional statistical guarantees with empirical evidence that predictions can help testing even when they would be unimpressive as standalone outcome predictors.
summary.tldr: A betting-based sequential test uses unlabeled-data predictions to improve power while retaining validity under stated shift assumptions.

title: Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Testing by Betting on Predictions

abstract: Why does contrastive learning with simple images and augmentations yield useful representations for downstream tasks? We address this question by analytically computing the optimal representation in terms of a contrastive loss for a range of basic augmentations and any image dataset with stationary statistics. We show that for certain augmentations the optimum can be attained by a CNN whose first layer filters are sinusoids, followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, global average pooling, and a final linear layer that performs partial whitening. We also show that the optimal weights in such CNNs for more complicated augmentations are still sinusoids. The frequencies of the sinusoids and their weights can be computed using a simple “waterfilling” algorithm given the dataset’s expected power spectrum. Experiments with different image datasets and augmentations show that such CNNs trained with SGD empirically learn sinusoids in their first layer and to perform partial whitening.

These observations support the proposed account of how image statistics and augmentation choices shape contrastive representations.

title: A Theory of Contrastive Learning with Natural Images

abstract: Reward models are central to large language model (LLM) post-training. However, past work has shown that they can reward spurious or undesirable attributes such as length, format, hallucinations, and sycophancy. In this work, we introduce and study the research problem of automatically finding reward model biases in natural language. We offer a simple approach of using an LLM to iteratively propose and refine candidate biases. Our method can recover known biases and surface novel ones: for example, we found that Skywork-V2-8B, a leading open-weight reward model, often mistakenly favors responses with redundant spacing and responses with hallucinated content. In addition, we show evidence that evolutionary iteration outperforms flat best-of-N search, and we validate the recall of our pipeline using synthetically injected biases. We hope our work contributes to further research on improving RMs through automated interpretability methods.

paragraphs: Reward models help guide language-model post-training by scoring candidate responses. Those scores can favor properties that do not make an answer better, such as unnecessary length, flattering agreement, or fabricated content. This paper asks whether an automated process can discover such unwanted preferences and describe them in natural language.

The proposed approach uses a language model to suggest possible biases and iteratively refine its candidates. This makes bias discovery a search process in which earlier candidates inform later ones. The authors report that the method recovers previously known biases and identifies new ones. In particular, Skywork-V2-8B often incorrectly preferred responses containing redundant spacing or hallucinated information.

The study provides evidence that evolutionary refinement works better than generating a fixed batch of candidates and selecting the best. It also tests discovery recall using deliberately injected synthetic biases, where the target behavior is known. These results suggest automated search can help inspect reward models for undesirable scoring patterns and provide concrete targets for further improvement.
summary.tldr: An iterative language-model search discovers unwanted reward-model preferences, including biases toward redundant spacing and hallucinated content.

title: Automatically Finding Reward Model Biases

abstract: In this paper, we study the private and robust alignment of language models from a theoretical perspective by establishing upper bounds on the suboptimality gap in both offline and online settings. We consider preference labels subject to privacy constraints and/or adversarial corruption, and analyze two distinct interplays between them: privacy-first and corruption-first. For the privacy-only setting, we show that log loss with an MLE-style algorithm achieves near-optimal rates, in contrast to conventional wisdom. For the joint privacy-and-corruption setting, we first demonstrate that existing offline algorithms in fact provide stronger guarantees—simultaneously in terms of corruption level and privacy parameters—than previously known, which further yields improved bounds in the corruption-only regime. In addition, we also present the first set of results for private and robust online alignment. Our results are enabled by new uniform convergence guarantees for log loss and square loss under privacy and corruption, which we believe have broad applicability across learning theory and statistics.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment can rely on preference labels that are affected by privacy requirements, adversarial corruption, or both. This paper asks how close alignment algorithms can get to their objective under those conditions. It develops theoretical upper bounds on the remaining suboptimality in both offline and online learning settings.

The analysis separates privacy-first and corruption-first arrangements, accounting for different ways the two effects interact. With privacy alone, a maximum-likelihood-style algorithm using log loss achieves near-optimal rates. With privacy and corruption together, the authors establish stronger guarantees for existing offline algorithms than were previously known, improving dependence on both privacy parameters and corruption levels.

The strengthened analysis also improves bounds when corruption is the only concern. In addition, the paper presents what the authors identify as the first results for jointly private and robust online alignment. New uniform convergence guarantees for log loss and square loss underpin these findings. The contribution is a sharper account of algorithmic reliability under the analyzed conditions, including improved guarantees for methods that already existed.
summary.tldr: New theoretical bounds strengthen guarantees for language-model alignment when preference labels face privacy constraints and adversarial corruption.

title: Improved Bounds for Private and Robust Alignment

abstract: Reward models are central to Large Language Model (LLM) alignment within the framework of RLHF. The standard objective used in reward modeling is the Bradley-Terry (BT) loss, which learns from pairwise data consisting of chosen and rejected responses. In this work, we analyze the per-sample gradient of BT-loss and show spurious learning signals due to representation distance. In particular, BT gradient norm scales with two distinct components: (1) prediction error, reflected by the difference in predicted rewards between chosen and rejected responses, and critically, (2) representation distance between the pair measured in the output space of the final layer. While the first term captures the intended training signal, the second term can significantly impact the update magnitude and misalign learning. Specifically, pairs with small representation distance often receive vanishingly weak updates, even when misranked, while pairs with large distance receive disproportionately strong updates. This leads to gradients from large-distance pairs overshadowing those from small-distance pairs, where fine-grained distinctions are especially important. To overcome this limitation, we propose NormBT, an adaptive pair-wise normalization scheme that rescales update to balance representation-driven effects and focuses learning signals on prediction error. NormBT is a lightweight, drop-in modification to BT loss with negligible overhead. Across various LLM backbones and datasets, NormBT improves reward model performance consistently, with notable gains of over 5% on the Reasoning category of RewardBench, which contains numerous fine-grained pairs.

paragraphs: Reward models learn to prefer chosen responses over rejected ones, commonly using the Bradley–Terry loss. This paper shows that the size of a pair’s learning update depends on more than prediction error. It also depends on the distance between the pair’s representations in the final layer’s output space.

That extra dependence can distort training. A misranked pair with nearby representations may receive a very weak update, while a distant pair receives a disproportionately strong one. Large-distance pairs can consequently dominate learning, even though distinguishing nearby responses is especially important for fine-grained judgments.

NormBT introduces adaptive normalization for each response pair to balance these distance-driven effects and focus learning more directly on prediction error. It is a lightweight modification to the existing loss with negligible overhead. Across several language-model backbones and datasets, the authors report consistent reward-model improvements, including gains exceeding 5% on RewardBench’s Reasoning category. That category contains many fine-grained pairs, aligning the observed benefit with the mechanism the paper identifies.
summary.tldr: NormBT normalizes preference-learning updates to reduce representation-distance bias and improve reward models’ handling of fine-grained response differences.

title: When Distance Distracts: Representation Distance Bias in BT-Loss for Reward Models

abstract: Formal verification provides strong guarantees of software correctness, but its adoption is limited by the high cost of writing precise formal specifications. While recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in theorem proving and verified code generation, their true ability to generate program specifications remains unclear. Existing evaluations require either verifying implementation conformance or proving semantic equivalence between specifications, both of which are formidably difficult and may conflate proof difficulty with specification quality. To address this problem, we introduce Coins, a Rocq based evaluation framework that assesses specification quality by instantiating specifications under evaluation on trusted test cases and generating concrete proof obligations. This design aligns with the asymmetric nature of formal reasoning, where successful proofs provide reliable evidence while proof failures are inherently ambiguous. Using Coins, we conduct a large scale study on HumanEval with a curated set of human written Rocq specifications. Our results show that specification generation remains a formidable challenge, and that verification complexity can obscure genuine differences in specification quality. Overall, we find that accurate specification evaluation, rather than model scaling alone, is central to understanding the power of LLMs for specification synthesis, and that test case based formal reasoning offers a more faithful and discriminative measure of progress.

paragraphs: Formal specifications describe the properties a program should satisfy, but writing them precisely is costly. Evaluating language models that generate specifications is also difficult. Checking implementation conformance or proving equivalence between specifications can mix two separate issues: the quality of a specification and the difficulty of proving facts about it.

Coins addresses this evaluation problem using Rocq. It instantiates candidate specifications on trusted test cases and creates concrete proof obligations. The design respects an important asymmetry: a successful proof supplies reliable evidence, while a failed proof can have several explanations. This makes proof outcomes useful without treating every failure as decisive evidence that a specification is wrong.

The findings emphasize evaluation as a prerequisite for understanding model capability. Test-case-based formal reasoning offers a more discriminating measure of progress, helping distinguish improvements in generated specifications from changes in how readily they can be verified.
summary.tldr: Coins evaluates generated formal specifications through trusted test cases and concrete proofs, helping separate specification quality from proof difficulty.

title: How Powerful are LLMs in Generating Formal Program Specifications?

abstract: Backpropagation (BP) remains the dominant training paradigm for deep neural networks, yet its reliance on global gradient propagation fundamentally induces update locking problem, enforcing strong inter-layer dependencies in parameter updates. To address this limitation, we propose Depth-progressive Monotonic Learning (DMoL), a training scheme that assigns layer-wise local belief objectives and incrementally refines them across network depth, enabling unlocked parameter updates. As a result, DMoL supports dynamic modification of network depth during training, adapting to available compute and device resources while maintaining stable optimization. We provide theoretical guarantees that layer-wise local belief objectives improve monotonically with increasing depth and converge exponentially. Empirically, DMoL consistently matches or outperforms BP across diverse tasks, yielding a 4.3% accuracy gain on CIFAR-100, mitigating over-smoothing in deep graph neural networks (+37.5% on Cora), and reducing the final loss by over 35% in diffusion model training, highlighting its robustness and flexibility as an alternative to BP. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ychAlbert/DMoL.

paragraphs: Global backpropagation couples parameter updates across a network's layers: updates depend on gradients propagated through the network. This dependency creates the update-locking problem. Depth-progressive Monotonic Learning, or DMoL, introduces local objectives for individual layers and progressively refines them across depth, allowing parameter updates without that global dependency.

The approach also permits network depth to change during training. The authors present this as a way to adapt to available computation and device resources while maintaining stable optimization. Their theoretical guarantees concern the local belief objectives: these improve monotonically as depth increases and converge exponentially. These guarantees describe the objectives themselves, rather than asserting that every additional layer must improve test accuracy.

Across the evaluated tasks, DMoL consistently matches or exceeds backpropagation. Reported results include a 4.3% accuracy gain on CIFAR-100, a 37.5% improvement on Cora alongside reduced over-smoothing in deep graph networks, and over 35% lower final loss in diffusion training. These findings support local training as a flexible alternative across several network applications.
summary.tldr: DMoL uses progressively refined local layer objectives to unlock parameter updates and support changing network depth during training.

title: Depth-Progressive Monotonic Learning without Global Backpropagation

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has recently driven major gains in long chain-of-thought reasoning large language models (LLMs), but the high inference cost of such models motivates distillation into smaller students. Most existing knowledge distillation (KD) methods are designed for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), relying on fixed teacher traces or teacher-student Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence based regularization. When combined with RL, these approaches often suffer from distribution mismatch and objective interference: teacher supervision may not align with the student’s evolving rollout distribution, and the KL regularizer can compete with reward maximization and require careful loss balancing. To address these issues, we propose RL-aware distillation (RLAD), which performs selective imitation during RL—guiding the student toward the teacher only when it improves the current policy update. Our core component,Trust Region Ratio Distillation (TRRD), replaces the teacher-student KL regularizer with a PPO/GRPO-style likelihood-ratio objective anchored to a teacher–old-policy mixture, yielding advantage-aware, trust-region-bounded distillation on student rollouts and naturally balancing exploration, exploitation, and imitation. Across diverse logic reasoning and math benchmarks, RLADconsistently outperforms offline distillation, standard GRPO, and KL-based on-policy teacher–student knowledge distillation.

paragraphs: Distilling a powerful reasoning model into a smaller student can reduce inference cost, but supervision designed for ordinary fine-tuning can conflict with reinforcement learning. Fixed teacher examples may poorly match the student’s changing outputs. A separate teacher-student divergence penalty can also compete with reward maximization, requiring careful balancing between imitation and task improvement.

RL-aware distillation makes imitation conditional on whether it helps the current policy update. Its Trust Region Ratio Distillation component replaces the usual KL penalty with a likelihood-ratio objective in the style of PPO or GRPO. The objective uses a mixture of the teacher and the student’s old policy as its anchor and operates on student-generated rollouts.

This construction makes distillation sensitive to advantages while bounding updates within a trust region. The authors describe it as balancing exploration, exploitation, and imitation within the policy-learning procedure. Across logic and mathematics benchmarks, RLAD consistently outperforms offline distillation, standard GRPO, and KL-based on-policy distillation, supporting the value of adapting teacher guidance to the student’s ongoing learning.
summary.tldr: RLAD selectively integrates teacher imitation into reinforcement-learning updates and improves reasoning over several distillation and RL baselines.

abstract: Machine learning methods are often applied to the problem of learning a map from a robot's sensor data, but they are rarely applied to the problem of learning a robot's motion model. The motion model, which can be influenced by robot idiosyncrasies and terrain properties, is a crucial aspect of current algorithms for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). In this paper we concentrate on generating the correct motion model for a robot by applying EM methods in conjunction with a current SLAM algorithm. In contrast to previous calibration approaches, we not only estimate the mean of the motion, but also the interdependencies between motion terms, and the variances in these terms. This can be used to provide a more focused proposal distribution to a particle filter used in a SLAM algorithm, which can reduce the resources needed for localization while decreasing the chance of losing track of the robot's position. We validate this approach by recovering a good motion model despite initialization with a poor one. Further experiments validate the generality of the learned model in similar circumstances.

paragraphs: A robot's motion model describes how it moves, including effects associated with the robot and terrain. This model is important for simultaneous localization and mapping, or SLAM. The paper focuses on learning that motion model, complementing the more commonly studied task of learning a map from sensor data.

The method combines expectation maximization with an existing SLAM algorithm. It estimates not only mean motion but also variances and interdependencies between motion terms. Those additional quantities describe uncertainty and how aspects of motion vary together. They can support a more focused proposal distribution for the particle filter used in SLAM.

A more focused proposal can reduce localization resource requirements and lower the chance of losing track of the robot's position. The authors validate the learning approach by recovering a good motion model after starting with a poor one. Further experiments support the learned model's generality in similar circumstances, keeping the transfer claim tied to comparable operating conditions rather than arbitrary changes in environment.
summary.tldr: EM-based learning within SLAM estimates motion averages, uncertainty, and dependencies, recovering a useful model even from poor initialization.

title: Learning probabilistic motion models for mobile robots

abstract: We consider the problem of decentralized detection under constraints on the number of bits that can be transmitted by each sensor. In contrast to most previous work, in which the joint distribution of sensor observations is assumed to be known, we address the problem when only a set of empirical samples is available. We propose a novel algorithm using the framework of empirical risk minimization and marginalized kernels, and analyze its computational and statistical properties both theoretically and empirically. We provide an efficient implementation of the algorithm, and demonstrate its performance on both simulated and real data sets.

We propose a novel algorithm using the framework of empirical risk minimization and marginalized kernels, and analyze its computational and statistical properties both theoretically and empirically. We provide an efficient implementation of the algorithm, and demonstrate its performance on both simulated and real data sets.

paragraphs: The paper addresses detection with multiple sensors when each sensor can transmit only a limited number of bits. These communication limits are part of the learning problem: the system must make useful detection or classification decisions despite restricted messages. The authors consider the setting where only observed samples are available to guide the design.

This differs from approaches that assume the joint probability distribution of the sensor observations is already known. The proposed algorithm instead combines empirical risk minimization with marginalized kernels. Its learning framework uses sample-based evidence to address the detection task while retaining the communication constraint as a defining feature of the problem.

The contribution includes an efficient implementation and both theoretical and empirical analysis of computational and statistical properties. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm on simulated and real datasets. The stated outcome is a developed and evaluated approach to learning decentralized detection from data. Its significance is in bringing limited communication and incomplete distributional knowledge into the same learning problem, rather than requiring a known joint observation model.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a sample-based kernel method for decentralized detection when each sensor has a limited communication budget.

title: Decentralized detection and classification using kernel methods

abstract: Unsupervised learning methods often involve summarizing the data using a small number of parameters. In certain domains, only a small subset of the available data is relevant for the problem. One-Class Classification or One-Class Clustering attempts to find a useful subset by locating a dense region in the data. In particular, a recently proposed algorithm called One-Class Information Ball (OC-IB) shows the advantage of modeling a small set of highly coherent points as opposed to pruning outliers. We present several modifications to OC-IB and integrate it with a global search that results in several improvements such as deterministic results, optimality guarantees, control over cluster size and extension to other cost functions. Empirical studies yield significantly better results on various real and artificial data.

paragraphs: Sometimes only a small part of a dataset is relevant to the problem being studied. One-class clustering seeks a useful subset by locating a dense region. This paper builds on One-Class Information Ball, an algorithm that models a small, highly coherent collection of points instead of approaching the task mainly through removing outliers.

The authors modify that algorithm and combine it with global search in a hybrid global-and-local approach. They report several benefits: deterministic results, optimality guarantees, control over cluster size, and support for additional cost functions. These changes address both the reliability of the search and the flexibility of the clustering objective.

Experiments on real and artificial data produce significantly better results. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and practical: the method expands how a coherent subset can be specified while strengthening the search used to find it. Its stated optimality guarantees concern the proposed search framework, and the empirical findings support the improvements on the datasets studied.
summary.tldr: A hybrid search improves One-Class Information Ball with deterministic results, optimality guarantees, cluster-size control, and broader cost functions.

title: Robust one-class clustering using hybrid global and local search

abstract: In this paper we present a novel algorithm, CarpeDiem. It significantly improves on the time complexity of Viterbi algorithm, preserving the optimality of the result. This fact has consequences on Machine Learning systems that use Viterbi algorithm during learning or classification. We show how the algorithm applies to the Supervised Sequential Learning task and, in particular, to the HMPerceptron algorithm. We illustrate CarpeDiem in full details, and provide experimental results that support the proposed approach.

We illustrate CarpeDiem in full details, and provide experimental results that support the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Learning systems that predict sequences can use the Viterbi algorithm during training or classification. The paper introduces CarpeDiem as a faster way to carry out that computation while retaining the optimality of the result. Here, the application called SSL is supervised sequential learning, where the predictions concern a sequence.

The key contribution is the combination of improved time complexity and preservation of the optimal answer. Computational savings therefore do not come from accepting a suboptimal result. Because Viterbi can be part of both learning and prediction, improving this computation has implications for systems at either stage, wherever the proposed algorithm applies.

The authors describe CarpeDiem in detail and show its application to supervised sequential learning, specifically the HMPerceptron algorithm. They also present experiments supporting the approach. Taken together, the stated complexity improvement and empirical evidence make this a contribution to the computational side of sequence learning: a central inference operation can become faster while preserving the quality criterion that the original algorithm guarantees.
summary.tldr: CarpeDiem improves on Viterbi’s time complexity while preserving optimality, with an application to supervised sequence learning.

title: CarpeDiem: an algorithm for the fast evaluation of SSL classifiers

abstract: The spike and slab Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) is defined by having both a real valued ``slab'' variable and a binary ``spike'' variable associated with each unit in the hidden layer. In this paper we generalize and extend the spike and slab RBM to include non-zero means of the conditional distribution over the observed variables conditional on the binary spike variables. We also introduce a term, quadratic in the observed data that we exploit to guarantee the all conditionals associated with the model are well defined -- a guarantee that was absent in the original spike and slab RBM. The inclusion of these generalizations improves the performance of the spike and slab RBM as a feature learner and achieves competitive performance on the CIFAR-10 image classification task. The spike and slab model, when trained in a convolutional configuration, can generate sensible samples that demonstrate that the model has capture the broad statistical structure of natural images.

The spike and slab model, when trained in a convolutional configuration, can generate sensible samples that demonstrate that the model has capture the broad statistical structure of natural images.

paragraphs: A spike-and-slab restricted Boltzmann machine pairs a binary spike variable with a real-valued slab variable in each hidden unit. This paper extends that image-modeling framework in two ways, aiming to improve its ability to learn useful features while strengthening the mathematical definition of its conditional distributions.

The first change allows the observed variables to have nonzero conditional means given the binary spikes. The second introduces a term quadratic in the observed data. The authors use that term to guarantee that all of the model's conditional distributions are well defined, a guarantee absent from the original formulation. These changes expand the model while addressing a specific mathematical issue.

The generalized model improves feature-learning performance and achieves competitive results on CIFAR-10 image classification. In a convolutional configuration, it also generates sensible image samples. The authors interpret those samples as evidence that the model has captured broad statistical structure in natural images. The classification and generation findings provide complementary evidence about its learned representation, without claiming that it captures every aspect of image structure.
summary.tldr: An extended spike-and-slab RBM guarantees well-defined conditionals, improves feature learning, and generates images reflecting broad natural-image structure.

title: Unsupervised Models of Images by Spikeand-Slab RBMs

abstract: Low-rank and sparse structures have been profoundly studied in matrix completion and compressed sensing. In this paper, we develop ``Go Decomposition'' (GoDec) to efficiently and robustly estimate the low-rank part $L$ and the sparse part $S$ of a matrix $X=L+S+G$ with noise $G$. GoDec alternatively assigns the low-rank approximation of $X-S$ to $L$ and the sparse approximation of $X-L$ to $S$. The algorithm can be significantly accelerated by bilateral random projections (BRP). We also propose GoDec for matrix completion as an important variant. We prove that the objective value $\|X-L-S\|_F^2$ converges to a local minimum, while $L$ and $S$ linearly converge to local optimums. Theoretically, we analyze the influence of $L$, $S$ and $G$ to the asymptotic/convergence speeds in order to discover the robustness of GoDec. Empirical studies suggest the efficiency, robustness and effectiveness of GoDec comparing with representative matrix decomposition and completion tools, e.g., Robust PCA and OptSpace.

paragraphs: GoDec separates a matrix into three parts: a low-rank component, a sparse component, and remaining noise. The low-rank part captures structure that can be represented compactly, while the sparse part accounts for a relatively small collection of entries. The goal is to estimate these two structured components efficiently even when the observed matrix also contains noise.

The algorithm alternates between two updates. It subtracts the current sparse estimate and finds a low-rank approximation, then subtracts the current low-rank estimate and finds a sparse approximation. Bilateral random projections can substantially accelerate this process. The paper also develops a matrix-completion variant, extending the approach to recovering a matrix from incomplete observations.

The analysis establishes convergence of the objective to a local minimum and linear convergence of the component estimates to local optima. It also examines how the components and noise affect convergence speed and robustness. Empirical comparisons with matrix decomposition and completion methods support GoDec’s efficiency, robustness, and effectiveness; the convergence claims remain local.
summary.tldr: GoDec alternates low-rank and sparse approximations to decompose noisy matrices efficiently, with local convergence guarantees and supportive empirical results.

title: GoDec: Randomized Lowrank & Sparse Matrix Decomposition in Noisy Case
